examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第5回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Grandfather's Old Radio

When Sota helped his grandmother clean the storage room, he found a small brown radio with a silver handle. "That was your grandfather's favorite radio forty years ago," his grandmother said. Sota turned the switch, but no sound came out.

Sota liked learning how machines worked. He asked if he could take the radio to Mr. Yamada, a retired electrician who lived next door. Mr. Yamada smiled and opened the back cover carefully. Inside, one thin wire had come loose, and dust covered the speaker.

For an hour, Mr. Yamada showed Sota how to brush away the dust gently and reconnect the wire safely. When they put new batteries in and turned the dial, clear jazz music filled the room! Sota was amazed by the warm sound.

That evening, Sota placed the working radio on the kitchen table. When his grandmother heard an old song from her youth, tears came to her eyes, and she thanked Sota again and again.

examples.script:
A Useful Map

Last summer, Ren moved to a small town with his family. He did not know anyone there. He liked riding his bicycle, so he often went out to find new places. One afternoon, he found a beautiful pond behind the station. He wanted to tell his grandmother about it, but she did not know how to get there.

Ren decided to draw a map of the town. First, he visited the library to find an old map. It showed the streets, but it did not show the new park or the pond. Ren rode around town again and took notes. He also talked to people at the shops. They told him about a quiet garden and a small bakery.

Ren put these places on his map. He drew pictures and used large letters because his grandmother could not read small writing easily. When the map was finished, he took her to the pond. She found the way by looking at his map.

Later, a librarian saw Ren's map. She asked him to make copies for the library. Ren was surprised, but he was happy to help. Now new people in town can take a free map from the library. Ren has also made friends with some children who used his map.

Pottery Workshop Trip

From: Nana
To: Aunt Keiko
Subject: Saturday's pottery class

Dear Aunt Keiko,
Thank you for inviting me to the pottery studio in Mashiko this Saturday! My mother said I can go with you. I have never made a cup on a potter's wheel before, so I am really excited.

What kind of clothes should I wear? Clay might get on my sleeves, so I plan to bring an old long-sleeved shirt and tie my hair back. Also, my father baked some walnut cookies tonight. I will bring a box for us to eat on the train!

I will wait in front of the north ticket gate at 8:45 a.m.

Love,
Nana

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第14回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Vegetable Stamp Postcards

During summer vacation, twelve-year-old Riku helped his mother cook curry for lunch. When she sliced the green tops off two okra pods and cut the root base off a bunch of komatsuna greens, Riku noticed something surprising: the cut okra looked like a five-pointed star, and the komatsuna stem looked like a blooming rose!

"Wait—don't throw those scraps into the bin yet!" Riku said. Remembering an art project from elementary school, he dried the vegetable ends on a paper towel, dipped them lightly into watercolor paint on a sponge, and pressed them onto blank white postcards.

Green okra stars and pink komatsuna roses filled the cards in minutes. Riku added a short summer greeting—"How are you doing in the August heat?"—and mailed one card each to his grandparents in Toyama and his uncle in Kobe.

Three days later, his grandmother called laughing. She had framed Riku's postcard beside the kitchen calendar and tried stamping bell-pepper rings herself!

examples.script:
Borrowing Tent Gear

From: Uncle Shin
To: Yuta
Subject: Your camping trip

Hi Yuta,
Your mother told me that you are going camping with your classmates next weekend. You are welcome to borrow my green tent! It is big enough for four people, and it is easy to set up.

I also have two warm sleeping bags and a bright lantern. Do you need them? I will clean the tent this Saturday morning, so you can come to my house on Saturday afternoon. Bring a large backpack to carry the lantern and small tools.

Before the trip, let's practice putting up the tent in my garden once. That way, you won't have trouble at the campsite!

Uncle Shin

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第8回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Vegetable Stamp Bag

Hina's art class had an interesting project in October: each student received a plain white cloth tote bag and had to decorate it using natural shapes. At first, Hina thought about pressing autumn leaves onto the cloth, just like many of her classmates.

That evening, while helping her father make curry, Hina watched him cut off the bottom of a green okra pod and the root end of a lotus root. When she looked at the leftover pieces on the cutting board, she noticed something surprising. The cut okra looked like a neat five-pointed star, and the lotus root had a ring of pretty holes like a flower!

Hina asked her father if she could wash and dry those vegetable ends instead of throwing them away. The next day in art class, she dipped the okra and lotus root into fabric paint—yellow, green, and dark blue—and stamped patterns across her bag.

Her classmates gathered around her desk in amazement. Hina gave the finished bag to her father so he could carry vegetables home from the market every week.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第3回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Borrowing Tent Gear

From: Uncle Shin
To: Yuta
Subject: Your camping trip

Hi Yuta,
Your mother told me that you are going camping with your classmates next weekend. You are welcome to borrow my green tent! It is big enough for four people, and it is easy to set up.

I also have two warm sleeping bags and a bright lantern. Do you need them? I will clean the tent this Saturday morning, so you can come to my house on Saturday afternoon. Bring a large backpack to carry the lantern and small tools.

Before the trip, let's practice putting up the tent in my garden once. That way, you won't have trouble at the campsite!

Uncle Shin

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Library Stamp Rally

Autumn Reading Week!
November 2 – November 13
Midori School Library

Borrow books during Autumn Reading Week and collect stamps on a special card! You get one stamp each time you borrow a book and write a two-line comment about it. Students who collect four stamps will receive a handmade bookmark from the library committee. Pick up your stamp card at the counter starting Monday!

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Borrowing Camp Gear

From: Riku
To: Uncle Shinji
Subject: Lantern for our camp

Hi Uncle Shinji,
How have you been? Next Saturday, my Boy Scout group is going to camp beside Lake Suwa for one night. Our leader asked each tent team to bring one battery lantern.

Mom told me that you have two LED lanterns in your garage. Could I borrow one of them this week? I can visit your house after soccer practice on Wednesday around 5:30 p.m. to pick it up. I will buy new batteries at the store on my way!

Best wishes,
Riku

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第11回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Borrowing Camping Chairs

From: Uncle Kenji
To: Sota
Subject: Folding chairs for Sunday's barbecue

Hi Sota,
Your dad told me your family is having a riverside barbecue with your soccer teammates this Sunday. Of course you can borrow our four green folding chairs and our cooler box!

On Saturday morning, Aunt Yoko and I will drive to your grandmother's farm, so we won't be home after nine a.m. Could you and your dad stop by tonight around seven thirty, or before eight thirty tomorrow morning? Also, ice packs are already freezing in our garage freezer—take as many as you need!

Have fun on Sunday,
Uncle Kenji

To: Haruna
Subject: Found your dolphin keychain!

Hi Haruna,
After you went home from our study session at my house today, my little brother found a silver dolphin keychain under the sofa cushion. Remember you got it at the aquarium in Okinawa last summer? I was so glad it wasn't lost on the street!

See you tomorrow,
Sora

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Useful Map

Last summer, Ren moved to a small town with his family. He did not know anyone there. He liked riding his bicycle, so he often went out to find new places. One afternoon, he found a beautiful pond behind the station. He wanted to tell his grandmother about it, but she did not know how to get there.

Ren decided to draw a map of the town. First, he visited the library to find an old map. It showed the streets, but it did not show the new park or the pond. Ren rode around town again and took notes. He also talked to people at the shops. They told him about a quiet garden and a small bakery.

Ren put these places on his map. He drew pictures and used large letters because his grandmother could not read small writing easily. When the map was finished, he took her to the pond. She found the way by looking at his map.

Later, a librarian saw Ren's map. She asked him to make copies for the library. Ren was surprised, but he was happy to help. Now new people in town can take a free map from the library. Ren has also made friends with some children who used his map.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第2回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Preparing for Grandma's Birthday

From: Kaho
To: Uncle Dan
Subject: Grandma's birthday dinner

Dear Uncle Dan,
Everyone in our house is excited about Grandma's seventieth birthday party this Sunday! Mom reserved a quiet room at Olive Restaurant near South Station for 5:30 p.m. Because parking near the station is expensive, Dad thinks taking the train will be easier for you.

My brother Shun and I are making a photo album of our family trips. Do you have any old photos of Grandma from when you and Mom were children? If you bring two or three photos on Sunday, we can put them on the first page.

Also, please don't tell Grandma about the album yet, because we want it to be a surprise! Call our house if you need directions from the station.

Love,
Kaho

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第2回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Rainy Day at the Pottery Studio

Last month, Toma went on a family trip to a mountain village famous for handmade pottery. On Saturday morning, they planned to hike to a waterfall. However, heavy rain started right after breakfast, so Toma felt disappointed inside the hotel lobby.

The hotel manager smiled and told Toma's parents about a small pottery studio five minutes away. "Visitors can make their own cups or bowls there, even without reservations," she said. Toma had never touched potter's clay before, so he became curious and agreed to try.

At the studio, a potter named Mr. Hori showed Toma how to shape wet clay on a spinning wheel. At first, Toma pressed too hard with his fingers, and the clay bent to one side. Mr. Hori gently helped him fix the shape and taught him to keep his hands steady. After thirty minutes, Toma finished making a round soup bowl for his mother.

Because the clay needed to dry and be baked in a hot kiln, Toma could not take the bowl home that day. Three weeks later, a cardboard box arrived at Toma's house. Inside was his shiny green soup bowl! His mother used it for dinner that evening, and Toma decided to visit the studio again next summer to make a plate for his father.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第3回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across the Sea

Last autumn, Ms. Green's English class started a postcard exchange with a school in New Zealand. Each student got a partner. Hina's partner was a boy named Liam. In her first postcard, Hina wrote about her town's autumn festival and drew a small red lantern. However, she was worried that her English sentences were too short.

Three weeks later, postcards arrived from New Zealand. Liam loved Hina's drawing! He sent a postcard with a picture of sheep on a green hill. He wrote, "In New Zealand, October is spring, so baby lambs are everywhere now." Hina was surprised because the seasons were opposite.

For her second card, Hina wanted to share more. She went to the park, picked up two yellow ginkgo leaves, and taped one onto a card after pressing it flat in a thick dictionary. She wrote five sentences about how the trees changed color in November.

In December, Liam sent a photo of his class display board. Hina's yellow leaf was in the center, and many students wrote nice comments around it. Hina felt proud and decided to write longer letters next year.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第13回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Repairing Grandfather's Wooden Clock

On the wall of thirteen-year-old Shun's living room hung an old octagonal wooden clock that had belonged to his great-grandfather. Every hour, its brass pendulum used to chime softly, until one winter morning the hands stopped at ten-fifteen.

Shun's mother thought they would have to throw it away because modern battery shops didn't fix wind-up clocks. That Saturday, however, Shun spotted a tiny shop near the shotengai arcade with a hand-painted sign: "Takahashi Watch & Clock Repair."

Inside, seventy-five-year-old Mr. Takahashi opened the back panel with a small screwdriver and smiled. "Nothing is broken," he told Shun. "Old oil inside the gears simply dried up in the cold." Letting Shun watch through a magnifying glass, he cleaned each brass wheel with a soft brush and added two tiny drops of fresh clock oil.

When the warm chime rang out again at home that evening, Shun's grandfather clapped with joy—and Shun decided he wanted to learn how mechanical things work too.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第15回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Bookshop Cat's Bookmark

Near fourteen-year-old Nanami's cram school stood an old secondhand bookshop called Kusunoki Books. Whenever Nanami had twenty minutes before her evening math class, she liked browsing its tall wooden shelves—especially because a plump orange cat named Kinako often napped on a cushion beside the cash register.

One rainy Tuesday, Nanami bought a mystery novel about a detective on a train. When the owner, Mrs. Hori, handed her the paper-wrapped book, she slipped a handmade bookmark inside. On it was a small rubber-stamp picture of Kinako wearing round glasses and reading!

"My granddaughter carved that eraser stamp for our shop's fiftieth anniversary this month," Mrs. Hori explained proudly. "There are four seasonal Kinako designs—spring cherry blossoms, summer watermelon, autumn acorns, and winter kotatsu."

Nanami loved the autumn acorn bookmark so much that she finished the mystery novel in four days—and brought her best friend Aoi to Kusunoki Books the very next week.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Rainy-Day Board Games

At Aoba Junior High School, students loved playing soccer outside during lunch break. On rainy weeks in June, however, the schoolyard was closed. Many students sat quietly at their desks or crowded the hallways with nothing to do.

Kotaro, a member of the student council, talked with his classmates about this problem. He remembered that his grandfather had taught him shogi and simple card games on rainy afternoons. Kotaro asked teachers if the council could open one empty classroom on the first floor as a "Rainy-Day Game Room" during lunch.

The principal liked the idea, as long as students followed clear rules: games had to finish five minutes before afternoon classes, and everyone had to put all pieces back in their boxes. Teachers and families donated chess sets, reversi boards, and word-card games.

On the first rainy Tuesday, more than thirty students from different grades visited the room. Seventh graders played reversi against ninth graders and made new friends. Soon, some students even looked forward to rainy days!

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Grandpa's Wooden Birdhouse

During spring break, twelve-year-old Mao stayed with her grandparents in Nagano for four days. Behind their house stood two tall apple trees. Every morning, Mao heard small wild birds singing in the branches, so she wanted to watch them more closely.

On the second day, her grandfather opened his small workshop and showed Mao some clean cedar boards left over from repairing a fence. "Why don't we build a birdhouse together?" he asked. He taught Mao how to measure the wood carefully with a metal ruler and smooth the edges with sandpaper.

Her grandfather made one important point: the round entrance hole had to be just three centimeters wide. If the hole was too big, crows might reach inside; if it was too small, even little chickadees could not enter. They hung the finished birdhouse on the lower branch of an apple tree and placed a dish of water nearby.

Before Mao went home on the fourth morning, a pair of small gray-and-white birds flew into the box carrying dry moss. Mao took a photo from the window and promised to visit again in summer.

Preparing for Mountain Hiking

From: Mr. Kato
To: Outdoor Club Members
Subject: Sunday's hike on Mount Takao

Hello everyone,
The weather forecast for this Sunday looks clear and cool! Let's meet in front of the ticket machine at Central Station at 7:40 a.m. Our train leaves at 7:55 a.m., so please do not be late.

We will eat lunch near the top of the mountain. Bring rice balls or sandwiches, a large bottle of water, and a plastic sheet to sit on. Even if the morning feels warm in town, the wind at the top is cold in November. Make sure to put a light jacket in your backpack.

See you on Sunday,
Mr. Kato

Borrowing Tent Gear

From: Uncle Shin
To: Yuta
Subject: Your camping trip

Hi Yuta,
Your mother told me that you are going camping with your classmates next weekend. You are welcome to borrow my green tent! It is big enough for four people, and it is easy to set up.

I also have two warm sleeping bags and a bright lantern. Do you need them? I will clean the tent this Saturday morning, so you can come to my house on Saturday afternoon. Bring a large backpack to carry the lantern and small tools.

Before the trip, let's practice putting up the tent in my garden once. That way, you won't have trouble at the campsite!

Uncle Shin

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第11回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Learning the Sign for "Delicious"

Every Wednesday afternoon, thirteen-year-old Ren stops at Hidamari Bakery near his junior high school to buy warm walnut rolls. Two months ago, a cheerful college student named Mr. Mori started working at the register. Small cards on the counter explained that Mr. Mori was deaf, so customers pointed to bread labels or held up fingers to show how many rolls they wanted.

Ren liked Mr. Mori's bright smile, yet he felt a little sad that he could only nod when leaving. That night, Ren borrowed an introductory Japanese Sign Language book with clear illustrations from the town library. He practiced three phrases in front of his mirror: "Hello," "Thank you," and "Last week's bread was delicious!"

The following Wednesday, after receiving his bag of walnut rolls, Ren tapped his right cheek lightly and touched his chin—the sign for "delicious"—followed by "thank you." Mr. Mori's eyes lit up with surprise. He signed back slowly, teaching Ren the sign for "bread."

Now Ren learns one new sign each week, and their thirty-second chat at the counter is his favorite part of Wednesday.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

SOUTH TOWN TRAFFIC CLUB
Free Junior Bicycle Safety Check
Date: Sunday, April 19 (9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.)
Place: South Elementary School Playground

Spring is a great season for cycling! Volunteer mechanics will check your brakes, tires, bell, and front light for free. If your tires need air or your chain needs oil, we will take care of it on the spot.

Students who pass all safety checks will receive a reflective sticker for their rear fender. No reservation is needed; just bring your bicycle before noon. If it rains, the event will be held next Sunday, April 26.

Town River Lantern Evening
Date: Saturday, August 8 (6:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.)
Place: Stepping-Stone Lawn beside Clearwater Bridge

Come celebrate summer evening by floating paper lanterns illuminated with reusable LED lights! From 5:30 p.m., visitors can decorate a wooden-base paper lantern with brush pens for 300 yen at the riverside tent.

Starry Sky Observation Night

WEST HILL SCIENCE CENTER
Starry Sky Observation Night
Date: Friday, October 16 (6:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.)
Location: Rooftop Terrace (3rd Floor)

Look at Saturn and autumn stars through our large telescopes! Center staff will explain how to find major constellations in the night sky. Admission is free for junior high school students and 300 yen for adults.

Because the rooftop gets cold at night, please wear a warm jacket. Do not use flashlights or bright phone screens on the terrace, as strong light makes it hard to see faint stars. If the sky is cloudy, a 45-minute planetarium show will be held on the first floor instead.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across Three Oceans

When Ms. Carter became the English teacher at Harbor Junior High School in April, many eighth-grade students felt shy about writing in English. Whenever she asked them to write three sentences in their notebooks, they worried so much about making small grammar mistakes that their pages stayed almost blank.

In May, Ms. Carter arranged a pen-pal project with two partner schools (one in New Zealand and one in Portugal) where students were also learning English as a global language. Instead of exchanging instant text messages, each student designed a handmade postcard introducing one local food or seasonal event from their town. Because space on a postcard was small, students felt relaxed and focused on sharing one clear idea.

When the first bundle of colorful cards arrived from New Zealand and Portugal in June, the classroom grew lively. Harbor students noticed that their new friends occasionally crossed out a word or used simple sentences, yet their drawings and descriptions of winter rugby matches in June and grilled sardine festivals were vivid and easy to enjoy.

Realizing that communication mattered more than perfection, the students began writing longer letters in autumn. Several students looked up English words on their own to explain how their town celebrated the autumn harvest.

At the end of the term, the class displayed copies of the postcards on the hallway board with a world map and yarn connecting the three towns. Even students who once feared writing three lines now look forward to opening the mail bag every month.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第8回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Benchmark on Sunset Hill

Behind Oak Junior High School stands Sunset Hill, a gentle climb that takes about twenty-five minutes to reach the top. Although the view of the harbor from the summit is wonderful, few older residents climbed the trail because there was nowhere to sit and rest halfway up.

In October, Mr. Kudo, who teaches woodworking in technology class, asked his ninth-grade students what they wanted to leave behind as a graduation project. One student, Yui, remembered walking up Sunset Hill slowly with her grandmother in spring and wishing there had been a sturdy bench near the big cedar tree halfway along the path. When Yui shared this memory, the whole class voted to build two wooden benches for the hill.

First, the class got permission from the city parks office. A city engineer visited the school to explain how outdoor benches must withstand rain, snow, and strong sunlight. Following her advice, the students chose local cedar wood, smoothed every sharp corner with sandpaper so nobody would get splinters, and brushed waterproof oil onto each board three times.

In February, thirty students carried the parts up the trail together and assembled the benches beside the big cedar tree. On the back of each bench, they carved a small message: "Take your time and enjoy the breeze." On graduation morning in March, Yui climbed Sunset Hill with her grandmother, and they sat side by side watching ferryboats cross the shining harbor.

Autumn Bird-Watching Morning Walk

GREEN LAKE NATURE PARK
Autumn Bird-Watching Morning Walk
Date: Sunday, October 18 (7:00 a.m. – 9:00 a.m.)
Meeting Spot: North Wooden Pier
Fee: 200 yen per person (free for students under 15)

October is the best season to watch wild ducks and swans arriving at Green Lake from the north! Park rangers will guide visitors quietly along the reed trail and explain how migrating birds find food before winter.

Ten pairs of binoculars are available to borrow at no extra cost, reserved on a first-come, first-served basis at the pier from 6:45 a.m. Please avoid wearing bright red or neon jackets, because sudden bright colors can frighten the birds away.

A visitor’s question

When Owen began helping at a small local museum, he learned the names of many old tools. He expected visitors to ask about them. Instead, several children asked how people used the tools in daily life. Owen could name each tool but could not explain its use clearly. The next week, he asked an older volunteer to show him. examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Help with the Garden Exhibition

From: Nora
To: Daniel
Subject: Garden exhibition

Hi Daniel,
Our class is preparing an exhibition about the school garden. You said you wanted to help, and I have a special job for you. We took photographs of the garden every week, but we do not have anyone to arrange them on the display boards. You are good at choosing pictures, so could you do that?

The exhibition was going to open on Thursday, but the hall will be used for a teachers' meeting that day. It will open on Friday instead. We must finish our work by Wednesday afternoon because the boards need to be checked.

Could you come to Room 5 after school on Tuesday? I will bring the photographs and some large sheets of paper. You only need to bring scissors. We can use the school's glue. If you cannot come, please email me before Monday evening so I can ask someone else.

Thanks,
Nora

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第3回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Maple Hill Nature Observation Day

MAPLE HILL NATURE DAY
Date: Saturday, May 16
Meeting Time & Place: 8:50 a.m. at the East School Gate (Bus leaves at 9:00 a.m.)
Participation Fee: 200 yen (for insurance and a trail map)

Join our science teachers to observe wild birds and spring leaves on Maple Hill! Please wear walking shoes and bring a hat, a water bottle, and a pocket notebook. There are no rubbish bins on the hill, so bring a small plastic bag to carry all snack wrappers back to school for sorting.

Rain Plan: If heavy rain is forecast on Friday afternoon, we will visit the Town Picture Gallery instead.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第5回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Starry Sky Observation Night

WEST HILL SCIENCE CENTER
Starry Sky Observation Night
Date: Friday, October 16 (6:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.)
Location: Rooftop Terrace (3rd Floor)

Look at Saturn and autumn stars through our large telescopes! Center staff will explain how to find major constellations in the night sky. Admission is free for junior high school students and 300 yen for adults.

Because the rooftop gets cold at night, please wear a warm jacket. Do not use flashlights or bright phone screens on the terrace, as strong light makes it hard to see faint stars. If the sky is cloudy, a 45-minute planetarium show will be held on the first floor instead.

Changing Our Interview Day

From: Mei
To: Toby
Subject: Bakery interview for the school paper

Hi Toby,
I just spoke on the phone with Mr. Baker, the owner of Sunflower Bread Shop, about our interview for the school newspaper. Originally, we planned to visit his shop after school this Wednesday. However, a group of elementary school children is visiting his kitchen that afternoon, so he asked if we could come on Thursday at 4:15 p.m. instead.

Mr. Baker said we may take two photos of the bread ovens, as long as we don't use a camera flash while staff are working. Since you are the photographer for our article, could you bring the club camera on Thursday?

I already wrote five interview questions in a shared notebook. Please read them during lunch break tomorrow and add one or two questions of your own. Let me know tonight if Thursday works for you!

Thanks,
Mei

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第6回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Umbrellas with Green Ribbons

At North Station Junior High School, sudden afternoon showers are common in June and September. For years, the school office kept twenty plain black umbrellas to lend to students who forgot theirs. Unfortunately, fewer than half of the umbrellas came back within a week. Students didn't mean to keep them; once a black umbrella stood in a family's umbrella stand at home, it looked just like everyone else's.

Last spring, the student welfare committee looked for a friendly way to solve this problem without making strict rules. One seventh-grade member, Riku, noticed how easily shoppers returned bright baskets at his neighborhood supermarket. Inspired by that, the committee tied a bright green cloth ribbon with a wooden tag onto the handle of every school umbrella. Each tag showed a cheerful turtle drawing and a number from one to twenty.

Instead of asking teachers to write down borrowers' names in a heavy book, the committee placed a whiteboard right inside the school entrance. When students borrowed an umbrella, they simply moved a numbered magnet from the "Ready" column to the "Out" column. Every morning as students walked into school, they passed the board and immediately remembered if a numbered turtle umbrella was still at their house.

During the rainy month of June, nineteen out of twenty umbrellas were returned the very next morning, and the last one came back on Friday after a student recovered from a cold. Other schools in the city heard about the turtle tags and visited North Station Junior High to learn how a small visual change encouraged everyone to cooperate.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across Three Oceans

When Ms. Carter became the English teacher at Harbor Junior High School in April, many eighth-grade students felt shy about writing in English. Whenever she asked them to write three sentences in their notebooks, they worried so much about making small grammar mistakes that their pages stayed almost blank.

In May, Ms. Carter arranged a pen-pal project with two partner schools (one in New Zealand and one in Portugal) where students were also learning English as a global language. Instead of exchanging instant text messages, each student designed a handmade postcard introducing one local food or seasonal event from their town. Because space on a postcard was small, students felt relaxed and focused on sharing one clear idea.

When the first bundle of colorful cards arrived from New Zealand and Portugal in June, the classroom grew lively. Harbor students noticed that their new friends occasionally crossed out a word or used simple sentences, yet their drawings and descriptions of winter rugby matches in June and grilled sardine festivals were vivid and easy to enjoy.

Realizing that communication mattered more than perfection, the students began writing longer letters in autumn. Several students looked up English words on their own to explain how their town celebrated the autumn harvest.

At the end of the term, the class displayed copies of the postcards on the hallway board with a world map and yarn connecting the three towns. Even students who once feared writing three lines now look forward to opening the mail bag every month.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第12回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Saving the Old Clock on Station Square

For forty-five years, a tall brass clock stood in the center of Willowbrook Station Square. Commuters checked its round white face every morning, and friends simply said, "Meet me under the brass clock," whenever they went shopping downtown. Two winters ago, however, ice damaged the gears inside, and the hands stopped at twenty minutes past four.

Because parts for such an old clock were no longer sold in stores, the city office considered taking the clock down and putting up a plain digital screen instead. When students in the technical high school's metalwork club heard the news in the local paper, they asked the city if they could inspect the broken gears with their club adviser, Mr. Hori, who had repaired factory machines for thirty years.

Inside the clock tower, the students discovered that only two bronze gear wheels had cracked. Over six weeks after school, they measured the worn teeth down to a tenth of a millimeter, drew computer plans, and shaped two new bronze gears on the school lathe. On the day they tested the mechanism, they also polished the tarnished brass post until it shone in the sunlight.

When the clock chimed five o'clock again on the first Saturday of May, more than two hundred townspeople gathered in the square and applauded. Today, a small plaque at the base thanks the high school club for keeping the town's favorite meeting spot alive.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第13回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Rain Plan for Our Walking History Tour

From: Mr. Shinohara, History Club Adviser
To: History Club Members
Subject: Tomorrow's castle-town walking tour

Hello everyone,
Thank you for preparing your short guide speeches for tomorrow's walking tour of the old castle-town district. Each member chose a fascinating spot to introduce!

According to this evening's weather forecast, light rain will begin around 11:00 a.m. tomorrow, though the early morning will be dry. Therefore, we will reverse the order of our schedule. Instead of visiting the Folk History Museum in the morning and walking outside in the afternoon, we will meet at East Gate Square at 8:45 a.m. and do the outdoor walking route first while the streets are dry. Then, at 11:15 a.m., we will eat an early lunch in the covered rest house beside the moat and spend the afternoon inside the museum.

Please bring a folding umbrella and put your speech notes inside a clear plastic folder so raindrops won't smudge the ink. See you at East Gate Square!

Mr. Shinohara

examples.script:
Recording How Beans Grow

In April, Class Three received permission to turn an unused strip of land beside the science room into a small learning garden. At first, several students complained that pulling weeds and carrying soil was tiring. Their science teacher, Mr. Aoki, suggested dividing the work into short ten-minute shifts before morning homeroom so nobody would feel overwhelmed.

On the first Monday of May, the students planted green bean seeds in four wooden boxes. At the beginning, some students watered the boxes twice a day because they thought more water would make the seeds grow faster. However, Mr. Aoki showed them that giving too much water could actually rot the seeds underground. The class made a simple chart to check the soil with their fingers before watering.

To keep the area tidy, the students also set up two recycling bins near the tap. Dry leaves and pulled weeds went into the brown bin to become compost, while empty plastic seedling pots were washed and placed in the blue bin so next year's class could reuse them.

Two weeks later, the first bright green shoots pushed through the soil. Every Friday afternoon, students sketched the plants and measured their height with rulers. Several students who rarely spoke in science lessons became enthusiastic about comparing their weekly drawings.

In June, the Town Picture Gallery invited local schools to display student projects. Class Three selected twelve detailed plant sketches along with a short explanation of their watering chart. The students hope visitors will see that even a narrow corner of a schoolyard can become a place for discovery.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across Three Oceans

When Ms. Carter became the English teacher at Harbor Junior High School in April, many eighth-grade students felt shy about writing in English. Whenever she asked them to write three sentences in their notebooks, they worried so much about making small grammar mistakes that their pages stayed almost blank.

In May, Ms. Carter arranged a pen-pal project with two partner schools (one in New Zealand and one in Portugal) where students were also learning English as a global language. Instead of exchanging instant text messages, each student designed a handmade postcard introducing one local food or seasonal event from their town. Because space on a postcard was small, students felt relaxed and focused on sharing one clear idea.

When the first bundle of colorful cards arrived from New Zealand and Portugal in June, the classroom grew lively. Harbor students noticed that their new friends occasionally crossed out a word or used simple sentences, yet their drawings and descriptions of winter rugby matches in June and grilled sardine festivals were vivid and easy to enjoy.

Realizing that communication mattered more than perfection, the students began writing longer letters in autumn. Several students looked up English words on their own to explain how their town celebrated the autumn harvest.

At the end of the term, the class displayed copies of the postcards on the hallway board with a world map and yarn connecting the three towns. Even students who once feared writing three lines now look forward to opening the mail bag every month.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第8回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Benchmark on Sunset Hill

Behind Oak Junior High School stands Sunset Hill, a gentle climb that takes about twenty-five minutes to reach the top. Although the view of the harbor from the summit is wonderful, few older residents climbed the trail because there was nowhere to sit and rest halfway up.

In October, Mr. Kudo, who teaches woodworking in technology class, asked his ninth-grade students what they wanted to leave behind as a graduation project. One student, Yui, remembered walking up Sunset Hill slowly with her grandmother in spring and wishing there had been a sturdy bench near the big cedar tree halfway along the path. When Yui shared this memory, the whole class voted to build two wooden benches for the hill.

First, the class got permission from the city parks office. A city engineer visited the school to explain how outdoor benches must withstand rain, snow, and strong sunlight. Following her advice, the students chose local cedar wood, smoothed every sharp corner with sandpaper so nobody would get splinters, and brushed waterproof oil onto each board three times.

In February, thirty students carried the parts up the trail together and assembled the benches beside the big cedar tree. On the back of each bench, they carved a small message: "Take your time and enjoy the breeze." On graduation morning in March, Yui climbed Sunset Hill with her grandmother, and they sat side by side watching ferryboats cross the shining harbor.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第11回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Town Bench Notebook

Near the small post office in Cedar Hill stood a long wooden bench under an apricot tree. Every afternoon, older residents rested there with shopping bags, and high school students waited nearby for the hillside bus. Yet the two groups rarely spoke to each other beyond a polite nod.

One rainy Sunday in April, a retired carpenter named Mr. Toda attached a small waterproof wooden box to the arm of the bench. Inside, he placed a thick notebook with a green cover and a pencil tied to a string. On the first page, he wrote: "Please leave a question, a local memory, or a small tip for the next person who sits here."

For the first few days, the pages stayed blank. Then a ninth-grade boy named Shun wrote, "Does anyone know how to keep tomato plants from falling over in strong wind?" The next afternoon, Shun opened the notebook and found a neat drawing of bamboo stakes tied in a triangle, signed by "Mrs. Kimura, three streets east." Below that, another student asked what Cedar Hill looked like before the supermarket was built, and three longtime residents filled two pages with stories about the old outdoor fish market.

By summer, the green notebook was full, and Mr. Toda had to add a second volume. More importantly, people sitting on the bench began recognizing handwriting and starting real conversations, sharing gardening advice, school concert dates, and even fresh apricots from the tree overhead.

From: Nanami
To: Sota
Subject: Colored vests for Grade 8 relay

Our physical education teacher, Mr. Kawai, asked our Field Day committee to check the numbered mesh vests ("pinnies") in the gym storage room today. When Reina and I counted them after school, we found plenty of red, yellow, and green vests for the eighth-grade class relay, but three of the blue vests had torn seams and missing numbers.

Luckily, the local youth soccer coach, who is Reina's uncle, said we may borrow a full set of ten clean blue vests for Field Day next Wednesday! Since you live right across the street from the community ground where his team practices on Sunday mornings, could you pick up the bag of blue vests from Coach Endo around 10:30 a.m. this Sunday?

After Field Day finishes on Wednesday, Reina and I will wash all ten vests at home and return them to her uncle, so you only need to bring the bag to school on Monday morning. Let me know if Sunday morning works!

Thanks,
Nanami

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第12回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Saving the Old Clock on Station Square

For forty-five years, a tall brass clock stood in the center of Willowbrook Station Square. Commuters checked its round white face every morning, and friends simply said, "Meet me under the brass clock," whenever they went shopping downtown. Two winters ago, however, ice damaged the gears inside, and the hands stopped at twenty minutes past four.

Because parts for such an old clock were no longer sold in stores, the city office considered taking the clock down and putting up a plain digital screen instead. When students in the technical high school's metalwork club heard the news in the local paper, they asked the city if they could inspect the broken gears with their club adviser, Mr. Hori, who had repaired factory machines for thirty years.

Inside the clock tower, the students discovered that only two bronze gear wheels had cracked. Over six weeks after school, they measured the worn teeth down to a tenth of a millimeter, drew computer plans, and shaped two new bronze gears on the school lathe. On the day they tested the mechanism, they also polished the tarnished brass post until it shone in the sunlight.

When the clock chimed five o'clock again on the first Saturday of May, more than two hundred townspeople gathered in the square and applauded. Today, a small plaque at the base thanks the high school club for keeping the town's favorite meeting spot alive.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第14回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Photographs in the Arcade Windows

For over fifty years, Sunrise Shopping Arcade had been the lively center of Willow Town. Recently, however, three family-owned stores had closed, and their shuttered front windows made the covered street look dim and lonely after school. Ninth-grader Hina walked through the arcade every day on her way home from violin lessons and wished the street felt welcoming again.

In October, Hina's social studies class began a project on local history. While visiting the town library's basement archive, Hina found boxes of black-and-white photographs taken in the 1970s. They showed children buying roasted chestnuts, snow piled outside the fish shop, and colorful paper decorations hanging from the arcade roof during summer festivals.

With permission from the library and the landlords of the empty shops, Hina and five classmates enlarged thirty photographs and displayed them neatly behind the glass of the closed storefronts. Beneath each photo, they taped a blank card asking passersby, "Do you remember this day? Tell us your story!"

Within a week, shoppers began stopping to read and write notes: "That boy holding the puppy is my grandfather!" and "This bakery made the best melon bread." On Saturdays, families came just to see the new comments, and two young bakers who visited the display liked the friendly atmosphere so much that they rented one of the empty shops the following spring.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第15回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Table Tennis in the Old School Gym

Five years ago, North Valley Elementary School closed because fewer children lived in the mountain village, and students began riding a school bus to a larger town nearby. Although the classrooms were turned into a small local library, the wooden gymnasium behind the building stayed locked and silent.

Last autumn, fourteen-year-old Soma found four dusty table-tennis tables folded up in the gym's storage room while helping his aunt return library books. Soma loved playing table tennis at his junior high school, yet he had nowhere to practice on weekends without taking a forty-minute bus ride.

Soma wrote a polite proposal to the village council suggesting a "Saturday Morning Open Gym." Retired carpenter Mr. Endo offered to check the floorboards and replace the torn nets, while Soma and two friends made simple posters inviting anyone from age seven to eighty. Only six people showed up on the first Saturday in November, but word spread quickly.

Soon, twenty villagers gathered every week. Older residents who had played table tennis in their twenties turned out to have tricky spin serves that surprised the teenagers, while the students eagerly picked up stray balls and taught beginners how to hold a paddle. On snowy winter mornings when mountain roads were quiet, the sound of bouncing white balls and laughter warmed the old gym once again.

A visitor’s question

When Owen began helping at a small local museum, he learned the names of many old tools. He expected visitors to ask about them. Instead, several children asked how people used the tools in daily life. Owen could name each tool but could not explain its use clearly. The next week, he asked an older volunteer to show him. Together they made short demonstration videos. Now Owen plays these videos during his tours. He still introduces the names, but he spends more time showing what the tools actually did.
The bridge (     ) by local workers about fifty years ago.
The benches in River Park (     ) painted by local volunteers last Sunday.
This river is much (     ) than it was twenty years ago thanks to local cleanups.
According (     ) the local newspaper, a new footbridge will open next spring.
It was careless (     ) me to leave my umbrella on the local train.
My cousin has belonged to the local swimming club (     ) last autumn.

examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第2回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Seeds for Next Month

Every Saturday morning, Emi visits the Maple Community Garden with her grandfather. Residents of different ages grow vegetables and flowers there together. Last Saturday, the sky was covered with dark clouds when they left home, so her grandfather reminded Emi to pack two light raincoats in her bag.

When they arrived at the garden, they saw Mr. Lee, an older neighbor, carrying a heavy wooden box full of seed packets. Because his back was hurting a little, Emi hurried over and helped him arrange the packets neatly on a long table under a tent. Mr. Lee thanked her and explained which flowers grew well in summer.

Twenty minutes later, large drops of rain suddenly began to fall. Everyone worked quickly as a team. While the adults covered the vegetable beds with plastic sheets, Emi and two other students moved the young flowerpots under the roof of the tool shed so the strong rain would not damage them.

After the rain stopped, Emi noticed a small bookshelf inside the shed. Garden members leave gardening books there so anyone can borrow them for two weeks. Emi chose a beginner's guide to growing sunflowers. Mr. Lee also gave her a packet of sunflower seeds as a thank-you gift.

On the way home, Emi asked her grandfather if they could clear a sunny corner of their own yard. Next month, she plans to plant the seeds there and keep a photo diary of how tall the sunflowers grow.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第10回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Maps You Can Touch

Last autumn, eighth-grade students at Hillside Junior High School visited the City Science Museum with a blind guest speaker, Mr. Nagai, who had talked to their class the week before about how he traveled safely around town. At the museum entrance, the students noticed something surprising: although there were colorful floor maps everywhere, none of them had raised lines or Braille labels that Mr. Nagai could read with his fingertips.

Back at school, four students in the craft club asked Mr. Nagai what kind of map truly helped him inside unfamiliar buildings. He explained that too many tiny details actually made a touch map confusing. What mattered most was clear textures, such as rough sandpaper strips for stairs, smooth raised tape for main hallways, and round wooden beads for restrooms and the information desk.

Over the next two months, the four students measured the first floor of their own school building, where guests often visited for concerts and parent meetings. They built a sturdy touch map on a wide wooden board using five distinct materials that felt completely different under a finger. Mr. Nagai tested their first version and suggested widening the space between hallway lines so two fingers could follow a route comfortably.

After the students improved the board and placed it inside the main entrance in January, not only visually impaired visitors but also young children and elderly grandparents stopped to trace the routes. Seeing how clear design helped everyone, the City Science Museum invited the students to share what they had learned with its exhibition staff.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第13回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Rain Plan for Our Walking History Tour

From: Mr. Shinohara, History Club Adviser
To: History Club Members
Subject: Tomorrow's castle-town walking tour

Hello everyone,
Thank you for preparing your short guide speeches for tomorrow's walking tour of the old castle-town district. Each member chose a fascinating spot to introduce!

According to this evening's weather forecast, light rain will begin around 11:00 a.m. tomorrow, though the early morning will be dry. Therefore, we will reverse the order of our schedule. Instead of visiting the Folk History Museum in the morning and walking outside in the afternoon, we will meet at East Gate Square at 8:45 a.m. and do the outdoor walking route first while the streets are dry. Then, at 11:15 a.m., we will eat an early lunch in the covered rest house beside the moat and spend the afternoon inside the museum.

Please bring a folding umbrella and put your speech notes inside a clear plastic folder so raindrops won't smudge the ink. See you at East Gate Square!

Mr. Shinohara

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Preparing Lunch for the Park Cleanup Team

From: Noah
To: Emi
Subject: Friday afternoon in the school kitchen

Hi Emi,
Thank you for joining our cooking team! As you know, community volunteers will gather early on Saturday morning to clean the pond in Central Park, and our class promised to prepare light lunch boxes for them.

We will meet in the school kitchen at 3:30 p.m. this Friday right after classes finish. I will bring fresh bread and sliced cheese from my uncle's bakery, and Hana is going to make warm carrot soup. Could you bring two clean dishcloths and a roll of aluminum foil? We need the foil to wrap the sandwiches neatly.

Also, we have to pack everything into cooler boxes before 5:00 p.m. because Mr. Takeda will lock the kitchen at 5:15 p.m. and store the boxes in the staff refrigerator overnight. Let me know if you can make it!

Best,
Noah

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across Three Oceans

When Ms. Carter became the English teacher at Harbor Junior High School in April, many eighth-grade students felt shy about writing in English. Whenever she asked them to write three sentences in their notebooks, they worried so much about making small grammar mistakes that their pages stayed almost blank.

In May, Ms. Carter arranged a pen-pal project with two partner schools (one in New Zealand and one in Portugal) where students were also learning English as a global language. Instead of exchanging instant text messages, each student designed a handmade postcard introducing one local food or seasonal event from their town. Because space on a postcard was small, students felt relaxed and focused on sharing one clear idea.

When the first bundle of colorful cards arrived from New Zealand and Portugal in June, the classroom grew lively. Harbor students noticed that their new friends occasionally crossed out a word or used simple sentences, yet their drawings and descriptions of winter rugby matches in June and grilled sardine festivals were vivid and easy to enjoy.

Realizing that communication mattered more than perfection, the students began writing longer letters in autumn. Several students looked up English words on their own to explain how their town celebrated the autumn harvest.

At the end of the term, the class displayed copies of the postcards on the hallway board with a world map and yarn connecting the three towns. Even students who once feared writing three lines now look forward to opening the mail bag every month.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第11回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Town Bench Notebook

Near the small post office in Cedar Hill stood a long wooden bench under an apricot tree. Every afternoon, older residents rested there with shopping bags, and high school students waited nearby for the hillside bus. Yet the two groups rarely spoke to each other beyond a polite nod.

One rainy Sunday in April, a retired carpenter named Mr. Toda attached a small waterproof wooden box to the arm of the bench. Inside, he placed a thick notebook with a green cover and a pencil tied to a string. On the first page, he wrote: "Please leave a question, a local memory, or a small tip for the next person who sits here."

For the first few days, the pages stayed blank. Then a ninth-grade boy named Shun wrote, "Does anyone know how to keep tomato plants from falling over in strong wind?" The next afternoon, Shun opened the notebook and found a neat drawing of bamboo stakes tied in a triangle, signed by "Mrs. Kimura, three streets east." Below that, another student asked what Cedar Hill looked like before the supermarket was built, and three longtime residents filled two pages with stories about the old outdoor fish market.

By summer, the green notebook was full, and Mr. Toda had to add a second volume. More importantly, people sitting on the bench began recognizing handwriting and starting real conversations, sharing gardening advice, school concert dates, and even fresh apricots from the tree overhead.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第15回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Table Tennis in the Old School Gym

Five years ago, North Valley Elementary School closed because fewer children lived in the mountain village, and students began riding a school bus to a larger town nearby. Although the classrooms were turned into a small local library, the wooden gymnasium behind the building stayed locked and silent.

Last autumn, fourteen-year-old Soma found four dusty table-tennis tables folded up in the gym's storage room while helping his aunt return library books. Soma loved playing table tennis at his junior high school, yet he had nowhere to practice on weekends without taking a forty-minute bus ride.

Soma wrote a polite proposal to the village council suggesting a "Saturday Morning Open Gym." Retired carpenter Mr. Endo offered to check the floorboards and replace the torn nets, while Soma and two friends made simple posters inviting anyone from age seven to eighty. Only six people showed up on the first Saturday in November, but word spread quickly.

Soon, twenty villagers gathered every week. Older residents who had played table tennis in their twenties turned out to have tricky spin serves that surprised the teenagers, while the students eagerly picked up stray balls and taught beginners how to hold a paddle. On snowy winter mornings when mountain roads were quiet, the sound of bouncing white balls and laughter warmed the old gym once again.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Wooden Book Box at Lake Green Camp

Last summer, my town opened a small outdoor library at Lake Green Camp so families staying in tents could enjoy reading without carrying heavy books from home. Volunteers built a weatherproof wooden box with a small slanted roof and placed it beside the camp dining hall. Campers were welcome to leave books they had finished reading and borrow any book from the box during their stay.

When my family stayed at the camp in August, it rained heavily on our second afternoon, canceling our canoeing lesson. Feeling bored inside our tent, my friend Jo and I walked over to the dining hall and opened the wooden book box for the first time. Inside, we discovered an illustrated guide to wild lakeside birds left by a previous camper, along with a handwritten note on the first page recommending a quiet lookout point behind the boat house.

As soon as the rain stopped the next morning, Jo and I visited that lookout point with the guide in hand. Within half an hour, we spotted three kinds of waterbirds shown in the book and sketched their feathers in our notebooks. Before leaving the camp on Sunday, we returned the bird guide and added two mystery novels of our own.

However, several first-time campers told the camp staff that they had walked past the dining hall without realizing what the wooden box was for. This spring, Jo and I offered to paint a bright sign and draw a simple camp map showing the box's location. The staff gladly accepted our idea, and our map now hangs right at the camp entrance.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第5回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Voice Guide Made by Students

Last autumn, the History Folk House in Cedar Town celebrated its fiftieth birthday. Inside the wooden house, visitors can see traditional kitchen tools, lanterns, and weaving machines used a century ago. However, the director, Ms. Ono, noticed that junior high and elementary school visitors often walked through the rooms in five minutes because the printed explanations used difficult historical words.

Ms. Ono invited the broadcasting club at Cedar Junior High School to help solve this problem. Six club members visited the folk house after school on Wednesdays for a month. First, they interviewed elderly volunteers to learn surprising stories, such as how families kept food cool before electric refrigerators existed. Next, the students rewrote those explanations in clear, friendly sentences for young visitors.

Recording the voice guide took more effort than the students had expected. When they listened to their first recordings, they realized they were reading too fast. Their club adviser suggested pausing for two seconds after important words so listeners could look closely at each object while listening. The students recorded all ten tracks again.

In December, QR codes were placed beside ten exhibits so visitors could listen to the two-minute student stories on borrowed tablets. During the winter holidays, twice as many children completed the quiz sheet at the exit as the year before. Now the club members are preparing an English version of three popular tracks for international guests visiting Cedar Town in spring.

Umbrellas with Green Ribbons

At North Station Junior High School, sudden afternoon showers are common in June and September. For years, the school office kept twenty plain black umbrellas to lend to students who forgot theirs. Unfortunately, fewer than half of the umbrellas came back within a week. Students didn't mean to keep them; once a black umbrella stood in a family's umbrella stand at home, it looked just like everyone else's.

Last spring, the student welfare committee looked for a friendly way to solve this problem without making strict rules. One seventh-grade member, Riku, noticed how easily shoppers returned bright baskets at his neighborhood supermarket. Inspired by that, the committee tied a bright green cloth ribbon with a wooden tag onto the handle of every school umbrella. Each tag showed a cheerful turtle drawing and a number from one to twenty.

Instead of asking teachers to write down borrowers' names in a heavy book, the committee placed a whiteboard right inside the school entrance. When students borrowed an umbrella, they simply moved a numbered magnet from the "Ready" column to the "Out" column. Every morning as students walked into school, they passed the board and immediately remembered if a numbered turtle umbrella was still at their house.

During the rainy month of June, nineteen out of twenty umbrellas were returned the very next morning, and the last one came back on Friday after a student recovered from a cold. Other schools in the city heard about the turtle tags and visited North Station Junior High to learn how a small visual change encouraged everyone to cooperate.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第13回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Quiet Shelf for Nervous Dogs

Sixteen-year-old Noa volunteered every Saturday at the Oakwood Animal Shelter, cleaning kennels and refilling water bowls. Most rescued dogs wagged their tails happily whenever visitors walked down the aisle, hoping to be adopted. At the far end of the room, however, two shy dogs named Marble and Pip always hid behind their blankets because the echoing barks in the concrete room frightened them.

One evening at home, Noa noticed how her own dog calmed down immediately whenever her mother played soft classical guitar music in the living room. Curious, Noa read an article by a veterinary behavior specialist explaining that slow instrumental melodies and even gentle human reading voices could lower stress in shelter animals.

With permission from the shelter manager, Ms. Kato, Noa started a twenty-minute "Story Time" each Saturday morning before visiting hours opened. Sitting on a cushion outside the shy dogs' pens, Noa and two younger volunteers read nature picture books aloud in calm, steady voices while soft guitar music played at low volume.

During the first week, Marble only peeked out from under his blanket. By the third week, both Marble and Pip walked right up to the front gate and rested their chins on the floor, listening peacefully. When families arrived at noon, visitors could finally see the dogs' gentle personalities, and before the end of autumn, both Marble and Pip had found warm new homes.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第14回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Photographs in the Arcade Windows

For over fifty years, Sunrise Shopping Arcade had been the lively center of Willow Town. Recently, however, three family-owned stores had closed, and their shuttered front windows made the covered street look dim and lonely after school. Ninth-grader Hina walked through the arcade every day on her way home from violin lessons and wished the street felt welcoming again.

In October, Hina's social studies class began a project on local history. While visiting the town library's basement archive, Hina found boxes of black-and-white photographs taken in the 1970s. They showed children buying roasted chestnuts, snow piled outside the fish shop, and colorful paper decorations hanging from the arcade roof during summer festivals.

With permission from the library and the landlords of the empty shops, Hina and five classmates enlarged thirty photographs and displayed them neatly behind the glass of the closed storefronts. Beneath each photo, they taped a blank card asking passersby, "Do you remember this day? Tell us your story!"

Within a week, shoppers began stopping to read and write notes: "That boy holding the puppy is my grandfather!" and "This bakery made the best melon bread." On Saturdays, families came just to see the new comments, and two young bakers who visited the display liked the friendly atmosphere so much that they rented one of the empty shops the following spring.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第15回（3本文・計10問）

Hi Riko,
Thanks for collecting the sports day and school trip photos from all four ninth-grade classes! I put the eighty photos into our slideshow software last night, and the whole video is about six minutes long.

When I showed a test version to Mr. Honda at lunch today, he really liked the order of the scenes, but he noticed two small things we should fix before Friday's rehearsal. First, three photos from Class 9C's chorus contest are a little dark, so I will brighten them tonight on my computer. Second, we still need one cheerful instrumental song to play during the club-activity section in the middle.

Since your older brother plays trumpet in the brass band club, do you think we could use the recording of their autumn concert march? Please ask him tonight if the band adviser allows us to use two minutes of that recording!

Talk to you tomorrow,
Kaito

examples.script:
The Wooden Book Box at Lake Green Camp

Last summer, my town opened a small outdoor library at Lake Green Camp so families staying in tents could enjoy reading without carrying heavy books from home. Volunteers built a weatherproof wooden box with a small slanted roof and placed it beside the camp dining hall. Campers were welcome to leave books they had finished reading and borrow any book from the box during their stay.

When my family stayed at the camp in August, it rained heavily on our second afternoon, canceling our canoeing lesson. Feeling bored inside our tent, my friend Jo and I walked over to the dining hall and opened the wooden book box for the first time. Inside, we discovered an illustrated guide to wild lakeside birds left by a previous camper, along with a handwritten note on the first page recommending a quiet lookout point behind the boat house.

As soon as the rain stopped the next morning, Jo and I visited that lookout point with the guide in hand. Within half an hour, we spotted three kinds of waterbirds shown in the book and sketched their feathers in our notebooks. Before leaving the camp on Sunday, we returned the bird guide and added two mystery novels of our own.

However, several first-time campers told the camp staff that they had walked past the dining hall without realizing what the wooden box was for. This spring, Jo and I offered to paint a bright sign and draw a simple camp map showing the box's location. The staff gladly accepted our idea, and our map now hangs right at the camp entrance.

Table Tennis in the Old School Gym

Five years ago, North Valley Elementary School closed because fewer children lived in the mountain village, and students began riding a school bus to a larger town nearby. Although the classrooms were turned into a small local library, the wooden gymnasium behind the building stayed locked and silent.

Last autumn, fourteen-year-old Soma found four dusty table-tennis tables folded up in the gym's storage room while helping his aunt return library books. Soma loved playing table tennis at his junior high school, yet he had nowhere to practice on weekends without taking a forty-minute bus ride.

Soma wrote a polite proposal to the village council suggesting a "Saturday Morning Open Gym." Retired carpenter Mr. Endo offered to check the floorboards and replace the torn nets, while Soma and two friends made simple posters inviting anyone from age seven to eighty. Only six people showed up on the first Saturday in November, but word spread quickly.

Soon, twenty villagers gathered every week. Older residents who had played table tennis in their twenties turned out to have tricky spin serves that surprised the teenagers, while the students eagerly picked up stray balls and taught beginners how to hold a paddle. On snowy winter mornings when mountain roads were quiet, the sound of bouncing white balls and laughter warmed the old gym once again.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across Three Oceans

When Ms. Carter became the English teacher at Harbor Junior High School in April, many eighth-grade students felt shy about writing in English. Whenever she asked them to write three sentences in their notebooks, they worried so much about making small grammar mistakes that their pages stayed almost blank.

In May, Ms. Carter arranged a pen-pal project with two partner schools (one in New Zealand and one in Portugal) where students were also learning English as a global language. Instead of exchanging instant text messages, each student designed a handmade postcard introducing one local food or seasonal event from their town. Because space on a postcard was small, students felt relaxed and focused on sharing one clear idea.

When the first bundle of colorful cards arrived from New Zealand and Portugal in June, the classroom grew lively. Harbor students noticed that their new friends occasionally crossed out a word or used simple sentences, yet their drawings and descriptions of winter rugby matches in June and grilled sardine festivals were vivid and easy to enjoy.

Realizing that communication mattered more than perfection, the students began writing longer letters in autumn. Several students looked up English words on their own to explain how their town celebrated the autumn harvest.

At the end of the term, the class displayed copies of the postcards on the hallway board with a world map and yarn connecting the three towns. Even students who once feared writing three lines now look forward to opening the mail bag every month.

examples.script:
Why Stadium Grass Needs Artificial Sunlight

Modern soccer stadiums are built with steep, covered stands that shelter tens of thousands of fans from rain and wind, while keeping cheers echoing loudly around the pitch. For the groundskeepers tending the natural grass field, however, those towering roofs create a stubborn problem: even at noon on a sunny day, large sections of turf remain in deep shadow.

Grass blades need sunlight for photosynthesis, especially in winter when matches tear up wet soil and natural daylight hours are short. Without enough light, shaded goal areas quickly turn muddy and bare. To keep the turf thick and safe for players' ankles, many stadiums wheel out wide aluminum rigs fitted with high-efficiency grow lamps between matches. Sensors in the soil measure temperature and moisture so lamps warm and illuminate only the weakest patches. This targeted care (21).

Although running grow rigs uses electricity, keeping natural turf healthy avoids costly mid-season resodding, where entire truckloads of grass must be stripped and replaced. Healthy roots hold the ground together, proving that great stadium architecture must consider (22) as carefully as spectator comfort.

Schedule and Costume Guide for the Autumn Choral Exchange

From: Clara Bennett, Regional Youth Choir Coordinator
To: Participating High School Choir Leaders
Subject: Next Saturday's joint concert at Civic Concert Hall

Dear choir leaders,
We are delighted that eight high school choirs will gather at Civic Concert Hall next Saturday, November 7, for our annual Autumn Choral Exchange. Please share the following final details with your members before Wednesday.

Although the public performance begins at 1:30 p.m., all choirs must check in at the north stage entrance between 9:45 a.m. and 10:15 a.m. Each school will have strictly twelve minutes on stage during the morning acoustic check, followed by a combined rehearsal of the closing song with all two hundred singers at 11:40 a.m.

Dressing rooms on the basement level are shared by two schools each, so please ask students not to bring large wheeled suitcases. Choirs may wear either their regular school uniforms or black-and-white concert attire; however, shoes with hard metal heels are prohibited by the hall manager because they scratch the cedar stage floor.

Finally, audience admission is free, and family members do not need tickets, though recording videos with tripods in the aisles is not allowed for fire-safety reasons. Let me know by Thursday evening if your pianist requires a page turner.

Warmly,
Clara Bennett

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第7回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Mist Vegetables Gently—and Leave Others Dry

Shoppers reaching for lettuce or broccoli in the produce aisle often hear a soft rumble of thunder from hidden speakers just before fine water droplets drift over the greens. Although the sound effect is playful, the misting system itself serves a practical purpose grounded in plant biology.

Even after harvest, leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, and parsley continue losing moisture through microscopic pores on their leaves. Because these greens have a large surface area and very thin outer skins, dry store air can leave them limp within hours, forcing grocers to throw away otherwise nutritious food. Periodic bursts of cool mist keep humidity high around the leaves and slow down wilting, while the brief sound warning lets customers step back so their sleeves stay dry.

Not every vegetable benefits from a shower, however. Onions, garlic, potatoes, and winter squash are stored in dry bins far from the mist nozzles. Evolved as underground bulbs or thick-skinned storage organs, these crops naturally resist drying out; getting them wet in a warm store actually encourages mold and premature sprouting. Tomatoes and mushrooms likewise spoil faster when damp.

In recent years, several grocery chains have replaced open misting with ultrasonic humidifiers that create fog droplets too tiny to wet surfaces. Because excess water no longer pools at the bottom of display trays, stores report less bacterial rot and longer shelf life.

Knowing how different vegetables respond to moisture helps shoppers at home too: leafy greens stay crisp wrapped in a slightly damp cloth in the fridge, whereas onions belong in a cool, dry basket.
