examples.script:
Why Bakery Windows Fog Up Less Than Before

On cold winter mornings, small bakeries face a practical display problem. Warm steam rising from fresh trays of bread meets the icy glass of the front window and turns into tiny water droplets. While a misty window looks cozy in picture books, shop owners dislike it when passersby cannot see which breads have just come out of the oven.

Turning up the heater near the glass dries the window, yet dry hot air also makes uncovered croissants and crusty loaves lose moisture faster. A baker in Matsumoto found a simpler fix after talking with a neighbor who repaired eyeglasses. By installing a quiet ceiling fan that kept air moving gently across the glass and leaving a two-centimeter vent open near the top frame, the shop prevented warm damp air from sitting still against the cold pane. This adjustment (21) without drying out the bread.

Keeping the window clear had a welcome effect on morning sales. Commuters walking to the station could spot steaming walnut rolls from across the street and step inside on impulse. Sometimes solving an everyday shop problem requires (22) rather than buying a bigger heater.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第7回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Libraries Lend Sewing Machines and Tools

For generations, people thought of public libraries solely as quiet halls lined with books, magazines, and newspapers. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have added an unexpected shelf near the checkout counter—one stocked with sewing machines, pruning shears, air-quality monitors, and cake pans.

The idea behind a "library of things" is straightforward. Many household tools are genuinely useful twice a year, yet sit gathering dust in a closet for the other fifty weeks. Buying a decent sewing machine just to hem two pairs of curtains is expensive, especially for students or young families living in compact apartments with little storage space. Borrowing equipment with an ordinary library card lets residents (21).

Sharing infrequent tools brings community benefits as well. Librarians often pair popular items with beginner workshops led by retired tailors or carpenters, turning solitary repairs into friendly learning sessions. In this way, lending practical tools extends a library's traditional mission: giving everyone equal access to (22) regardless of income.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第15回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Manhole Covers Are Almost Always Round

Walk down almost any city street in the world, and the heavy cast-iron plates covering underground sewer and utility shafts share one unmistakable shape: they are round. Meanwhile, sidewalk grates for rainwater, subway ventilation panels, and telecom curb boxes are often rectangular. That contrast is no accident of tradition—civil engineers settled on circular manhole covers for hard-headed safety and practical reasons.

Consider what happens when workers lift a fifty-kilogram rectangular lid to climb down a ladder. Turned diagonally, a rectangle is narrower across its short side than across its corner-to-corner diagonal, meaning a careless slip could send the heavy iron plate plunging edge-first onto a technician below. A circle, by contrast, has the exact same diameter at every angle; resting on a slightly narrower circular lip inside the frame, a round cover physically (21).

Round lids simplify manufacturing and street work too. Foundries can turn circular rims smoothly on a lathe, workers never have to rotate a heavy cover to match corners when putting it back, and one worker can roll a round plate on its edge like a wheel instead of straining their back. Geometry here quietly protects (22).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第3回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Public Libraries Are Lending Household Tools

When people think of a public library, they naturally picture rows of novels, study desks, and children's picture books. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have quietly added a very different section: shelves stocked with electric drills, sewing machines, hedge trimmers, and kitchen food dehydrators that residents can borrow with an ordinary library card.

The idea grew out of a simple observation about modern apartments. Many tools are essential for an occasional task, such as putting up a bookshelf, hemming curtains, or pruning a backyard tree, yet sit unused in closets for the other 364 days of the year. Buying decent equipment is expensive, and small apartments rarely have extra storage space. Sharing durable tools across a neighborhood reduces both household spending and manufacturing waste.

In the port city of Westhaven, the central library launched its "Tool Corner" three years ago with forty donated items inspected by retired electricians and carpenters. Before borrowing power tools for the first time, residents watch a five-minute safety video and sign an agreement promising to return items clean. A modest late fee encourages borrowers to bring popular items back on schedule so weekend projects are not delayed for the next person.

Interestingly, library staff noticed an unexpected benefit. Residents who visited initially to borrow a sewing machine or bicycle repair stand often left with craft manuals, gardening guides, or cookbooks as well, bringing first-time adult visitors into the building.

Running a tool library still requires dedicated space and regular maintenance checks, so not every small branch can store heavy garden equipment. Even so, Westhaven's experience shows that libraries have always been about sharing knowledge and practical resources that strengthen daily community life.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第5回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Public Clocks Still Matter in the Smartphone Era

Almost everyone walking through a train station plaza or town square today carries an exact atomic-synced clock in a coat pocket. At first glance, spending municipal money to maintain large analog clocks on towers, schools, and park posts might seem outdated. Yet when cities remove broken public clocks instead of repairing them, residents surprisingly often petition to bring them back.

One reason is practical convenience in moments when hands are occupied. A parent holding a toddler's hand, a cyclist waiting at an intersection, or a commuter carrying grocery bags in winter gloves can check a clock face in half a second without unzipping a pocket. Even more importantly, pulling out a smartphone just to check the time frequently leads to unintended distraction—one glance at a notification banner, and five minutes vanish.

Urban designers point to a subtler social role as well. Unlike a private screen, a public clock creates a shared reference point in physical space. Saying "Let's meet under the station clock at two" gives friends and visitors an unmistakable landmark visible from across a crowded square. During major power or cellular outages following storms, wind-up or battery-backed tower clocks have also continued marking time calmly when digital displays went dark.

Maintaining outdoor clocks does require skilled hands. Gears exposed to freezing rain, sea breeze, and nesting birds must be cleaned and lubricated regularly, and fewer young technicians train in turret clockwork today. To keep costs manageable, some towns pair modern solar-charged movements behind historic dial faces, preserving the familiar look while simplifying upkeep.

Far from being mere nostalgia, a well-placed town clock quietly supports punctual, unhurried movement through shared streets.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第7回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Mist Vegetables Gently—and Leave Others Dry

Shoppers reaching for lettuce or broccoli in the produce aisle often hear a soft rumble of thunder from hidden speakers just before fine water droplets drift over the greens. Although the sound effect is playful, the misting system itself serves a practical purpose grounded in plant biology.

Even after harvest, leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, and parsley continue losing moisture through microscopic pores on their leaves. Because these greens have a large surface area and very thin outer skins, dry store air can leave them limp within hours, forcing grocers to throw away otherwise nutritious food. Periodic bursts of cool mist keep humidity high around the leaves and slow down wilting, while the brief sound warning lets customers step back so their sleeves stay dry.

Not every vegetable benefits from a shower, however. Onions, garlic, potatoes, and winter squash are stored in dry bins far from the mist nozzles. Evolved as underground bulbs or thick-skinned storage organs, these crops naturally resist drying out; getting them wet in a warm store actually encourages mold and premature sprouting. Tomatoes and mushrooms likewise spoil faster when damp.

In recent years, several grocery chains have replaced open misting with ultrasonic humidifiers that create fog droplets too tiny to wet surfaces. Because excess water no longer pools at the bottom of display trays, stores report less bacterial rot and longer shelf life.

Knowing how different vegetables respond to moisture helps shoppers at home too: leafy greens stay crisp wrapped in a slightly damp cloth in the fridge, whereas onions belong in a cool, dry basket.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第9回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Old Bridges Were Built with Roofs

Travel through rural valleys in Switzerland, Austria, North America, or parts of Japan, and you may cross a wooden bridge that looks remarkably like a long narrow barn floating above a river. Tourists often assume the roof and side walls were added so travelers and horses could stay dry during sudden storms—or so nervous farm animals would not fear the rushing water below.

While shelter was a pleasant bonus, carpenters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries had a much more practical structural reason: protecting the heavy timber trusses underneath from rot. An uncovered wooden bridge exposed to rain, snow, and summer sun typically needed major replacement within fifteen to twenty years. Water seeped into joints where beams met, froze and expanded in winter, and invited wood-eating fungi.

Adding a lightweight roof and shingle siding cost extra lumber at the start, yet shielded the load-bearing beams from moisture. When minor roof shingles wore out, villagers could replace them cheaply without closing the bridge or rebuilding its main frame. Protected this way, many covered timber bridges lasted eighty to over a hundred years—four or five times longer than open wooden spans.

When affordable steel and reinforced concrete arrived in the twentieth century, engineers no longer needed roofs to weatherproof bridges. Nevertheless, communities that preserved historic covered bridges have gained unexpected value: calm pedestrian crossings, local landmarks, and living lessons in resource-saving craftsmanship.

Sometimes the smartest way to make a structure endure is not choosing a rarer material, but keeping everyday weather off its bones.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 長文読解練習（基礎ウォームアップ・2本文・計4問）
examples.script:
Borrowing tools, not buying them

At the Willow Tool Room, residents can borrow things such as drills and long ladders. At first, people chose an item online and collected it whenever the room was open. Volunteers soon noticed a problem: some people arrived without knowing how to carry a large item safely. The room now asks borrowers to describe their transport plans before a booking is confirmed. A volunteer may suggest a smaller item or a different collection time. The room has not introduced a delivery service. Its aim is to keep borrowing practical without asking volunteers to travel around town. The new question adds a step to booking, but fewer borrowers now have to return home empty-handed.

examples.script:
Schedule and Costume Guide for the Autumn Choral Exchange

From: Clara Bennett, Regional Youth Choir Coordinator
To: Participating High School Choir Leaders
Subject: Next Saturday's joint concert at Civic Concert Hall

Dear choir leaders,
We are delighted that eight high school choirs will gather at Civic Concert Hall next Saturday, November 7, for our annual Autumn Choral Exchange. Please share the following final details with your members before Wednesday.

Although the public performance begins at 1:30 p.m., all choirs must check in at the north stage entrance between 9:45 a.m. and 10:15 a.m. Each school will have strictly twelve minutes on stage during the morning acoustic check, followed by a combined rehearsal of the closing song with all two hundred singers at 11:40 a.m.

Dressing rooms on the basement level are shared by two schools each, so please ask students not to bring large wheeled suitcases. Choirs may wear either their regular school uniforms or black-and-white concert attire; however, shoes with hard metal heels are prohibited by the hall manager because they scratch the cedar stage floor.

Finally, audience admission is free, and family members do not need tickets, though recording videos with tripods in the aisles is not allowed for fire-safety reasons. Let me know by Thursday evening if your pianist requires a page turner.

Warmly,
Clara Bennett

Instructions for the Astronomical Choir Recording

From: Mr. Shinohara, Chorus Club Director
To: Chorus Club Members
Subject: Sunday's recording session in the civic auditorium

Dear members,
This Sunday afternoon, a local radio technician will record two of our songs in the civic auditorium for the winter youth music broadcast. Because the auditorium's microphones are sensitive enough to pick up rustling cloth and clicking jewelry, please wear soft cotton shirts without zippers, metal buttons, or bracelets.

We will enter through the backstage door on the west side at 1:15 p.m.; the front glass doors will stay locked because no audience is attending. Warm-up exercises begin at 1:30 p.m., and recording runs from 2:15 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.

Cold winter air dries vocal cords quickly, so bring a bottle of plain room-temperature water. Please avoid milk tea or sweet juice right before singing, as sugar and dairy can coat your throat and make clear high notes harder. Cough drops may be used during breaks, not while standing on the risers.

Let's enjoy making a recording we'll remember!
Mr. Shinohara

examples.script:
The quiet label

A small theatre once put a "quiet performance" label on certain shows. Staff expected it to welcome people who disliked sudden noise. However, a visitor explained that the label was unclear: did it mean the audience had to remain completely silent, or that the sound from the stage would be softer? The theatre asked several visitors to review its website. It then replaced the short label with a description of what would be different. These performances now use lower sound levels and leave a few lights on. Visitors may step outside and return. The theatre still offers ordinary performances, but it no longer expects a single label to explain every change.

examples.script:
Why Stadium Grass Needs Artificial Sunlight

Modern soccer stadiums are built with steep, covered stands that shelter tens of thousands of fans from rain and wind, while keeping cheers echoing loudly around the pitch. For the groundskeepers tending the natural grass field, however, those towering roofs create a stubborn problem: even at noon on a sunny day, large sections of turf remain in deep shadow.

Grass blades need sunlight for photosynthesis, especially in winter when matches tear up wet soil and natural daylight hours are short. Without enough light, shaded goal areas quickly turn muddy and bare. To keep the turf thick and safe for players' ankles, many stadiums wheel out wide aluminum rigs fitted with high-efficiency grow lamps between matches. Sensors in the soil measure temperature and moisture so lamps warm and illuminate only the weakest patches. This targeted care (21).

Although running grow rigs uses electricity, keeping natural turf healthy avoids costly mid-season resodding, where entire truckloads of grass must be stripped and replaced. Healthy roots hold the ground together, proving that great stadium architecture must consider (22) as carefully as spectator comfort.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第9回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Coastal Towns Paint Lighthouses in Distinct Stripes

Postcards of seacoasts often show a tall white lighthouse standing on a rocky headland. Travel along an actual coastline, however, and you quickly notice that neighboring lighthouses rarely look identical: one wears bold red-and-white horizontal bands, another spirals like a black-and-white barber pole, and a third is painted solid yellow.

At night, sailors identify lighthouses by their unique flash rhythm—for instance, two quick flashes every ten seconds. During daylight hours, however, a flashing lamp is hard to spot against bright sky or sea glare. Before satellite navigation existed, captains steering along a foggy coast with binoculars needed an unmistakable visual daytime marker, known to mariners as a "daymark." Giving adjacent towers contrasting patterns ensured that (21).

Background scenery also guides color choice. A pure white tower stands out sharply against dark pine forests, yet vanishes against chalk cliffs or winter snowdrifts, where red bands remain vivid. Even today, when ships carry digital chart plotters, maritime authorities maintain these painted daymarks as (22) whenever electronics fail at sea.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第11回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Wooden Cutting Boards Stay Popular in Professional Kitchens

When smooth plastic cutting boards entered home kitchens decades ago, many cooks assumed traditional wooden boards would soon disappear. Plastic boards were light, inexpensive, and easy to load into hot dishwashers. Yet walk into bakeries, sushi counters, and restaurant prep rooms today, and thick end-grain boards made of hinoki cypress, maple, or ginkgo wood remain a chef's favorite surface.

Knife care is the first reason cooks stay loyal to wood. Hard glass, stone, or stiff plastic dulls a finely sharpened steel edge quickly because the blade slams into an unyielding surface on every chop. Wood fibers, particularly when arranged vertically like bristles on a brush, part slightly under the knife edge and spring back afterward. This gentle cushion lets chefs (21).

Food-safety experiments also surprised early skeptics. Deep knife grooves in old plastic boards can trap moisture and bacteria even after a quick wash, whereas dry natural wood pulls liquid droplets inward via capillary action, leaving surface microbes without the water they need to multiply. Provided cooks wash a wooden board promptly and stand it upright to dry, traditional timber offers (22).

Preparing Bicycles for the Lake Charity Ride

From: Lake Aoi Charity Ride Committee
To: Youth Category Riders
Subject: Helmet labels and water-station rules for Sunday

Dear riders,
Only five days remain until our 30-kilometer Lake Aoi Charity Ride! The weather outlook for Sunday is mild and dry, with light morning wind.

When you pick up your rider packet on Saturday afternoon (1:00 p.m. – 5:00 p.m. at Lakeshore Park Tent A), you will receive two matching number stickers: place the small sticker on the front of your helmet and wrap the long sticker around your seat post so marshals can record your checkpoint times.

To keep plastic waste off the lakeshore, our three rest stations will not hand out disposable paper or plastic cups. Instead, volunteers will refill riders' own bicycle water bottles from chilled tanks, along with sliced bananas and salt candies. Please arrive at the start corral by 8:15 a.m. with a full bottle.

Ride safely and enjoy the lake views!
Event Committee

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第10回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Pocket Parks Cool Busy Neighborhoods

When city governments talk about expanding green space, residents often picture sprawling central parks with boating ponds and long jogging loops. Finding ten empty hectares inside an already crowded district, however, is nearly impossible. Instead, urban planners from Tokyo to Madrid are turning tiny leftover plots—a vacant corner lot, a former gas station, or two unused parking spaces—into "pocket parks."

Measuring smaller than a tennis court, a single pocket park may hold just four shade trees, a permeable brick path, a drinking fountain, and three wooden benches. Modest as that sounds, grouping dozens of small green oases a five-minute walk apart changes how a neighborhood feels in summer. Tree canopies block direct solar heat on asphalt, while soil beds soak up sudden downpours that would otherwise flood storm drains.

Social researchers have noticed equally important human effects. Large destination parks require a planned weekend trip for elderly residents or parents with toddlers, whereas a bench beneath zelkova trees fifty meters from a grocery store invites spontaneous ten-minute rests every day. Regular eye contact among neighbors watering flower beds also builds informal community trust.

Maintaining thirty scattered mini-parks can stretch municipal gardening crews thin if handled centrally. Successful cities solve this by pairing public tree pruning with neighborhood "park friends" volunteers who sweep leaves, plant seasonal bulbs, and report broken lights.

Grand city parks remain irreplaceable treasures, yet weaving tiny green pockets into everyday streets proves that nature does not have to be huge to transform urban life.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第1回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
A Museum You Can Hear

At the Riverside Museum, most visitors once followed signs from one glass case to another. They read short descriptions of old tools, clothes, and furniture, then moved on. The objects were interesting, but the museum staff noticed that many visitors did not stay long. Few people understood how the objects had been used in daily life.

To change this, the museum invited local residents to record stories about familiar objects. One woman described the sound of the sewing machine her mother used at home. A retired baker explained why a wooden tray had a particular shape. These recordings were added to a small audio player that visitors could borrow at the entrance. The aim was not to replace the written descriptions but to provide another way to explore the collection.

The first recordings were long and difficult to follow. Staff had assumed that visitors would listen to complete interviews. In practice, people wanted to move at their own speed. The museum therefore divided the interviews into short sections. Each section focused on one object and lasted less than two minutes. Visitors could choose only the stories that interested them.

The new system also changed the relationship between the museum and the town. Residents who had rarely visited came to hear their relatives' recordings. Some brought photographs or offered to share their own memories. The museum checked these stories against old records before using them, because personal memories are not always exact.

A visitor survey later showed that people were spending more time in the museum. However, the director did not regard longer visits as the only sign of success. She was more pleased that visitors were asking new questions about everyday life in the past. The museum now plans to add stories from younger residents as well. The staff believe that objects which seem ordinary today may help future visitors understand the present.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第9回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Old Bridges Were Built with Roofs

Travel through rural valleys in Switzerland, Austria, North America, or parts of Japan, and you may cross a wooden bridge that looks remarkably like a long narrow barn floating above a river. Tourists often assume the roof and side walls were added so travelers and horses could stay dry during sudden storms—or so nervous farm animals would not fear the rushing water below.

While shelter was a pleasant bonus, carpenters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries had a much more practical structural reason: protecting the heavy timber trusses underneath from rot. An uncovered wooden bridge exposed to rain, snow, and summer sun typically needed major replacement within fifteen to twenty years. Water seeped into joints where beams met, froze and expanded in winter, and invited wood-eating fungi.

Adding a lightweight roof and shingle siding cost extra lumber at the start, yet shielded the load-bearing beams from moisture. When minor roof shingles wore out, villagers could replace them cheaply without closing the bridge or rebuilding its main frame. Protected this way, many covered timber bridges lasted eighty to over a hundred years—four or five times longer than open wooden spans.

When affordable steel and reinforced concrete arrived in the twentieth century, engineers no longer needed roofs to weatherproof bridges. Nevertheless, communities that preserved historic covered bridges have gained unexpected value: calm pedestrian crossings, local landmarks, and living lessons in resource-saving craftsmanship.

Sometimes the smartest way to make a structure endure is not choosing a rarer material, but keeping everyday weather off its bones.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第15回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Hospital Gardens Speed Patient Recovery

Throughout much of the mid-twentieth century, modern hospital architecture prioritized sterile efficiency above all else. Landscaped courtyards that once surrounded nineteenth-century infirmaries were paved over for parking decks and diagnostic wings, leaving patient rooms facing blank brick walls or air-conditioning shafts.

A turning point arrived in 1984 when environmental psychologist Roger Ulrich examined ten years of surgical recovery charts at a suburban Pennsylvania hospital. Patients recovering from identical gallbladder operations had been assigned randomly to rooms along one corridor: half looked out on a small stand of deciduous trees, while the other half faced a plain brown brick wall. Patients with the tree view requested significantly fewer strong painkillers, reported lower anxiety to nurses, and went home nearly a full day sooner on average.

Follow-up clinical studies in Japan, Sweden, and the United States confirmed that visual and physical contact with greenery lowers stress hormones such as cortisol and steadies heart rate—not only in patients, but also among exhausted ICU nurses and family caregivers taking ten-minute breaks.

Today, architects design "healing gardens" onto hospital rooftops and inner courtyards with careful medical input. Smooth, glare-free paths accommodate wheelchairs and IV poles safely; fragrant herbs and seasonal blossoms help stroke patients rebuild sensory orientation, while toxic or heavy-pollen plants are excluded near allergy wards.

Greenery cannot replace skilled surgeons or antibiotics, of course, yet restoring nature to hospital grounds treats the human nervous system alongside the illness.

Why Libraries Lend Sewing Machines and Tools

For generations, people thought of public libraries solely as quiet halls lined with books, magazines, and newspapers. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have added an unexpected shelf near the checkout counter—one stocked with sewing machines, pruning shears, air-quality monitors, and cake pans.

The idea behind a "library of things" is straightforward. Many household tools are genuinely useful twice a year, yet sit gathering dust in a closet for the other fifty weeks. Buying a decent sewing machine just to hem two pairs of curtains is expensive, especially for students or young families living in compact apartments with little storage space. Borrowing equipment with an ordinary library card lets residents (21).

Sharing infrequent tools brings community benefits as well. Librarians often pair popular items with beginner workshops led by retired tailors or carpenters, turning solitary repairs into friendly learning sessions. In this way, lending practical tools extends a library's traditional mission: giving everyone equal access to (22) regardless of income.

examples.script:
Why Public Libraries Are Lending Household Tools

When people think of a public library, they naturally picture rows of novels, study desks, and children's picture books. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have quietly added a very different section: shelves stocked with electric drills, sewing machines, hedge trimmers, and kitchen food dehydrators that residents can borrow with an ordinary library card.

The idea grew out of a simple observation about modern apartments. Many tools are essential for an occasional task, such as putting up a bookshelf, hemming curtains, or pruning a backyard tree, yet sit unused in closets for the other 364 days of the year. Buying decent equipment is expensive, and small apartments rarely have extra storage space. Sharing durable tools across a neighborhood reduces both household spending and manufacturing waste.

In the port city of Westhaven, the central library launched its "Tool Corner" three years ago with forty donated items inspected by retired electricians and carpenters. examples.script:
How Curved Sidewalk Corners Shape Street Safety

Most pedestrians never think twice about the shape of a street corner where two sidewalks meet. Yet traffic engineers know that the radius of that curve—whether it forms a sharp ninety-degree turn or a wide, sweeping arc—has a direct effect on how fast cars turn and how safely people cross.

During the mid-twentieth century, many cities widened intersection corners into gentle curves so large trucks and buses could turn without slowing down much. While convenient for vehicles, wide curves had two drawbacks for walkers. First, drivers could swing around corners at twenty-five or thirty kilometers per hour while looking mainly for oncoming cars rather than people in the crosswalk. Second, rounding off the corner pushed the curb back, making the painted crosswalk several meters longer for children and older residents to cross.

In recent years, urban planners have been tightening residential and school-zone corners again. A tighter curb forces passenger cars to slow to walking pace before turning, giving drivers an extra second or two to spot someone stepping off the sidewalk. Extending the corner slightly—a design often called a "curb bulb"—also shortens the crossing distance and lets pedestrians see past parked cars without stepping into traffic.

What about fire engines and delivery trucks that still need room to turn? Engineers solve this in creative ways. On some corners, they build a low, textured stone apron beside the curb: ordinary cars stay off the bumpy surface, while the wide wheels of an emergency vehicle can roll slowly over it when necessary.

Small geometric changes in concrete rarely make headlines, yet reshaping a single corner can calm an entire neighborhood crossing every day of the year.

A small theatre once put a "quiet performance" label on certain shows. Staff expected it to welcome people who disliked sudden noise. However, a visitor explained that the label was unclear: did it mean the audience had to remain completely silent, or that the sound from the stage would be softer? The theatre asked several visitors to review its website. It then replaced the short label with a description of what would be different. These performances now use lower sound levels and leave a few lights on. Visitors may step outside and return. The theatre still offers ordinary performances, but it no longer expects a single label to explain every change.

examples.script:
Why Coastal Towns Paint Lighthouses in Distinct Stripes

Postcards of seacoasts often show a tall white lighthouse standing on a rocky headland. Travel along an actual coastline, however, and you quickly notice that neighboring lighthouses rarely look identical: one wears bold red-and-white horizontal bands, another spirals like a black-and-white barber pole, and a third is painted solid yellow.

At night, sailors identify lighthouses by their unique flash rhythm—for instance, two quick flashes every ten seconds. During daylight hours, however, a flashing lamp is hard to spot against bright sky or sea glare. Before satellite navigation existed, captains steering along a foggy coast with binoculars needed an unmistakable visual daytime marker, known to mariners as a "daymark." Giving adjacent towers contrasting patterns ensured that (21).

Background scenery also guides color choice. A pure white tower stands out sharply against dark pine forests, yet vanishes against chalk cliffs or winter snowdrifts, where red bands remain vivid. Even today, when ships carry digital chart plotters, maritime authorities maintain these painted daymarks as (22) whenever electronics fail at sea.

examples.script:
Why Bakeries Slash Bread Dough Before Baking

Look closely at a crusty French baguette or country loaf, and you will notice diagonal cuts running neatly across the golden top. Home bakers often assume these slashes—known professionally as "scoring"—are merely a baker's artistic signature. While distinct patterns do help identify different loaves, a sharp blade actually solves a basic physics problem inside a hot oven.

The moment raw dough hits a hot baking stone, yeast activity surges and trapped water turns into steam, causing the loaf to puff up rapidly during the first ten minutes. Meanwhile, dry oven heat quickly hardens the outer skin into a firm crust. If no cuts have been made, expanding gas pushes against the weakest random spot on the side or bottom, tearing an uneven blowout and leaving the interior dense in one half and hollow in the other. Scoring creates deliberate expansion joints so the loaf (21).

Angle and depth matter too. Holding the blade nearly flat creates a thin flap of dough that peels back into a crisp, caramelized ridge prized for flavor. Thus, a two-second cut just before baking controls both (22).

examples.script:
How Botanical Gardens Use Wood Libraries

When visitors stroll through a botanical garden or natural history museum, pressed leaves and dried blossoms in herbarium cabinets usually come to mind as plant collections. Tucked away in climate-controlled basements from Kew Gardens in London to Kyoto and Madison, Wisconsin, however, researchers curate a lesser-known archive that looks like a carpenter's dream bookshelf: thousands of polished rectangular blocks of wood shelved spine-out like hardcover novels, known as a "xylarium."

Carved from documented trees collected around the globe over the past two centuries, each block records a species' unique cellular architecture. Slice a sliver of wood thinner than tissue paper and place it under a microscope, and its water-conducting vessels, rays, and growth rings form a fingerprint as distinctive as human DNA—even decades after a tree was felled and turned into furniture or flooring.

That anatomical library now plays a frontline role against illegal logging, one of the world's most destructive wildlife crimes. Rare tropical rosewoods, mahoganies, and ebonies protected by international treaties look nearly identical to legal plantation timber once sawn into smooth planks and stacked inside shipping containers. Customs officers at ports used to rely on paper export certificates that smugglers easily forged.

By training portable machine-vision cameras and chemical spectrometers on verified xylarium blocks, wood anatomists have given border inspectors field tools that identify protected tree species on the dock within minutes.

Old museum blocks have helped art historians and luthiers too—dating medieval oak panels and matching repair wood for historic bridges—proving that carefully cataloged specimens gain unexpected value long after they are collected.

Why Public Clocks Still Matter in the Smartphone Era

Almost everyone walking through a train station plaza or town square today carries an exact atomic-synced clock in a coat pocket. At first glance, spending municipal money to maintain large analog clocks on towers, schools, and park posts might seem outdated. Yet when cities remove broken public clocks instead of repairing them, residents surprisingly often petition to bring them back.

One reason is practical convenience in moments when hands are occupied. A parent holding a toddler's hand, a cyclist waiting at an intersection, or a commuter carrying grocery bags in winter gloves can check a clock face in half a second without unzipping a pocket. Even more importantly, pulling out a smartphone just to check the time frequently leads to unintended distraction—one glance at a notification banner, and five minutes vanish.

Urban designers point to a subtler social role as well. Unlike a private screen, a public clock creates a shared reference point in physical space. Saying "Let's meet under the station clock at two" gives friends and visitors an unmistakable landmark visible from across a crowded square. During major power or cellular outages following storms, wind-up or battery-backed tower clocks have also continued marking time calmly when digital displays went dark.

Maintaining outdoor clocks does require skilled hands. Gears exposed to freezing rain, sea breeze, and nesting birds must be cleaned and lubricated regularly, and fewer young technicians train in turret clockwork today. To keep costs manageable, some towns pair modern solar-charged movements behind historic dial faces, preserving the familiar look while simplifying upkeep.

Far from being mere nostalgia, a well-placed town clock quietly supports punctual, unhurried movement through shared streets.

examples.script:
How Pocket Parks Cool Busy Neighborhoods

When city governments talk about expanding green space, residents often picture sprawling central parks with boating ponds and long jogging loops. Finding ten empty hectares inside an already crowded district, however, is nearly impossible. Instead, urban planners from Tokyo to Madrid are turning tiny leftover plots—a vacant corner lot, a former gas station, or two unused parking spaces—into "pocket parks."

Measuring smaller than a tennis court, a single pocket park may hold just four shade trees, a permeable brick path, a drinking fountain, and three wooden benches. Modest as that sounds, grouping dozens of small green oases a five-minute walk apart changes how a neighborhood feels in summer. Tree canopies block direct solar heat on asphalt, while soil beds soak up sudden downpours that would otherwise flood storm drains.

Social researchers have noticed equally important human effects. Large destination parks require a planned weekend trip for elderly residents or parents with toddlers, whereas a bench beneath zelkova trees fifty meters from a grocery store invites spontaneous ten-minute rests every day. Regular eye contact among neighbors watering flower beds also builds informal community trust.

Maintaining thirty scattered mini-parks can stretch municipal gardening crews thin if handled centrally. Successful cities solve this by pairing public tree pruning with neighborhood "park friends" volunteers who sweep leaves, plant seasonal bulbs, and report broken lights.

Grand city parks remain irreplaceable treasures, yet weaving tiny green pockets into everyday streets proves that nature does not have to be huge to transform urban life.

How Quiet Floors Help Hospital Patients Recover

When patients stay overnight in a hospital, uninterrupted sleep is one of the strongest aids to healing. Ironically, hospital wards have long been among the hardest places to sleep soundly. Alongside necessary medical monitors, everyday corridor sounds—squeaking supply carts, echoing footsteps on hard vinyl tiles, and clicking door latches—repeatedly wake light sleepers.

Acoustic researchers measuring ward noise found that sudden peaks in sound disturb sleep far more than a low, steady hum. A metal cart rolling over a tiny seam in a hard floor can send a sharp sixty-five-decibel clatter into nearby rooms, raising a sleeping patient's heart rate even if the person does not fully remember waking up.

To tackle this problem without sacrificing hygiene, hospital designers have rethought flooring and hardware from the ground up. New rubber-composite floors cushion footsteps and cart wheels while remaining seamless and easy to disinfect—unlike carpets, which trap dust and spills. Equally simple mechanical changes help: replacing metal trash-can lids with slow-closing dampers and fitting supply carts with soft polyurethane casters cut corridor noise spikes nearly in half during pilot studies.

Staff well-being improves alongside patient rest. Nurses walking ten kilometers per shift on cushioned rubber floors report less knee and back fatigue, and quieter hallways reduce misunderstandings when doctors discuss medication doses.

Thoughtful hospital design recognizes that recovery depends not only on advanced medicine, but also on a calm sensory environment.

A Museum You Can Hear

At the Riverside Museum, most visitors once followed signs from one glass case to another. They read short descriptions of old tools, clothes, and furniture, then moved on. The objects were interesting, but the museum staff noticed that many visitors did not stay long. Few people understood how the objects had been used in daily life.

To change this, the museum invited local residents to record stories about familiar objects. One woman described the sound of the sewing machine her mother used at home. A retired baker explained why a wooden tray had a particular shape. These recordings were added to a small audio player that visitors could borrow at the entrance. The aim was not to replace the written descriptions but to provide another way to explore the collection.

The first recordings were long and difficult to follow. Staff had assumed that visitors would listen to complete interviews. In practice, people wanted to move at their own speed. The museum therefore divided the interviews into short sections. Each section focused on one object and lasted less than two minutes. Visitors could choose only the stories that interested them.

The new system also changed the relationship between the museum and the town. Residents who had rarely visited came to hear their relatives' recordings. Some brought photographs or offered to share their own memories. The museum checked these stories against old records before using them, because personal memories are not always exact.

A visitor survey later showed that people were spending more time in the museum. However, the director did not regard longer visits as the only sign of success. She was more pleased that visitors were asking new questions about everyday life in the past. The museum now plans to add stories from younger residents as well. The staff believe that objects which seem ordinary today may help future visitors understand the present.

examples.script:
Why Public Libraries Are Lending Household Tools

When people think of a public library, they naturally picture rows of novels, study desks, and children's picture books. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have quietly added a very different section: shelves stocked with electric drills, sewing machines, hedge trimmers, and kitchen food dehydrators that residents can borrow with an ordinary library card.

The idea grew out of a simple observation about modern apartments. Many tools are essential for an occasional task, such as putting up a bookshelf, hemming curtains, or pruning a backyard tree, yet sit unused in closets for the other 364 days of the year. Buying decent equipment is expensive, and small apartments rarely have extra storage space. Sharing durable tools across a neighborhood reduces both household spending and manufacturing waste.

In the port city of Westhaven, the central library launched its "Tool Corner" three years ago with forty donated items inspected by retired electricians and carpenters. Before borrowing power tools for the first time, residents watch a five-minute safety video and sign an agreement promising to return items clean. A modest late fee encourages borrowers to bring popular items back on schedule so weekend projects are not delayed for the next person.

Interestingly, library staff noticed an unexpected benefit. Residents who visited initially to borrow a sewing machine or bicycle repair stand often left with craft manuals, gardening guides, or cookbooks as well, bringing first-time adult visitors into the building.

Running a tool library still requires dedicated space and regular maintenance checks, so not every small branch can store heavy garden equipment. Even so, Westhaven's experience shows that libraries have always been about sharing knowledge and practical resources that strengthen daily community life.

examples.script:
How Quiet Floors Help Hospital Patients Recover

When patients stay overnight in a hospital, uninterrupted sleep is one of the strongest aids to healing. Ironically, hospital wards have long been among the hardest places to sleep soundly. Alongside necessary medical monitors, everyday corridor sounds—squeaking supply carts, echoing footsteps on hard vinyl tiles, and clicking door latches—repeatedly wake light sleepers.

Acoustic researchers measuring ward noise found that sudden peaks in sound disturb sleep far more than a low, steady hum. A metal cart rolling over a tiny seam in a hard floor can send a sharp sixty-five-decibel clatter into nearby rooms, raising a sleeping patient's heart rate even if the person does not fully remember waking up.

To tackle this problem without sacrificing hygiene, hospital designers have rethought flooring and hardware from the ground up. New rubber-composite floors cushion footsteps and cart wheels while remaining seamless and easy to disinfect—unlike carpets, which trap dust and spills. Equally simple mechanical changes help: replacing metal trash-can lids with slow-closing dampers and fitting supply carts with soft polyurethane casters cut corridor noise spikes nearly in half during pilot studies.

Staff well-being improves alongside patient rest. Nurses walking ten kilometers per shift on cushioned rubber floors report less knee and back fatigue, and quieter hallways reduce misunderstandings when doctors discuss medication doses.

Thoughtful hospital design recognizes that recovery depends not only on advanced medicine, but also on a calm sensory environment.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第4回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Teaching Buses and Trains to Wait Two Minutes

Missing a rural connecting bus by ninety seconds can turn a twenty-minute commute into an hour-long wait on a windy platform. In large cities, where another train arrives every four minutes, tight transfers rarely matter. Along regional rail lines and suburban bus corridors, however, vehicles run far less frequently, so a single delayed train can strand dozens of passengers who needed that connection.

Historically, bus drivers had no reliable way to know whether an approaching train was running two minutes late or twenty. Waiting blindly risked making every downstream stop late and causing passengers further along the route to miss their own appointments. As a result, most operators instructed drivers to depart strictly by the printed clock, even if a train was just pulling into the station.

Low-cost GPS trackers and shared dispatch screens have begun changing this rigid rule. In several mid-sized European and Japanese cities, trains and connecting buses now exchange live location updates automatically. If a train is delayed by three minutes or less—and the bus schedule has enough cushion on a quiet stretch of road to make up that time—the screen on the driver's dashboard flashes a "hold" request. Meanwhile, an announcement inside the train tells transferring riders that their bus is waiting at Stand 2, preventing dangerous sprinting on station stairs.

Of course, holding a bus is not always wise. When heavy snow delays a train by fifteen minutes, holding every feeder bus would paralyze the entire local network. Dispatch software therefore sets clear upper limits, typically three to five minutes, and prioritizes the last evening runs when no later bus exists.

Passenger surveys in towns using smart-hold rules show a notable jump in trust toward public transit. Knowing that operators coordinate across vehicles makes people far more willing to leave their cars at home for two-seat journeys.

A Second Life for Sports Gear

Many children try a new sport at school, only to outgrow their shoes, rackets, or protective pads within a single year. Because brand-new equipment can be costly, some families hesitate to let children try unfamiliar sports. Noticeably usable gear often ends up sitting in closets long after young players have moved on.

In the town of Brookside, two high school coaches started a seasonal "Gear Swap Day" at the public gym. Families donate clean sports items they no longer need, and any child in town can select suitable equipment at no charge. Before anything is placed on the tables, volunteer coaches inspect helmets, straps, and soles carefully. Their priority is to (21). Items that are worn out or damaged are recycled rather than passed on.

Over the past two years, participation in beginner sports classes in Brookside has risen steadily. Parents say children feel freer to experiment when trying a sport does not require an expensive initial purchase. For the coaches, the swap has proved (22), helping young residents stay active regardless of household budgets.

examples.script:
Why Bakery Windows Fog Up Less Than Before

On cold winter mornings, small bakeries face a practical display problem. Warm steam rising from fresh trays of bread meets the icy glass of the front window and turns into tiny water droplets. While a misty window looks cozy in picture books, shop owners dislike it when passersby cannot see which breads have just come out of the oven.

Turning up the heater near the glass dries the window, yet dry hot air also makes uncovered croissants and crusty loaves lose moisture faster. A baker in Matsumoto found a simpler fix after talking with a neighbor who repaired eyeglasses. By installing a quiet ceiling fan that kept air moving gently across the glass and leaving a two-centimeter vent open near the top frame, the shop prevented warm damp air from sitting still against the cold pane. This adjustment (21) without drying out the bread.

Keeping the window clear had a welcome effect on morning sales. Commuters walking to the station could spot steaming walnut rolls from across the street and step inside on impulse. Sometimes solving an everyday shop problem requires (22) rather than buying a bigger heater.

From: Luis, Festival Coordinator
To: Volunteers
Subject: Please read before Saturday

Dear volunteers,
Thank you for helping at our international food festival. There have been two important changes. First, heavy rain is expected, so the festival will take place inside the community center rather than in the park. The center has enough space for all the food tables, but the entrance is narrow. Please arrive at the back door to help move supplies.

Second, the local bus company cannot provide the extra morning service we requested. Some visitors may arrive later than planned. We will therefore begin serving food at 11:30 instead of 11:00. Volunteers should still arrive at 9:00, as originally arranged. We need that time to set up the tables and check the kitchen equipment.

If you are helping at a food table, please bring a clean apron. We will provide gloves and name tags. Volunteers at the information desk do not need aprons. Those who have not yet chosen a job should contact me by Thursday evening.

Finally, please avoid bringing your own cars because parking spaces must be kept for delivery vehicles. The number 6 bus stops directly outside the center. I will send a map with the entrance marked tomorrow.

Best wishes,
Luis

examples.script:
Why Small Bakeries Are Changing Their Schedules

In many towns, traditional bakeries used to display full trays of every kind of bread from early morning until closing time. Customers appreciated seeing abundant choices even late in the afternoon. Behind the scenes, however, keeping shelves full all day meant that unsold loaves frequently had to be thrown away at night, increasing ingredient costs and food waste.

Recently, a growing number of independent bakers have moved away from this model. At Sunrise Crust Bakery, for example, the owner noticed from sales records that crusty dinner rolls sold mostly after four o'clock, whereas fruit pastries were popular before ten in the morning. Instead of baking everything at dawn and hoping it would sell, the bakery began baking smaller batches tailored to each time of day.

At first, the owner worried that customers would complain if a particular item ran out early. When the bakery placed a simple chalkboard schedule outside the door showing what came out of the oven at 8:00 a.m., noon, and 4:00 p.m., customers reacted positively. Commuters started timing their visits to buy warm bread straight from the oven.

To handle the small amount of bread still left at closing time, Sunrise Crust partnered with a nearby evening soup kitchen and offered next-morning "surprise bags" at half price. While small-batch baking requires more careful planning by kitchen staff, the owner found that cutting daily waste allowed the shop to buy higher-quality local flour without raising prices.

Food researchers note that customers' expectations play a major role in reducing retail waste. When shoppers understand that an empty tray late in the day reflects careful production rather than poor service, neighborhood shops can operate far more sustainably.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第6回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Curved Sidewalk Corners Shape Street Safety

Most pedestrians never think twice about the shape of a street corner where two sidewalks meet. Yet traffic engineers know that the radius of that curve—whether it forms a sharp ninety-degree turn or a wide, sweeping arc—has a direct effect on how fast cars turn and how safely people cross.

During the mid-twentieth century, many cities widened intersection corners into gentle curves so large trucks and buses could turn without slowing down much. While convenient for vehicles, wide curves had two drawbacks for walkers. First, drivers could swing around corners at twenty-five or thirty kilometers per hour while looking mainly for oncoming cars rather than people in the crosswalk. Second, rounding off the corner pushed the curb back, making the painted crosswalk several meters longer for children and older residents to cross.

In recent years, urban planners have been tightening residential and school-zone corners again. A tighter curb forces passenger cars to slow to walking pace before turning, giving drivers an extra second or two to spot someone stepping off the sidewalk. Extending the corner slightly—a design often called a "curb bulb"—also shortens the crossing distance and lets pedestrians see past parked cars without stepping into traffic.

What about fire engines and delivery trucks that still need room to turn? Engineers solve this in creative ways. On some corners, they build a low, textured stone apron beside the curb: ordinary cars stay off the bumpy surface, while the wide wheels of an emergency vehicle can roll slowly over it when necessary.

Small geometric changes in concrete rarely make headlines, yet reshaping a single corner can calm an entire neighborhood crossing every day of the year.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第12回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Botanical Illustrators Still Draw Plants by Hand

Modern smartphones and macro cameras can photograph an orchid petal in a fraction of a second, capturing millions of pixels of color. Given such effortless technology, visitors to natural history museums are often surprised to learn that botanists naming a newly discovered plant species still commission black-and-white pen-and-ink illustrations drawn by hand.

A single photograph, however sharp, shows only one individual plant at one moment in time. In the wild, a flower may bloom in April while its seed pod matures in August, or one leaf may be chewed by insects while a diagnostic root tuber stays hidden underground. Even worse, camera lenses struggle with depth of field at close range: focusing sharply on tiny pollen stamens blurs the stem hairs two centimeters behind them.

A trained botanical illustrator overcomes all of these limits on one sheet of paper. Consulting closely with the botanist—and often examining pressed herbarium specimens under a microscope—the artist combines buds, open blossoms, cross-sections of fruit, and magnified seed textures side by side in crystal-clear focus. Unnecessary shadows and distracting background leaves are omitted so another scientist a century later can verify the exact vein pattern that distinguishes the species from close relatives.

Digital tablets have certainly joined traditional crow-quill pens on many illustrators' desks, making revisions cleaner. Yet the core skill remains human observation rather than button-pressing: deciding which tiny details matter scientifically.

Far from competing, photography and hand illustration complement each other—photos record living color in habitat, while botanical line art preserves clear structural truth.

examples.script:
Audio Labels in the Supermarket

For shoppers with poor eyesight, choosing between dozens of similar-looking cans and boxes in a supermarket can be exhausting. Price tags on shelf edges are often printed in tiny type, and packaging designs change frequently without warning. Even regular customers may hesitate to pick up an unfamiliar brand if they cannot easily check cooking instructions or allergy warnings.

To address this problem, a regional grocery chain tested small raised QR stickers on its own-brand food packages. Unlike ordinary promotional codes that open long marketing pages, these tactile stickers can be located by touch and scanned from a wide angle. A smartphone immediately reads aloud the product name, weight, expiry rule, and allergy ingredients. (18), shoppers do not need to align the camera precisely with a small symbol.

Feedback from visually impaired testers led to one further improvement. Early versions read every piece of text from top to bottom, forcing listeners to wait thirty seconds before hearing whether an item contained nuts or dairy. Designers reorganized the spoken order so critical safety details came first, making the labels (19).

Unexpectedly, other customers began using the stickers too, including elderly shoppers who had left reading glasses at home and foreign residents checking unfamiliar ingredients. Designing for a specific barrier ended up creating (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第9回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Escalators Have Brushes Along Their Sides

Look down at the bottom edges of almost any subway or department-store escalator, and you will notice rows of stiff black nylon bristles sticking inward from both side panels. Many riders casually use them to dust off their shoes—or assume the brushes are there to sweep candy wrappers off the moving steps. In fact, engineers added skirt brushes after investigating a serious mechanical hazard.

Between each moving metal step and the stationary side wall sits a tiny gap just a few millimeters wide. Without a physical barrier, soft rubber rain boots, trailing coat drawstrings, or long shopping bags resting right against the wall can get pulled into that gap by friction as the steps descend. Once fabric or rubber wedges inside, the escalator must halt abruptly. (18), a subtle sensory warning was needed to keep feet a few centimeters toward the center.

Stiff nylon bristles solve the problem gently through human reflexes. Whenever a passenger's shoe or pant leg brushes against the bristles, the light tickling sensation prompts the person to shift inward automatically without looking down. (19), the bristles physically deflect loose shoelaces before they can reach the narrow metal clearance.

Safety authorities made side brushes mandatory on new escalators in many countries after injury rates dropped sharply in early trials. Sometimes the best engineering safeguard is not a loud alarm, but (20).

examples.script:
Keeping Track of City Trees

On a summer afternoon, a tree-lined street can feel quite different from a nearby road without shade. Trees also provide places for birds and insects to live. Yet city officials often have incomplete information about the trees they are responsible for. Paper records may be old, and different departments may keep separate lists. This can make it difficult to decide where care is most urgently needed.

In one city, a group of residents offered to help create a shared tree record. Volunteers walked along public streets and entered basic information into a mobile form. They recorded each tree's location, took a photograph, and noted visible signs of damage. They were not asked to judge whether a tree was safe. That decision remained the responsibility of trained specialists.

The first month produced thousands of entries, but some were unreliable. A tree near a street corner might be recorded by two teams, while a photograph taken from far away might show the wrong tree. Rather than simply count the entries, the project leader introduced a checking stage. Teams compared neighboring records, and specialists reviewed reports of possible disease. Each confirmed tree received a single identification number.

The resulting map changed how the city planned its work. Officials had previously responded mainly to requests from residents. However, some neighborhoods made many requests while others made few, even when their trees were in poor condition. The new record allowed officials to compare areas more fairly. It also revealed streets where there were very few trees at all.

The project did not mean that every neighborhood could immediately receive new trees. Planting requires money, and there must be enough space underground for roots as well as above ground for branches. In some streets, water pipes and cables limited the available space. Officials had to explain why a request could not always be accepted.

For volunteers, the main lesson was that collecting information was only the beginning. The value of the record depended on checking it, keeping it current, and using it to answer practical questions. The group now revisits a different area each month. Its members hope that a record built through public participation will remain useful because people understand both its purpose and its limits.

examples.script:
An open rehearsal with a closed door

The Riverbank Orchestra wanted more local residents to attend its rehearsals. It made admission free and advertised that no knowledge of classical music was needed. Yet the audience remained mostly unchanged. A student volunteer suggested speaking to people who had never attended, rather than asking regular visitors what they enjoyed. These conversations revealed a practical problem: the building entrance was locked once rehearsal began, so anyone delayed at work could not enter. The orchestra arranged for a volunteer to remain near the entrance during the first half hour. Attendance increased, particularly among people working nearby. The free admission still mattered, but it had not solved the timing problem. The orchestra now checks whether its arrangements match the daily routines of the people it hopes to welcome.

How Bamboo Scaffolding Still Rises Around High-Rise Towers

Visitors stepping onto the streets of Hong Kong for the first time often look up in disbelief: encasing forty-story glass skyscrapers are intricate lattices of golden bamboo poles lashed together with black nylon strips. In an era of steel cranes and aluminum frames, traditional bamboo scaffolding remains a thriving engineering craft.

Speed, weight, and flexibility explain bamboo's staying power in dense subtropical cities. Thick giant-timber bamboo stalks weigh a fraction as much as steel pipes yet boast remarkable tensile strength along their hollow fibers. Experienced scaffolders carry bundles easily up narrow stairwells and tie custom grids around irregular balconies or curved neon signs without welding or heavy bolts. (21), a skilled crew can wrap a mid-rise facade far faster and at lower cost than with rigid metal tubing.

Typhoon winds reveal another surprising advantage. Whereas rigid steel frames can transmit violent gusts into building anchors or snap suddenly, properly braced bamboo flexes slightly with the wind to absorb energy. Safety standards are far from casual, however: Hong Kong building codes specify pole thickness, curing age, steel wall-anchors, and formal apprenticeships. (22), many modern projects use a hybrid approach—steel brackets at the base supporting bamboo lattices above.

Combining renewable fast-growing grass with rigorous safety engineering shows that traditional materials can (23).

examples.script:
Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind

In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).

A New Plan for the Exhibition

From: Elena Brooks, Project Leader
To: Student Exhibition Team
Subject: Final arrangements

Dear team,
Thank you for preparing the exhibition on the history of our neighborhood. After looking through your work, the community center has agreed to lend us its main hall. This will allow us to display larger photographs than we could in the school corridor. However, the hall is available for only one weekend, so we must finish setting up by Friday evening and remove everything on Sunday after closing.

We originally planned to borrow display boards from the town office. Unfortunately, they are needed for another event. The center has offered lightweight stands instead. These cannot hold heavy objects, so please do not bring the old tools you collected. Use photographs of them, with short explanations of what they were used for. Your interviews with residents can still be played through the small speakers.

Please send your final captions to me by Monday. I will check them for unclear dates and names, not change your choice of topics. If a resident has asked not to be named, use a description such as "a former shop owner." We have permission to show the donated photographs during the exhibition, but not to post them on social media.

I also need two volunteers to welcome visitors on Saturday morning. You do not have to know every part of local history. Your main task will be to explain the arrangement of the exhibition and direct visitors to the appropriate section. Please reply by tomorrow if you can help.

Elena

examples.script:
How Repair Cafés Extend Product Lifespans and Neighborhood Ties

Buy an electric toaster, desk fan, or winter coat today, and a single snapped switch or stuck zipper often sends the entire item to the trash bin. Manufacturers frequently seal plastic housings with glue rather than screws, while commercial repair shops must charge labor fees that rival the price of a cheap replacement. Across more than two thousand towns worldwide—having started in Amsterdam in 2009—community volunteers have built a welcoming response: the monthly "Repair Café."

Held in libraries, church basements, or civic centers on Saturday afternoons, a Repair Café pairs retired engineers, tailors, carpenters, and tech-savvy students with neighbors carrying broken household goods. Visitors pay nothing except optional donations for spare fuses or thread. Crucially, the café is not a drop-off counter; owners pull up a chair and hold the flashlight or screwdriver alongside the fixer. (21), demystifying how a coffee maker or bicycle brake works gives people confidence to tackle minor upkeep at home.

Volunteer groups log every attempted repair in a shared international database, successfully reviving roughly two-thirds of items brought in. Beyond keeping tons of metals and textiles out of landfills, those records now inform "right-to-repair" lawmakers pressing appliance makers to supply spare parts and screw-together designs. (22), elderly craftspeople living alone gain a lively monthly venue where younger neighbors genuinely value their decades of practical skill.

Sharing tools over a cup of tea shows how local grassroots action can (23).

examples.script:
Why Repair Instructions Matter Before You Buy

When consumers shop for a toaster, a desk fan, or a cordless vacuum cleaner, they usually compare price, weight, and battery life. Rarely do they ask what will happen three years later when a switch wears out or a battery loses strength. Yet millions of small household appliances are discarded every year not because their motors have failed, but because replacing a single inexpensive part requires special tools or sealed cases cannot be opened safely.

In response, several consumer groups and regional governments have introduced "repairability scores" displayed right beside product prices in electronics stores. Instead of giving a vague environmental badge, the score rates five concrete factors from one to ten: how easily a product can be taken apart, whether spare parts are sold to the public, how many years those parts remain available, how much they cost relative to a new machine, and whether clear repair manuals can be downloaded for free.

When the scoring system first appeared, some manufacturers argued that shoppers cared only about low upfront prices and would ignore technical ratings. Early retail data suggested otherwise. Even customers who never intended to use a screwdriver themselves began choosing models with higher scores, viewing repairability as a sign of honest engineering and long-term durability.

More importantly, the visibility of low scores prompted manufacturers to change design habits before products ever reached store shelves. Engineers replaced glue with standard screws in several popular appliances and published step-by-step part diagrams online. A company might willingly tolerate a complaint buried in customer service emails, whereas a low number printed on every price tag directly affected sales.

Specialists caution that a label alone does not guarantee fewer discarded appliances. Local repair shops still need affordable parts and trained technicians, and consumers may still replace working machines when new features look appealing. Even so, making repair information visible at the moment of purchase shifts attention from how cheaply an item is made to how responsibly it can be kept in use.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第9回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
How Seed Vaults Keep Crop Diversity Alive Underground

Walk through a modern supermarket, and the fruit and vegetable section looks wonderfully varied. Yet agricultural historians point out a quiet vulnerability behind that colorful display: globally, just nine plant species account for nearly two-thirds of all crop production, and farmers within each crop increasingly plant a handful of high-yielding commercial varieties. While uniform crops simplify harvesting and transport, genetic uniformity carries risk. If a new fungal disease or prolonged drought strikes a widely planted wheat or potato variety, entire regions can lose harvests simultaneously.

Over previous centuries, peasant farmers maintained thousands of local "landrace" varieties—grains and beans adapted to salty coastal soil, high mountain frost, or short desert rains. When farms switch to modern commercial seeds, those hardy older varieties can vanish within a single generation unless someone preserves viable seeds.

That is the mission of over a thousand seed banks worldwide, backed up by the Svalbard Global Seed Vault deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway. Sealed in moisture-proof foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, orthodox seeds such as wheat, rice, and lentils slow their metabolism so dramatically that they remain capable of sprouting for decades or even centuries. Permafrost surrounding the Arctic rock tunnel provides natural refrigeration even if external power temporarily fails.

Even the coldest vault is not a "set-and-forget" museum, however. Seeds slowly lose vigor over time and must periodically be thawed, planted in soil, harvested fresh, and frozen anew. Moreover, tropical crops with moist, fleshy seeds—such as cacao, mango, and avocado—cannot survive standard freezing at all; scientists preserve their diversity in living field collections or ultra-cold liquid nitrogen.

Safeguarding ancient seeds is ultimately forward-looking work: traits hidden in an obscure mountain grain today may hold the exact drought resistance breeders need fifty years from now.

examples.script:
Borrowing time

A city library introduced appointments for help with digital devices. Each appointment lasted twenty minutes. Staff could keep to the schedule easily when a visitor had one simple question. However, some visitors needed to explain a longer series of problems before staff understood the situation. Extending every appointment would have reduced the number of people the library could serve. Instead, the library added a short conversation at the booking stage. Staff now ask what the visitor hopes to do, rather than only which device they own. They can then choose a standard slot or arrange a longer session. The system is not perfect: some problems still take longer than expected. Nevertheless, fewer sessions now end before the main difficulty has even been identified.

From: M. Kurata, Bird Conservation Group
To: Student Survey Volunteers
Subject: Observation points and quiet-zone rules for Saturday

Dear student volunteers,
Thank you for joining our winter waterfowl count at Ashihara Marsh this Saturday morning. Migratory ducks and wild geese feed near the reed beds soon after sunrise, so we will meet at the south parking shelter at 6:40 a.m. and walk to our four wooden hides in small groups.

Each group includes an experienced spotter with a high-powered scope; your job is to record species counts every fifteen minutes on the waterproof clipboards provided. Please switch your phones to silent mode and turn screen brightness all the way down before entering a hide, as sudden flashes of white light through the viewing slots can startle resting flocks.

Because two hides stand over shallow water, icy breezes come up through the floorboards. Wear wool socks—two thin pairs trap more warmth than one tight thick pair—and bring a thermos of warm drink if you like, though strongly scented soup should wait until we return to the shelter at 9:30 a.m.

Best regards,
M. Kurata

examples.script:
Why Repair Instructions Matter Before You Buy

When consumers shop for a toaster, a desk fan, or a cordless vacuum cleaner, they usually compare price, weight, and battery life. Rarely do they ask what will happen three years later when a switch wears out or a battery loses strength. Yet millions of small household appliances are discarded every year not because their motors have failed, but because replacing a single inexpensive part requires special tools or sealed cases cannot be opened safely.

In response, several consumer groups and regional governments have introduced "repairability scores" displayed right beside product prices in electronics stores. Instead of giving a vague environmental badge, the score rates five concrete factors from one to ten: how easily a product can be taken apart, whether spare parts are sold to the public, how many years those parts remain available, how much they cost relative to a new machine, and whether clear repair manuals can be downloaded for free.

When the scoring system first appeared, some manufacturers argued that shoppers cared only about low upfront prices and would ignore technical ratings. Early retail data suggested otherwise. Even customers who never intended to use a screwdriver themselves began choosing models with higher scores, viewing repairability as a sign of honest engineering and long-term durability.

More importantly, the visibility of low scores prompted manufacturers to change design habits before products ever reached store shelves. Engineers replaced glue with standard screws in several popular appliances and published step-by-step part diagrams online. A company might willingly tolerate a complaint buried in customer service emails, whereas a low number printed on every price tag directly affected sales.

Specialists caution that a label alone does not guarantee fewer discarded appliances. Local repair shops still need affordable parts and trained technicians, and consumers may still replace working machines when new features look appealing. Even so, making repair information visible at the moment of purchase shifts attention from how cheaply an item is made to how responsibly it can be kept in use.
