examples.script:
Why Cities Are Uncovering Buried Streams

Beneath the asphalt of almost every major city flow dozens of forgotten brooks and small rivers. During periods of rapid urban growth in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, engineers routinely encased neighborhood streams in underground concrete pipes—known as culverts—to gain flat land for roads, prevent rubbish dumping, and move rainwater out of town as fast as possible. Out of sight, these waterways vanished from maps and local memory alike.

Climate pressures and aging pipes are now prompting municipalities to reverse course through a practice called "daylighting"—lifting buried streams back into open air. Ironically, the old concrete channels designed to prevent localized puddles often worsen flooding downstream during intense modern cloudbursts. Smooth underground pipes shoot storm runoff forward all at once, overwhelming river junctions below. An open channel lined with stones, curves, and terraced banks slows the water down and gives high flows safe room to spread.

Bringing water back to the surface transforms urban neighborhoods in quieter months as well. Shaded streamside paths run several degrees cooler than surrounding streets on August afternoons, while riffles oxygenate the water enough for dragonflies, minnows, and herons to return within a remarkably short time. Shopkeepers along famous daylighting projects—from Seoul to Zurich—have seen foot traffic rise as once-noisy traffic lanes become pleasant places to linger.

Daylighting is not feasible everywhere, of course. Where apartment blocks or subway tunnels sit directly atop a culvert, rerouting the stream through an adjacent park strip or widening parallel greenways may be the only practical option, and upstream street runoff must be filtered through gravel beds before entering the open brook.

Even modest stretches of uncovered water remind residents that a city is built atop living geography rather than a blank concrete slab.

Borrowing More Than Books

A small library wanted to attract residents who rarely borrowed books. Instead of expanding its shelves, it began lending useful household objects, including a sewing machine and a set of gardening tools. The staff hoped that residents could try an object before deciding whether to buy one. People could also borrow items they needed only occasionally.

At first, the library accepted almost every donated object. This created an unexpected problem. Some items were missing parts, while others required repairs that the staff could not perform. The service soon became difficult to manage. The library therefore introduced a rule: every object had to be inspected before it was accepted. (18), donations became easier to handle, even though the library received fewer of them.

Another concern was that borrowers might return objects late. The library considered charging large fines, but staff worried this would discourage people from trying the service. Instead, borrowers received a reminder a day before an item was due. If they needed more time, they could request an extension unless someone else was waiting. The library found that clear communication was (19).

The service is still small. Staff have not claimed that it will replace shopping or solve all the town's waste problems. However, residents have started discussing which objects could usefully be shared. For the library, one important result has been (20). People who had never met now exchange advice about using and repairing the objects they borrow.

examples.script:
Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind

In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).

examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Pack Berries in Vented Clamshell Boxes

Pick up a container of strawberries, raspberries, or blueberries at the market, and you will almost always find them sitting in a clear hinged plastic box perforated with narrow slots along the lid and base. Shoppers sometimes wish berries came in sealed airtight tubs or simple paper bags, yet post-harvest food scientists designed those slotted "clamshell" boxes around how delicate fruit breathes.

Even after leaving the vine, fresh berries remain living tissue: they consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide, heat, and water vapor. Seal warm berries inside an airtight container, and moisture condenses on the lid within an hour, creating damp droplets where gray mold spores multiply overnight. Conversely, loose paper bags crush soft raspberries during truck transport and hide bruised fruit at the bottom. Slotted clamshells cushion berries against bumps while letting cold refrigerator air flow straight through the stack. (18), berries reach home kitchens days fresher with far less spoilage.

Packaging waste is a real concern, of course. Because sticky label glue once ruined recycling batches, many producers now stamp product codes directly onto 100% recycled PET lids or test molded-pulp baskets with breathable cellulose windows. (19), shoppers should resist washing berries until right before eating—rinsing them days early traps water between seeds and speeds decay.

Balancing protective airflow with cleaner materials helps farmers and households alike (20).

How Ice Stupas Store Winter Water for Spring Crops

High in the cold desert valleys of Ladakh in northern India, farmers receive less than ten centimeters of rain a year. For centuries, villages depended on summer meltwater trickling down from mountain glaciers to irrigate barley, peas, and apricot trees. As smaller low-altitude glaciers have retreated, however, streams now run dry during critical planting weeks in April and May, only to surge later in July.

Building concrete reservoirs at four thousand meters is costly, and shallow ponds freeze solid or evaporate quickly in fierce high-altitude sun. In 2013, local engineer Sonam Wangchuk tested an ingenious geometric alternative: piping unused winter stream water downhill by gravity and spraying it upward into subzero night air. Freezing as it falls, the spray builds a towering cone of ice thirty meters tall, shaped like a traditional Buddhist monument or stupa. (21), a cone exposes far less surface area to spring sunshine per liter of ice than a flat pond does.

Because of that compact shape, an ice stupa melts slowly throughout April, May, and June—releasing steady trickles of water right when young barley shoots need moisture most. Local youths maintain the pipes without electric pumps, since height difference alone creates water pressure. (22), villages can store millions of liters of winter runoff using simple hardware-store pipes.

Ice stupas cannot replace glacier conservation on a global scale, yet they give mountain communities (23) while adapting to shifting snowmelt seasons.

examples.script:
How Hospital Courtyards Support Recovery

For much of the late twentieth century, hospital architecture prioritized compact efficiency: air-conditioned towers with short walking distances for staff, wipe-clean corridors, and sealed windows. Courtyards and gardens, once common around older infirmaries, were often paved over for parking or extra diagnostic wings. Over the past twenty years, however, medical planners have been bringing greenery back into the heart of hospital buildings—not merely as decoration, but as a practical aid to care.

Interest grew after clinical studies compared patients recovering from similar surgeries in rooms facing trees with those facing blank brick walls. Patients with a view of foliage tended to report less discomfort, sleep more steadily, and transition home slightly sooner. Subsequent research in rehabilitation wards showed that accessible outdoor courtyards motivated patients learning to walk again: reaching a sunlit bench beside seasonal flowers felt like a meaningful goal compared with counting tiles down a fluorescent hallway.

Designing an effective hospital garden requires far more care than planting a public park. Paths must be wide, level, and glare-free so IV poles and wheelchairs roll without jolting. Strongly scented lilies or heavy pollen-producing trees can bother patients sensitive to smells after chemotherapy, so landscape architects favor gentle textures, rustling bamboo, trickling water, and herbs whose fragrance appears only when someone chooses to brush a leaf. Shaded seating pockets also give family members and nurses a quiet five-minute refuge to reset emotionally between difficult conversations.

Skeptics understandably ask whether garden maintenance belongs in tight healthcare budgets. Yet hospitals that track staff turnover and visitor satisfaction increasingly treat well-designed courtyards as shared infrastructure. When nurses have a calm place to step outside on break and patients move more willingly during physical therapy, modest landscaping pays quiet returns across the whole institution.

examples.script:
How Wildlife Overpasses Reconnect Divided Forests

On highway maps, a new four-lane expressway cutting across a mountain range looks like a thin ribbon just thirty meters wide. To deer, bears, badgers, and forest tortoises living on either side, however, unfenced high-speed traffic—or twin rows of tall crash fencing—acts like an impassable concrete canyon. Wildlife biologists studying roads over the past forty years found that slicing one large forest into isolated patches does far more harm than roadkill collisions alone.

Cut off from neighboring valleys, small animal populations lose access to seasonal food—such as low-valley oak acorns in autumn—and begin inbreeding within a few generations, weakening genetic resistance to disease. Early highway engineers tried installing narrow concrete drainage pipes beneath roads, assuming animals would crawl through them. While foxes and raccoons adapted quickly to dark tunnels, cautious grazing mammals such as elk and deer refused to enter cramped spaces where predators might ambush them.

Canada's Banff National Park pioneered a bolder answer in the 1990s along the Trans-Canada Highway: wide, soil-covered "wildlife overpasses" fifty meters broad, planted with native shrubs, pine trees, and log piles so the bridge looks and smells like a continuous forest clearing from an animal's eye level. Low earth berms along the sides block headlight glare and tire roar from trucks passing underneath.

Motion-triggered infrared cameras across Banff's six overpasses and thirty-eight underpasses have recorded more than two hundred thousand safe crossings by grizzlies, wolves, moose, and lynx, slashing large-mammal vehicle collisions by over eighty percent—a major win for human driver safety and auto insurers as well.

Today, countries from the Netherlands and Germany to Japan and the United States build green bridges into new road budgets from the start, proving that transport networks and wildlife corridors can share the same landscape.

How Ferries Cut Fuel Use with Wind Rotor Sails

When people picture wind-powered ships, they usually imagine canvas sails billowing from wooden masts. Modern car ferries and cargo vessels look nothing like nineteenth-century clippers, yet a growing number now carry tall, spinning white cylinders on their decks to capture wind energy alongside regular engines.

These cylinders, known as rotor sails, rely on a physical principle familiar to baseball pitchers and tennis players. When a motor spins the vertical cylinder slowly in a crosswind, air speeds up on one side of the drum and slows down on the other. The resulting pressure difference pushes the ship forward at right angles to the wind. Because the motor spinning the cylinder uses only a tiny fraction of the thrust generated, ferries crossing windy straits can throttle back their main diesel engines. (21), operators on North Sea routes have recorded fuel savings of eight to fifteen percent.

Unlike fabric sails, rotor cylinders require no extra deck crew to hoist or fold when squalls hit; bridge computers adjust rotation speed automatically as wind direction changes. (22), some designs tilt flat onto the deck at the push of a button so the ship can pass safely beneath low harbor bridges.

Rotor sails cannot power a heavy ferry on calm days, nor are they meant to work alone. Rather, combining aerodynamic physics with modern automation gives shipping lines (23) while cleaner fuels are still scaling up.

How Ice Stupas Store Winter Water for Spring Crops

High in the cold desert valleys of Ladakh in northern India, farmers receive less than ten centimeters of rain a year. For centuries, villages depended on summer meltwater trickling down from mountain glaciers to irrigate barley, peas, and apricot trees. As smaller low-altitude glaciers have retreated, however, streams now run dry during critical planting weeks in April and May, only to surge later in July.

Building concrete reservoirs at four thousand meters is costly, and shallow ponds freeze solid or evaporate quickly in fierce high-altitude sun. In 2013, local engineer Sonam Wangchuk tested an ingenious geometric alternative: piping unused winter stream water downhill by gravity and spraying it upward into subzero night air. Freezing as it falls, the spray builds a towering cone of ice thirty meters tall, shaped like a traditional Buddhist monument or stupa. (21), a cone exposes far less surface area to spring sunshine per liter of ice than a flat pond does.

Because of that compact shape, an ice stupa melts slowly throughout April, May, and June—releasing steady trickles of water right when young barley shoots need moisture most. Local youths maintain the pipes without electric pumps, since height difference alone creates water pressure. (22), villages can store millions of liters of winter runoff using simple hardware-store pipes.

Ice stupas cannot replace glacier conservation on a global scale, yet they give mountain communities (23) while adapting to shifting snowmelt seasons.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第12回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Why Traditional Terraced Rice Fields Matter Beyond Harvests

Carved step by step into steep hillsides across Japan, the Philippines, southern China, and Indonesia, stone-and-earth terraced paddies—known in Japanese as tanada—look like shimmering mirrors in May and golden staircases in September. Built by hand over centuries where flat valley land was scarce, many mountain terraces now face abandonment because narrow, curved plots cannot accommodate large ride-on harvesters and aging farming populations find steep stone walls exhausting to maintain.

Judged strictly by tons of rice produced per hour of labor, tiny hillside paddies can never compete with vast laser-leveled plains. Yet hydrologists and municipal planners downstream have begun calculating the hidden public services those stepped fields perform every rainy season. Thousands of low earth bunds act collectively like a staircase of miniature check dams: instead of hurtling down bare slopes in destructive mudslides, typhoon rain pauses briefly in paddy after paddy, filtering slowly into mountain aquifers that feed clear village springs all winter.

Biodiversity thrives in that mosaic of shallow water and stone walls too. Rare frogs, dragonflies, and aquatic beetles that vanished from concrete-lined lowland canals depend on warm, pesticide-light terrace pools to breed, while wild herbs cling to dry stone risers.

Keeping terraces alive requires sharing the burden beyond individual farm households. Across Japan, "tanada ownership" programs invite city families to pay a modest annual fee and join four seasonal weekends—planting seedlings, weeding, harvesting by hand, and sharing freshly steamed rice with veteran farmers. Elsewhere, chefs pay premium prices for mineral-rich mountain-spring rice, and rural towns train young volunteers in dry-stone wall repair.

Preserving terraced hillsides is not mere nostalgia; it sustains living green infrastructure that protects valleys and culture together.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第15回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
How Roman Aqueducts Moved Water by Gravity Alone

Postcard photos of ancient Roman engineering almost always feature soaring multi-tiered stone arches—like the Pont du Gard in southern France or the Aqueduct of Segovia in Spain—striding dramatically across sunlit river valleys. Looking at those monumental bridges, casual travelers often assume Roman aqueducts ran entirely above ground on stone stilts. In reality, arches made up less than ten percent of most aqueduct routes; the other ninety percent wound invisibly through stone-lined channels buried half a meter to several meters underground.

Keeping channels underground made practical sense: buried conduits stayed cool, resisted evaporation, kept dirt and grazing animals out of drinking water, and required far less quarried stone than tall arches. What made Roman hydraulic engineering extraordinary was that the entire fifty- or eighty-kilometer journey from mountain spring to city fountain relied solely on gravity, without a single mechanical pump.

Surveyors had to maintain an almost imperceptibly gentle downward slope—often dropping just fifteen to thirty centimeters per kilometer, or less than the thickness of a textbook over the length of a soccer field. Too steep a gradient turned flowing water into a scouring torrent that eroded mortar walls; too flat a channel let stagnant pools deposit silt.

Without spirit levels or laser sights, Roman engineers used a wooden T-shaped instrument called a chorobates: a six-meter beam fitted with plumb bobs on its legs and a shallow water trough carved along its top to judge true horizontal even on windy hillsides. Where a deep valley blocked the path, arches carried the channel level across; where a ridge intervened, miners chiseled straight tunnels guided by vertical air shafts.

Delivering millions of liters daily to public baths, street fountains, and workshops, gravity-fed aqueducts sustained urban populations rarely matched again in Europe until the nineteenth century.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第3回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Recipes Sometimes Fail at High Altitude

Travelers staying in a mountain cabin two thousand meters above sea level are often puzzled when a familiar family recipe turns out strangely. Spaghetti takes longer to soften in boiling water, while a sponge cake that rises beautifully near the coast may puff up too fast in the oven and then collapse in the middle.

The cause is lower atmospheric pressure. At sea level, the weight of the air above pushes down on a pot of water, keeping molecules in liquid form until the temperature reaches 100 degrees Celsius. High in the mountains, thinner air exerts less pressure, so water begins boiling at around 93 degrees. Turning up the stove flame only produces more steam; it cannot make the boiling water any hotter. (21), foods cooked by boiling simply need extra minutes to finish.

Baking involves the same physics in reverse. Bubbles of steam and gas inside cake batter expand more forcefully when external air pressure is weak. Before the flour and eggs have time to set into a firm structure, the batter stretches too thin and sinks. Experienced mountain bakers compensate by reducing leavening powder slightly and raising oven temperature a little so the structure firms up sooner. (22), adding a spoonful of extra liquid prevents the batter from drying out in thin, dry mountain air.

Understanding these adjustments turns kitchen frustration into a practical science lesson. A recipe written in a coastal city assumes invisible environmental conditions. Once cooks recognize (23), they can adapt their methods confidently wherever they travel.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第11回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
How Bamboo Scaffolding Still Rises Around High-Rise Towers

Visitors stepping onto the streets of Hong Kong for the first time often look up in disbelief: encasing forty-story glass skyscrapers are intricate lattices of golden bamboo poles lashed together with black nylon strips. In an era of steel cranes and aluminum frames, traditional bamboo scaffolding remains a thriving engineering craft.

Speed, weight, and flexibility explain bamboo's staying power in dense subtropical cities. Thick giant-timber bamboo stalks weigh a fraction as much as steel pipes yet boast remarkable tensile strength along their hollow fibers. Experienced scaffolders carry bundles easily up narrow stairwells and tie custom grids around irregular balconies or curved neon signs without welding or heavy bolts. (21), a skilled crew can wrap a mid-rise facade far faster and at lower cost than with rigid metal tubing.

Typhoon winds reveal another surprising advantage. Whereas rigid steel frames can transmit violent gusts into building anchors or snap suddenly, properly braced bamboo flexes slightly with the wind to absorb energy. Safety standards are far from casual, however: Hong Kong building codes specify pole thickness, curing age, steel wall-anchors, and formal apprenticeships. (22), many modern projects use a hybrid approach—steel brackets at the base supporting bamboo lattices above.

Combining renewable fast-growing grass with rigorous safety engineering shows that traditional materials can (23).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第13回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Coin Edges Have Tiny Vertical Ridges

Run your fingernail around the rim of a hundred-yen or fifty-yen coin—or an American quarter or dime—and you feel dozens of crisp vertical grooves, whereas ten-yen and five-yen coins feel completely smooth. Cashiers and vending-machine engineers appreciate that texture today, yet "reeded edges" were invented more than three centuries ago to stop a widespread financial crime.

In seventeenth-century Europe, high-value coins were struck from pure silver or gold whose metal was worth exactly the face value stamped on the coin. Dishonest traders took advantage of soft precious metals by "clipping"—shaving tiny slivers of silver off the irregular edges of hundreds of coins before spending them at full value and melting the scraps into bullion bars. Over time, clipped coins grew noticeably smaller and lighter, undermining trust in everyday commerce. (18), Britain's Royal Mint—guided in the 1690s by warden Isaac Newton—introduced collar dies that stamped uniform grooves around every silver and gold coin's circumference.

With milled ridges in place, shaving even half a millimeter off a coin's rim immediately erased the grooves and exposed the tampering at a glance. Modern coins use cupronickel alloys rather than pure silver, so clipping for bullion is long gone. (19), reeded edges remain invaluable because they let blind and visually impaired shoppers distinguish denominations instantly by touch inside a purse.

Tiny ridges around a coin show how an anti-counterfeiting fix evolved into (20).

examples.script:
Why Repair Instructions Matter Before You Buy

When consumers shop for a toaster, a desk fan, or a cordless vacuum cleaner, they usually compare price, weight, and battery life. Rarely do they ask what will happen three years later when a switch wears out or a battery loses strength. Yet millions of small household appliances are discarded every year not because their motors have failed, but because replacing a single inexpensive part requires special tools or sealed cases cannot be opened safely.

In response, several consumer groups and regional governments have introduced "repairability scores" displayed right beside product prices in electronics stores. Instead of giving a vague environmental badge, the score rates five concrete factors from one to ten: how easily a product can be taken apart, whether spare parts are sold to the public, how many years those parts remain available, how much they cost relative to a new machine, and whether clear repair manuals can be downloaded for free.

When the scoring system first appeared, some manufacturers argued that shoppers cared only about low upfront prices and would ignore technical ratings. Early retail data suggested otherwise. Even customers who never intended to use a screwdriver themselves began choosing models with higher scores, viewing repairability as a sign of honest engineering and long-term durability.

More importantly, the visibility of low scores prompted manufacturers to change design habits before products ever reached store shelves. Engineers replaced glue with standard screws in several popular appliances and published step-by-step part diagrams online. A company might willingly tolerate a complaint buried in customer service emails, whereas a low number printed on every price tag directly affected sales.

Specialists caution that a label alone does not guarantee fewer discarded appliances. Local repair shops still need affordable parts and trained technicians, and consumers may still replace working machines when new features look appealing. Even so, making repair information visible at the moment of purchase shifts attention from how cheaply an item is made to how responsibly it can be kept in use.

examples.script:
Why Mapmakers Deliberately Straightened Subway Lines

Early transit maps of major cities in the 1910s and 1920s tried faithfully to show every twist of a railway line atop an accurate street map. As networks expanded, however, the results became nearly unreadable. Central business districts were crammed with tiny overlapping station names, while long suburban branches stretched off the edges of pocket folders.

In 1931, an electrical engineering draftsman named Harry Beck noticed something crucial while sketching London's Underground during a layoff. Once passengers descend beneath the pavement, they cannot see curving streets or rivers anyway; what they really need to know is which line to board, how many stops remain, and where two lines intersect. Drawing inspiration from electrical circuit diagrams—where wires are arranged neatly at horizontal, vertical, and forty-five-degree angles regardless of physical length—Beck compressed distant suburbs and enlarged the crowded center.

Transit managers initially rejected Beck's draft as too radical, fearing riders would misjudge walking distances on the surface. When the Underground printed a small trial run in 1933, however, commuters embraced its clarity immediately. Within decades, Tokyo, Paris, New York, and Sydney adopted similar schematic diagrams.

The trade-off managers worried about never completely vanished, though. Tourists consulting a schematic subway diagram sometimes take two train transfers to travel between stations that sit just four hundred meters apart above ground. To bridge this gap, several modern transit apps and station boards now blend both worlds—keeping clean geometric lines while adding dotted ten-minute walking arcs or subtle river contours.

Beck's insight remains a classic lesson in information design: leaving out geographic detail that does not serve the user's immediate task can make complex systems far easier to navigate.

examples.script:
How Seed Vaults Keep Crop Diversity Alive Underground

Walk through a modern supermarket, and the fruit and vegetable section looks wonderfully varied. Yet agricultural historians point out a quiet vulnerability behind that colorful display: globally, just nine plant species account for nearly two-thirds of all crop production, and farmers within each crop increasingly plant a handful of high-yielding commercial varieties. While uniform crops simplify harvesting and transport, genetic uniformity carries risk. If a new fungal disease or prolonged drought strikes a widely planted wheat or potato variety, entire regions can lose harvests simultaneously.

Over previous centuries, peasant farmers maintained thousands of local "landrace" varieties—grains and beans adapted to salty coastal soil, high mountain frost, or short desert rains. When farms switch to modern commercial seeds, those hardy older varieties can vanish within a single generation unless someone preserves viable seeds.

That is the mission of over a thousand seed banks worldwide, backed up by the Svalbard Global Seed Vault deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway. Sealed in moisture-proof foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, orthodox seeds such as wheat, rice, and lentils slow their metabolism so dramatically that they remain capable of sprouting for decades or even centuries. Permafrost surrounding the Arctic rock tunnel provides natural refrigeration even if external power temporarily fails.

Even the coldest vault is not a "set-and-forget" museum, however. Seeds slowly lose vigor over time and must periodically be thawed, planted in soil, harvested fresh, and frozen anew. Moreover, tropical crops with moist, fleshy seeds—such as cacao, mango, and avocado—cannot survive standard freezing at all; scientists preserve their diversity in living field collections or ultra-cold liquid nitrogen.

Safeguarding ancient seeds is ultimately forward-looking work: traits hidden in an obscure mountain grain today may hold the exact drought resistance breeders need fifty years from now.

Instructions for Participating in the River Salmon Fry Release

From: Kitagawa Watershed Conservation Association
To: Registered Families and High School Volunteers
Subject: Bucket acclimatization rule for Sunday's salmon fry release

Dear participants,
Thank you for joining our annual chum salmon fry release at Kitagawa River Park this Sunday at 10:00 a.m.! Over the winter, student volunteers tended fertilized eggs in chilled hatchery trays, and twelve thousand five-centimeter young salmon are now ready to begin their journey to the Pacific.

When you receive your small plastic bucket of fry at the riverside tent, please do NOT pour the fish straight into the river right away. Hatchery tank water is nine degrees Celsius, whereas sunlit river shallows may be three degrees warmer or cooler; a sudden temperature shock stuns tiny fish and leaves them vulnerable to birds.

Instead, crouch safely at the gravel edge, dip half your bucket into the river to mix river water in gradually over two minutes, and then tilt the rim gently underwater so the fry swim out on their own. Life jackets will be lent to all children under twelve.

Kitagawa Conservation Staff

Guidelines for Borrowing Roof-Snow Measurement Kits

From: Kitano Town Winter Safety Division
To: Neighborhood Association Snow Wardens
Subject: Calibrating borrowed snow-core tubes before December patrols

Dear Snow Wardens,
Thank you for volunteering to monitor roof-snow loads on elderly residents' homes this winter. Measuring snow depth with a ruler alone can be dangerously misleading: forty centimeters of fluffy January powder weighs far less than forty centimeters of rain-soaked February pack, which can quietly overload older timber rafters.

Starting Monday, each district warden may pick up a lightweight aluminum snow-core tube and hanging spring scale at Town Hall Annex Room 104. Push the hollow tube straight down to the roof eaves marker, lift out a vertical cylinder of snow, and weigh it on the hook scale to read water-equivalent load in kilograms per square meter.

Before every morning patrol, hang the empty dry tube on the scale and turn the top brass ring until the pointer reads exactly zero; trapped ice inside the barrel will inflate readings. Please log figures on the shared tablet form by noon.

Winter Safety Division

examples.script:
When fewer messages are not better

A housing association introduced an online repair form to reduce the time staff spent answering telephone calls. After three months, calls had fallen sharply, and managers initially described the change as a success. A maintenance worker, however, noticed that some serious problems were reaching the repair team later than before. Interviews suggested that residents sometimes abandoned the form because it required them to identify the technical category of a fault. They could describe a leaking ceiling but did not know which category to choose. The association simplified the form and restored a clearly advertised telephone option. Calls increased again, but fewer urgent repairs were reported late. The form had still saved staff time on routine requests. What changed was the measure of success: managers began examining how quickly problems reached the appropriate team, rather than treating every avoided call as a benefit.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第10回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Why Museums Control Light Exposure with Strict "Lux Budgets"

Step from a sunlit sculpture court into a gallery displaying Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints, medieval illuminated manuscripts, or nineteenth-century watercolor landscapes, and the room can feel surprisingly dim—almost like twilight. Visitors occasionally wonder whether the museum is cutting electricity costs. Conservators have a far more urgent motive: light itself is an invisible chemical force that permanently fades organic pigments and weakens paper fibers.

Unlike oil paintings on canvas or glazed ceramics—whose mineral pigments locked in linseed oil or glass tolerate moderate museum lighting well—plant dyes, insect inks, silk threads, and watercolor washes contain fragile molecular bonds. Photons of light, especially high-energy ultraviolet rays and blue wavelengths, snap those bonds one by one. Worse still, photochemical damage is strictly cumulative and irreversible: exposing a delicate Hiroshige print to bright gallery lamps for one week causes roughly the same fading as ten weeks under lamps one-tenth as bright, and no rest in a dark vault afterward can bring lost blues or purples back.

To balance public enjoyment today against preservation for centuries ahead, major museums manage fragile works under an annual "lux-hour budget." Illuminance is capped at just fifty lux—roughly a fifth of normal office brightness—with all ultraviolet filtered out. Curators also track how many hours each print spends on display; once a work reaches its yearly allowance, say three months, it returns to dark climate-controlled storage while a companion print takes its place.

Modern LEDs free of ultraviolet heat, paired with motion sensors or velvet curtains that visitors lift briefly inside display cases, stretch those precious light budgets further than ever.

Dim rooms and rotating exhibitions may test a visitor's patience, yet they ensure our grandchildren will still see the artist's original colors rather than pale ghosts.

examples.script:
Why Escalators and Stairs Use Contrasting Step Edges

Commuters hurrying through brightly lit rail stations rarely notice the narrow yellow or metallic strip running along the front edge of every stair and escalator step. Often mistaken for simple trim or anti-slip tape alone, these high-contrast strips—known in accessibility codes as step nosings—play a vital perceptual role in preventing falls.

When an entire staircase is built from uniform gray granite or stainless steel, overhead lighting can make adjacent steps blend visually into a single flat ramp, especially for older adults, tired evening travelers, or people with low vision. Descending stairs requires the brain to judge the exact drop and forward edge of the top and bottom steps within a fraction of a second. Marking each edge with a band whose brightness differs sharply from the tread surface breaks that optical illusion. (18), walkers place their heels more accurately without slowing down.

Color choice matters more than decoration. Pale beige strips on light limestone look stylish in architectural photos, yet offer almost no luminance contrast under cloudy skylight. Building guidelines therefore measure light reflectance values rather than hue alone, ensuring the strip remains distinct even in dim emergency lighting. (19), embedding gritty mineral particles into the nosing strip adds traction right where shoe soles pivot.

Combining visual clarity with physical grip demonstrates how inclusive design (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第8回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
How Salt Marshes Protect Coasts and Store Carbon

For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, tidal salt marshes—low coastal grasslands flooded twice daily by seawater—were dismissed by planners as muddy wasteland. Across Europe, East Asia, and North America, thousands of hectares were drained behind dikes to create pasture, factory sites, or port landfills.

Only after costly storm surges battered reclaimed shorelines did engineers measure what had been lost. Dense mats of salt-tolerant cordgrass and rushes act like a giant natural sponge and brake: friction from millions of flexible stems slows incoming storm waves and lowers flood peaks before water reaches inland homes. Unlike rigid concrete walls, healthy marshes trap river sediment on every tide, allowing the ground surface to build upward gradually over decades. (21), coastal towns behind wide marshes often spend far less on seawall repairs.

Climate researchers uncovered a second superpower hidden in the mud below. On land, fallen forest leaves decompose in oxygen-rich soil and release most of their carbon back into the air within years. Waterlogged marsh mud contains almost no oxygen, however, slowing microbial decay to a crawl. Dead marsh roots accumulate in thick peat layers meters deep, locking carbon away for centuries—a process scientists call "blue carbon." (22), restoring breached dikes to let tides return revives nursery habitats for young flounder and crabs.

Protecting surviving tidal marshes is therefore no luxury; it represents (23).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第15回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Concert Pianists Care About Bench Height

Watch a solo pianist walk onstage before a concerto, and you may see the performer spend thirty seconds turning dual side knobs on the padded bench—testing a single chord, rising slightly, and adjusting the seat by barely half a centimeter before nodding to the conductor. Audience members sometimes read this ritual as nervous perfectionism, yet biomechanics specialists say millimeter changes in bench height transform both tone production and injury risk.

Unlike typing at an office laptop, playing grand-piano repertoire demands transferring upper-body weight fluidly through relaxed shoulders, forearms, and finger pads into eighty-eight weighted wooden keys. If a bench sits two centimeters too low, a pianist must shrug the shoulders upward or bend the wrists below key level, choking leverage during thunderous chords and straining forearm tendons over two-hour programs. (18), perching too high forces the player to hunch forward, tiring lower-back muscles and making delicate soft passages harder to control.

Pedal geometry complicates the equation further. Taller pianists with long legs often push the bench slightly farther back from the keyboard so their right ankle can pivot smoothly on the damper pedal without cramping, which in turn changes elbow angles at the keys. Backstage technicians at major halls therefore keep numbered hydraulic or screw benches logged by artist preference. (19), traveling soloists who play different pianos every week carry a pocket tape measure to match seat-to-key distance precisely.

Those quiet turns of a bench knob before the first note show how musical artistry (20).

examples.script:
Rethinking How Cities Measure Bus Punctuality

Most city bus networks judge their performance by a familiar standard: whether each bus arrives at stops at the exact minute printed on the timetable. On quiet suburban routes that run twice an hour, this measure makes complete sense. Missing the 9:10 bus means waiting thirty minutes in the cold, so passengers check the clock before leaving home.

On busy urban corridors where buses are scheduled every five or six minutes, however, passengers behave differently. Commuters rarely consult a timetable; they simply walk to the stop expecting a bus to appear shortly. Yet heavy traffic frequently causes a frustrating pattern known as "bus bunching." If one bus is delayed for ninety seconds by a delivery van, slightly more passengers gather at the next stop. Boarding takes longer, delaying that bus further, while the following bus encounters almost empty stops and catches up. Soon two or three buses travel nose to tail, followed by a fifteen-minute gap.

Curiously, under traditional punctuality rules, an operator could try to keep drivers tied to fixed clock times even after traffic disrupted the pattern, or penalize drivers who paused briefly to restore spacing. When transit planners in Harborview analyzed passenger complaints, they realized riders on high-frequency routes did not care which specific bus they boarded; they cared about how long they waited on the sidewalk.

Harborview subsequently switched its evaluation of six-minute routes from timetable adherence to "headway regularity," which means keeping the time interval between consecutive buses steady. Dispatchers gained authority to ask an ahead-of-schedule bus to wait forty seconds at a transfer hub so a gap would not widen downstream. Digital signs at stops also began showing "Every 6 minutes" alongside live countdowns rather than long lists of clock times.

Average waiting times fell by nearly twenty percent without adding extra vehicles or drivers. Nevertheless, transit specialists note that headway management works only when routes are frequent and dispatchers communicate clearly with passengers on board; nobody likes sitting at a stop for forty seconds unless the driver explains why. Choosing the right metric, they conclude, depends on matching measurement to how passengers actually experience a journey.

examples.script:
Our centre used less electricity this summer than last summer. This may sound like evidence that the new lights saved a great deal of energy. However, the centre was also closed for two weeks, and the weather was cooler. We will compare electricity use during similar opening hours before estimating the contribution of the lights. This does not mean the lights were ineffective; it means the total reduction cannot all be attributed to them yet.
Question. Why is the speaker delaying a conclusion about the lights?
examples.translation: センターの今年の夏の電力使用量は昨夏より減りました。新しい照明が大きく節電した証拠に思えるかもしれません。しかし、2週間の休館もあり、気温も低めでした。照明の効果を見積もる前に、開館時間が似た条件での使用量を比べます。照明が無効だったという意味ではなく、減少分の全てをまだ照明に帰することはできないという意味です。

examples.script:
The Value of an Unfinished List

A coastal town began recording the wildlife found in its public gardens. Volunteers were asked to photograph insects and upload their observations to a shared website. The project attracted many enthusiastic participants, and its first map appeared to show that the central park had far more kinds of insects than any other garden. Some officials suggested concentrating future planting there.

A coordinator examined the observation records more carefully. The central park was close to a bus stop and had a popular cafe, so volunteers visited it frequently. Several smaller gardens had been visited only once. The map therefore reflected not only where insects lived but also (21). Treating every blank area on the map as an absence of wildlife would have been misleading.

The coordinator arranged visits to the less popular gardens and asked participants to spend a similar amount of time at each location. Specialists helped check photographs of insects that were difficult to identify. The revised map still had gaps, but the team marked these openly rather than filling them with guesses. (22), users could distinguish between an area where few insects had been seen and an area that had not yet been studied adequately.

The town eventually used the record to plan a wider network of flowering plants across its gardens. It did not wait until the list contained every possible species. Nevertheless, officials learned to treat the map as a developing source of evidence, not a complete picture. The project's usefulness depended on (23). A visually impressive map was valuable only if its limits were understood.

examples.script:
When Soil Microbes Leave Clues for Archaeologists

Archaeologists searching for ancient timber buildings often face a frustrating reality: in damp, mild climates, wooden posts rot away completely within centuries, leaving neither stone walls nor brick foundations behind. Traditionally, excavators locate vanished halls by scraping away topsoil and looking for faint dark circles—known as postholes—where decayed wood stained the earth.

Visual stains, however, can be hard to distinguish from animal burrows or tree roots. Recently, geoarchaeologists have begun analyzing the DNA and chemical traces of soil bacteria living in buried layers. Centuries of human or livestock activity alter soil phosphorus, acidity, and organic matter in lasting ways. Even two thousand years after a wooden stable disappeared, the microbial community thriving in that patch of dirt differs measurably from the microbes three meters outside the wall. (21), researchers can tell whether a vanished room once housed cattle, stored grain, or served as a clean sleeping area.

Sampling tiny cores of soil with a hand auger also protects fragile sites. Rather than digging wide trenches across an entire meadow, teams test small pinprick samples first to map where activity was concentrated. (22), full excavation can be limited to the corners most likely to answer historical questions.

Microbial mapping does not replace trowels and pottery analysis, of course. Still, reading living microscopic ecosystems allows archaeologists to (23) long after timber walls have turned back to dust.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第2回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Notice Regarding the Archive Digitization Project

From: Marcus Vance, Head Archivist
To: Part-Time Scanning Assistants
Subject: Updated procedures for the newspaper collection

Dear assistants,
Thank you for your steady work digitizing our nineteenth-century town newspapers. Over the past month, our online archive has already been used by local high schools and historical researchers. As we move on to the older 1870–1885 volumes next Monday, we need to adjust two workflow rules to protect fragile paper.

First, please stop using the automatic sheet feeder completely. Even single pages from the 1870s are brittle along the margins and may tear if pulled by rollers. Every page must be placed by hand onto the overhead flatbed camera. This will reduce the number of pages scanned per hour, so we have removed the daily page target that applied last month. Quality and preservation take priority over speed.

Second, when an article contains faded ink that optical software cannot read reliably, please mark the file with the tag "MANUAL-CHECK" rather than guessing the missing words yourself. Our senior historians will review flagged pages every Thursday.

White cotton gloves turned out to reduce finger sensitivity and actually caused more accidental creases, so please wash and dry your hands thoroughly before each shift instead of wearing gloves. Let me know if you need training on the overhead camera before Monday.

Sincerely,
Marcus Vance

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第1回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Who Benefits from a Quieter Street?

Reducing traffic on a residential street may seem an uncomplicated improvement. Fewer vehicles can mean less noise, cleaner air, and more space for people walking or cycling. Yet the evaluation of a traffic scheme depends on where its boundaries are drawn. A street that becomes quieter may sit beside another that receives the diverted vehicles. An assessment limited to the first street can therefore tell a convincing but incomplete story.

Suppose a district introduces barriers that prevent through-traffic from using several residential roads. Initial monitoring shows a sharp decline in vehicles inside the area. Residents living near the barriers report that children can cross more easily and that conversations are no longer interrupted by engine noise. These are genuine benefits, not merely perceptions to be dismissed. However, residents along the main roads outside the area report longer queues. They question why their experience is absent from the first evaluation.

One response is to enlarge the monitoring area. This is necessary, but a larger average alone may still obscure important differences. If a substantial improvement for several thousand people outweighs a smaller deterioration for a few hundred, the overall figure may look favorable. That calculation does not by itself establish whether the distribution of costs is acceptable, especially if those facing deterioration already experience the greatest pollution. Choosing a measurement boundary is therefore not a neutral substitute for considering fairness.

Timing introduces another complication. Drivers may initially follow familiar routes and later change their journey, travel at another hour, or choose another means of transport. The first week may consequently exaggerate permanent disruption. Conversely, waiting for people to adapt cannot justify disregarding persistent problems indefinitely. An evaluation should state in advance when it will be repeated and which findings would trigger a change. Otherwise, every unfavorable result can be described as temporary and every favorable result as final.

A credible process combines measurements with ways for affected people to challenge the interpretation. Residents may identify a school entrance that monitors have missed or explain why a supposedly convenient alternative route is unusable for someone with limited mobility. Their accounts do not replace traffic counts, but they can reveal what the counts fail to capture.

The choice is not simply between accepting every scheme and rejecting any scheme with uneven effects. It is between treating evaluation as a defense of a completed decision and using it to revise that decision. A project can retain its original aims while adding protection for neighboring roads, adjusting delivery access, or removing a barrier that causes disproportionate harm. A quieter street is worth pursuing, but the claim of success becomes stronger when it accounts for people beyond that street.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第2回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Negative Scientific Results Deserve Publication

Pick up almost any prominent scientific journal and you will read predominantly about experiments that worked: a compound that slowed disease progression in mice, a teaching intervention that raised test scores, or a catalyst that accelerated a chemical reaction. Studies in which a plausible hypothesis produced no statistically meaningful effect are far more likely to remain unpublished in laboratory drawers, a phenomenon methodologists call the "file-drawer problem."

This publication pattern rarely stems from deliberate dishonesty. Journals compete for attention and citations, editors favor striking breakthroughs, and researchers under career pressure understandably prioritize manuscripts with a high chance of acceptance. Writing up a rigorous null result takes nearly as much time as writing up a positive discovery, yet brings far less professional recognition. Individual incentives therefore align to filter out negative findings.

The collective cost to science, however, is substantial. When five independent laboratories test the same promising idea and four find no effect while one obtains a positive result by chance, publishing only the fifth study creates a distorted impression of effectiveness. Other teams may then spend years and public grant money repeating dead-end experiments they had no way of knowing had already failed. Worse still, clinical or policy reviews that pool published studies risk overestimating the benefits of an intervention.

One promising reform is the "registered report." Under this format, peer reviewers evaluate a study's research question, sample size, and experimental protocol before data are collected. If the design is sound and the question important, the journal commits in principle to publishing the paper regardless of how the numbers turn out, provided the researchers follow the approved plan. Early evaluations suggest that registered reports contain a much higher proportion of null findings than conventional journals while maintaining high methodological quality.

Registered reports do not suit purely exploratory research where methods evolve mid-experiment, nor do they eliminate the need for replication. Yet they address a structural flaw that exhortations to individual virtue cannot fix alone: shifting prestige from whether a result looks dramatic to whether an investigation was worth conducting and carefully executed.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第3回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
When Regional Dialects Enter Civic Services

Standardized national languages have historically simplified administration, schooling, and interregional commerce. Yet in regions where distinct dialects or minority varieties remain woven into everyday family life, conducting all public services exclusively in the standard form can create subtle barriers that officials rarely notice. Over the past two decades, hospitals, courts, and emergency hotlines in several countries have begun reassessing how local speech varieties function in high-stakes interactions.

Medical consultations illustrate why informal fluency matters. Older patients who read national broadcasts effortlessly may still describe pain intensity, dizziness, or emotional distress using regional idioms that lack one-to-one equivalents in textbook phrasing. When clinicians unfamiliar with local usage ask patients to "state symptoms plainly," speakers often shorten their explanations out of embarrassment, omitting timing or severity cues critical to diagnosis. Recruiting staff able to understand regional speech—or training practitioners in common local expressions—has improved history-taking accuracy without abandoning standard clinical records.

Skeptics sometimes worry that accommodating regional varieties in public offices will fragment civic cohesion or trap young speakers outside national labor markets. Experience from bilingual and bidialectal school programs suggests that this fear rests on a false choice. Students taught explicitly how local grammar differs from the standard register typically master formal writing more confidently than peers whose home speech is dismissed as careless slang. Naming the contrast turns unconscious habit into deliberate stylistic control.

Civic recognition also carries practical resilience benefits during disasters. Weather warnings or evacuation instructions delivered partly in trusted local phrasing often reach elderly residents faster than stiff bureaucratic bulletins, yet they work best when paired with unambiguous written maps and standard terminology for outside rescue teams. Rather than pitting regional speech against national intelligibility, effective public institutions treat repertoire—knowing when each register serves clarity—as a civic asset.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第1回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Learning from a Pilot Without Copying It

A successful pilot project is often presented as a miniature version of a future policy. If a service works for a small group, expanding it appears to be a matter of securing enough money and reproducing the same arrangement elsewhere. This picture is appealing to decision-makers because it turns uncertainty into an apparently manageable problem of scale. Unfortunately, the conditions that make a pilot succeed may be precisely those that cannot be reproduced simply by increasing its budget.

Consider a pilot designed to help residents navigate complicated housing applications. A small team operates from a familiar community center, and its coordinator has long-standing relationships with both local families and officials. Staff can telephone a particular official to clarify an unusual case, and residents who distrust formal agencies may approach the coordinator because a neighbor recommends her. None of these features is captured by a description that says only "advice provided at a local center."

When the service is expanded, new offices may be established quickly, but relationships take time. The original coordinator may also have exercised considerable judgment about which rules could be interpreted flexibly and which required strict compliance. A standardized handbook can preserve some of this knowledge, but not necessarily the ability to recognize a new situation. If policymakers copy only the visible procedure, they may reproduce its appearance while losing the mechanisms that made it effective.

This does not render pilots useless. Rather, it changes what should be learned from them. Evaluation needs to identify not only whether an outcome improved but also how the improvement occurred. Were staff reducing delays because they simplified paperwork, because they knew whom to contact, or because the pilot received exceptional attention from senior officials? These explanations imply different prospects for expansion. A process that depends on an unusual level of senior attention may be harder to sustain than one based on a broadly applicable change in application forms.

There is also a danger in selecting only the most enthusiastic communities for a pilot and then treating their results as representative. Such communities may contribute unpaid labor, adapt buildings, or solve problems informally. These contributions can be legitimate strengths of the pilot, but they should not disappear from the account of its costs. Expansion to areas without the same resources may require additional funding or a different design.

A useful next step may therefore be a deliberately varied second trial, rather than immediate nationwide adoption. This trial can test the service in places with different staffing, relationships, and levels of local support. Some adaptations should be permitted, provided the essential mechanism and the reason for each change are documented. Uniformity of every visible detail is not the same as fidelity to the project's purpose.

Ultimately, the most responsible claim for a pilot is rarely that it has eliminated uncertainty. It has made certain assumptions more testable and exposed conditions that deserve attention. Policymakers can then decide which elements should be preserved, which require investment, and which must change. Scaling a project intelligently is a process of learning across settings, not transporting a finished object from one place to another.

examples.script:
A Standard Is Not a Setting

When a public agency purchases a digital service, adopting a technical standard can appear to resolve the question of accessibility. A supplier certifies that its product complies, the certificate is filed, and the agency proceeds with installation. Standards are indispensable because they establish common expectations that would otherwise have to be negotiated separately for every purchase. However, a certificate describes a product under specified conditions, not every future interaction between that product and its users.

Imagine a booking system that works correctly when tested in isolation. During installation, an agency adds a short time limit, requires documents available only as scanned images, and places essential instructions on another website. Each decision may seem administratively convenient. Taken together, they can create obstacles that were absent from the original test. A compliant product has not necessarily produced (22).

User testing after installation is therefore essential, but it must be organized carefully. Inviting only experienced staff to complete familiar tasks is unlikely to reveal the difficulties faced by someone using assistive technology or encountering the process for the first time. Agencies need feedback from people whose circumstances differ, and a procedure for acting on that feedback. (23), collecting complaints without assigning responsibility for resolving them merely documents exclusion rather than reducing it.

This does not mean that technical standards should be discarded. They provide a necessary baseline and make suppliers accountable for features within their control. The problem arises when meeting a baseline is treated as the end of the agency's responsibility. Accessibility is sustained through procurement, configuration, testing, and maintenance. An effective approach consequently requires agencies to (24), rather than regard accessibility as a property that can be purchased once and then forgotten.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第5回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
When Municipal Procurement Shapes Green Markets

Discussions of environmental policy usually spotlight household choices—carrying reusable bags, sorting bottles, or turning down thermostats—alongside national taxes and regulations. Between individual shoppers and lawmakers, however, sits an economic actor whose routine purchasing decisions quietly steer entire industries: public procurement. Across most industrialized nations, central ministries, cities, public hospitals, and school districts spend between twelve and twenty percent of gross domestic product buying everything from concrete and streetlamps to school meals and fleet vehicles.

For emerging low-carbon technologies, the hardest barrier is rarely laboratory invention; it is crossing the commercial gap between costly small-batch prototypes and affordable mass production. Private contractors understandably hesitate to retool a cement plant or electrify heavy refuse trucks if customer demand looks uncertain. When a coalition of cities commits to buying low-clinker concrete for bridge decks over five years, suppliers gain the predictable order book needed to finance new kilns and train crews, driving unit costs down for private builders as well.

Using public tenders to encourage innovation requires careful contract design, though. Traditional bidding rules often specify exact materials and award contracts solely to the lowest upfront price—a formula that locks in familiar high-emission products even when cleaner alternatives cost less to run over twenty years. Conversely, writing specifications around a single patented process risks shutting out rival approaches and inflating taxpayer bills. Forward-looking agencies therefore set performance outcomes—such as maximum embodied carbon per square meter or lifetime energy consumption—and let competing engineers propose how best to meet them.

Verifying those claims demands administrative capacity that small towns rarely possess alone. Regional purchasing consortia and standardized third-party environmental product declarations have become crucial, allowing rural school boards and clinics to apply rigorous lifecycle criteria without hiring specialist engineers of their own.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第8回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
The Subtle Pitfalls of Algorithmic Dynamic Pricing

Airlines and hotels have adjusted fares according to season and remaining capacity for half a century; travelers readily accept that a beach room costs more in August than in rainy November, or that booking a seat the night before departure carries a premium. Powered by real-time inventory software and electronic shelf labels, however, rapid "dynamic pricing" has begun spreading into everyday arenas—from commuter toll lanes and ride-hailing apps to concert tickets, restaurant menus, and even neighborhood supermarkets.

In textbook microeconomics, flexible prices allocate scarce goods efficiently. Raising ride-hail fares during a Friday downpour entices off-duty drivers onto the streets while nudging price-sensitive riders with umbrellas toward the subway, shrinking wait times for people with urgent trips. Similarly, automated markdowns on yogurt or fish approaching its sell-by date at seven p.m. curb food waste while rewarding thrifty evening shoppers.

Yet behavioral economists warn that treating every consumer transaction like a live stock exchange overlooks how deeply long-term retail relationships depend on perceived fairness. In classic surveys pioneered by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues, respondents judged it acceptable for a hardware store to discontinue a seasonal discount when snow shovels ran low, yet overwhelmingly condemned raising the regular price of shovels the morning after a blizzard. Consumers distinguish sharply between rationing scarce luxuries and exploiting sudden necessity.

Opaque algorithms compound that resentment when prices jump unpredictably within minutes or appear personalized to a shopper's battery level or postcode. Firms chasing short-term surge revenue in staple goods have repeatedly suffered reputational backlashes far costlier than the extra margin earned on a busy afternoon. Smart pricing design therefore pairs transparency and clear upper caps with genuine customer value—using discounts to smooth off-peak demand rather than ambushing captive buyers.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 長文読解練習（基礎ウォームアップ・2本文・計4問）
examples.script:
An appeal that was available only on paper

A regional agency began using a scoring tool to prioritise applications for home adaptations. Applicants could request a review if they believed the score overlooked their circumstances. The agency described this review process as a safeguard, pointing to the existence of an appeal form. An independent evaluation found, however, that applicants were given only their overall score, not the factors that had produced it. Someone could suspect an error without knowing what evidence would correct it. The evaluators did not recommend disclosing every technical detail of the software. Instead, they proposed giving applicants a concise explanation of the relevant factors, access to the information recorded about them, and a named contact who could amend factual mistakes. The distinction was important: transparency was being treated not as the release of the largest possible quantity of information, but as support for a meaningful opportunity to challenge a decision. After a pilot, more appeals identified verifiable errors, although the total number of appeals changed little. The evaluation cautioned that this was evidence of a more usable review process, not proof that the underlying prioritisation policy was fair in every respect.

examples.script:
Why Handwritten Notes Aid Memory Selectively

Few classroom habits have sparked livelier debate over the past decade than whether students learn more effectively by writing lecture notes with a pen or typing them on a laptop. Early laboratory studies drew wide publicity after reporting that laptop users, despite producing longer transcripts, scored worse on conceptual questions than peers who wrote by hand. Many educators swiftly interpreted those findings as proof that physical pen strokes possess an inherent cognitive magic.

Subsequent replication trials and finer-grained experiments, however, painted a more nuanced picture. Typing is fast enough that diligent students often slip into "verbatim transcription"—recording a lecturer's sentences word for word almost like a courtroom stenographer, without pausing to digest what the argument means. Handwriting, by contrast, lags far behind normal speaking speed. Unable to capture every syllable, note-takers are forced to listen for main claims, condense examples into brief phrases, and draw arrows linking cause and effect. The memory advantage stems primarily from this real-time mental reorganization rather than from friction between ink and paper.

That distinction carries practical consequences. When researchers explicitly instructed laptop users to summarize ideas in their own words instead of transcribing verbatim, much of the gap on conceptual tests narrowed—though keyboard users still faced two stubborn disadvantages: formatting diagrams or equations mid-sentence is awkward on keys, and connected screens tempt attention with incoming messages. Conversely, copying textbook paragraphs word for word by hand yields surprisingly poor recall despite tired wrists.

Effective study strategies therefore depend less on banning devices outright than on matching medium to task. Digital files excel when organizing bibliography quotes or searching months of seminar records, whereas pen, paper, or stylus tablets shine whenever learners need to map unfamiliar relationships freely and force themselves to paraphrase on the fly.

examples.script:
When Academic Journals Publish Null Results

Open almost any prestigious science or psychology journal, and the table of contents brims with breakthroughs: a compound that shrinks tumors in mice, a classroom technique that boosts test scores, or a catalyst that doubles battery life. Rarely will you read a headline announcing that a plausible hypothesis made no measurable difference at all. Behind that lopsided reading list lies a long-standing distortion known to methodologists as the "file-drawer problem."

For decades, peer reviewers and editors favored eye-catching positive findings while rejecting rigorous studies whose outcomes were statistically flat, leaving disappointed researchers to tuck negative data away in desk drawers. That habit quietly skews collective knowledge. If twenty laboratories independently test whether a herbal extract improves memory, and nineteen find zero effect while one sees a fluke improvement by chance, publishing only that lone success misleads doctors and patients alike. (22), other scientists waste years and grant money repeating failed experiments nobody warned them about.

To correct this bias, a growing coalition of journals has introduced "Registered Reports." Under this format, reviewers judge a study's research question, sample size, and statistical plan BEFORE a single measurement is collected. Once the protocol passes peer review, the journal commits in principle to publishing the paper regardless of how the numbers turn out, provided the team follows its approved plan. (23), shifting evaluation from flashy outcomes to methodological rigor removes the temptation to cherry-pick favorable data.

Null results rarely win newspaper headlines, yet making them visible is vital to helping science (24).

This publication pattern rarely stems from deliberate dishonesty. Journals compete for attention and citations, editors favor striking breakthroughs, and researchers under career pressure understandably prioritize manuscripts with a high chance of acceptance. Writing up a rigorous null result takes nearly as much time as writing up a positive discovery, yet brings far less professional recognition. Individual incentives therefore align to filter out negative findings.

The collective cost to science, however, is substantial. When five independent laboratories test the same promising idea and four find no effect while one obtains a positive result by chance, publishing only the fifth study creates a distorted impression of effectiveness. Other teams may then spend years and public grant money repeating dead-end experiments they had no way of knowing had already failed. Worse still, clinical or policy reviews that pool published studies risk overestimating the benefits of an intervention.

One promising reform is the "registered report." Under this format, peer reviewers evaluate a study's research question, sample size, and experimental protocol before data are collected. If the design is sound and the question important, the journal commits in principle to publishing the paper regardless of how the numbers turn out, provided the researchers follow the approved plan. Early evaluations suggest that registered reports contain a much higher proportion of null findings than conventional journals while maintaining high methodological quality.

Registered reports do not suit purely exploratory research where methods evolve mid-experiment, nor do they eliminate the need for replication. Yet they address a structural flaw that exhortations to individual virtue cannot fix alone: shifting prestige from whether a result looks dramatic to whether an investigation was worth conducting and carefully executed.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第5回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Handwritten Notes Aid Memory Selectively

Few classroom habits have sparked livelier debate over the past decade than whether students learn more effectively by writing lecture notes with a pen or typing them on a laptop. Early laboratory studies drew wide publicity after reporting that laptop users, despite producing longer transcripts, scored worse on conceptual questions than peers who wrote by hand. Many educators swiftly interpreted those findings as proof that physical pen strokes possess an inherent cognitive magic.

Subsequent replication trials and finer-grained experiments, however, painted a more nuanced picture. Typing is fast enough that diligent students often slip into "verbatim transcription"—recording a lecturer's sentences word for word almost like a courtroom stenographer, without pausing to digest what the argument means. Handwriting, by contrast, lags far behind normal speaking speed. Unable to capture every syllable, note-takers are forced to listen for main claims, condense examples into brief phrases, and draw arrows linking cause and effect. The memory advantage stems primarily from this real-time mental reorganization rather than from friction between ink and paper.

That distinction carries practical consequences. When researchers explicitly instructed laptop users to summarize ideas in their own words instead of transcribing verbatim, much of the gap on conceptual tests narrowed—though keyboard users still faced two stubborn disadvantages: formatting diagrams or equations mid-sentence is awkward on keys, and connected screens tempt attention with incoming messages. Conversely, copying textbook paragraphs word for word by hand yields surprisingly poor recall despite tired wrists.

Effective study strategies therefore depend less on banning devices outright than on matching medium to task. Digital files excel when organizing bibliography quotes or searching months of seminar records, whereas pen, paper, or stylus tablets shine whenever learners need to map unfamiliar relationships freely and force themselves to paraphrase on the fly.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第1回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Who Benefits from a Quieter Street?

Reducing traffic on a residential street may seem an uncomplicated improvement. Fewer vehicles can mean less noise, cleaner air, and more space for people walking or cycling. Yet the evaluation of a traffic scheme depends on where its boundaries are drawn. A street that becomes quieter may sit beside another that receives the diverted vehicles. An assessment limited to the first street can therefore tell a convincing but incomplete story.

Suppose a district introduces barriers that prevent through-traffic from using several residential roads. Initial monitoring shows a sharp decline in vehicles inside the area. Residents living near the barriers report that children can cross more easily and that conversations are no longer interrupted by engine noise. These are genuine benefits, not merely perceptions to be dismissed. However, residents along the main roads outside the area report longer queues. They question why their experience is absent from the first evaluation.

One response is to enlarge the monitoring area. This is necessary, but a larger average alone may still obscure important differences. If a substantial improvement for several thousand people outweighs a smaller deterioration for a few hundred, the overall figure may look favorable. That calculation does not by itself establish whether the distribution of costs is acceptable, especially if those facing deterioration already experience the greatest pollution. Choosing a measurement boundary is therefore not a neutral substitute for considering fairness.

Timing introduces another complication. Drivers may initially follow familiar routes and later change their journey, travel at another hour, or choose another means of transport. The first week may consequently exaggerate permanent disruption. Conversely, waiting for people to adapt cannot justify disregarding persistent problems indefinitely. An evaluation should state in advance when it will be repeated and which findings would trigger a change. Otherwise, every unfavorable result can be described as temporary and every favorable result as final.

A credible process combines measurements with ways for affected people to challenge the interpretation. Residents may identify a school entrance that monitors have missed or explain why a supposedly convenient alternative route is unusable for someone with limited mobility. Their accounts do not replace traffic counts, but they can reveal what the counts fail to capture.

The choice is not simply between accepting every scheme and rejecting any scheme with uneven effects. It is between treating evaluation as a defense of a completed decision and using it to revise that decision. A project can retain its original aims while adding protection for neighboring roads, adjusting delivery access, or removing a barrier that causes disproportionate harm. A quieter street is worth pursuing, but the claim of success becomes stronger when it accounts for people beyond that street.
