examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第12回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Surge Pricing Provokes Moral Outrage

To a textbook microeconomist, raising prices dynamically when demand suddenly outstrips supply looks like plain common sense. If a torrential rainstorm hits a commuter rail station at six p.m. and three hundred drenched passengers compete for thirty nearby taxis, tripling fares does two useful things at once: travellers who can easily wait indoors stay put, while off-duty drivers two neighborhoods away gain a strong incentive to head toward the storm. Within half an hour, the queue clears.

In real life, however, dynamic "surge pricing" regularly triggers furious public backlash—especially when hardware stores raise snow-shovel prices after a blizzard or ride-hailing apps quadruple fares during transit breakdowns. Behavioral economists led by Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler traced this anger to an unwritten social norm they termed "reference-transaction fairness." Consumers accept that companies raise prices when wholesale costs rise—say, if cocoa beans double in price after crop disease. Exploiting a sudden spike in customer desperation without any matching rise in the seller's own costs, by contrast, violates deep intuitive rules of community reciprocity. (22), firms that cash in on a one-week emergency often forfeit years of hard-won customer loyalty.

Smart operators therefore look for ways to allocate scarce capacity without appearing predatory. Ride-hailing platforms cap multipliers during declared natural disasters while paying drivers bonuses out of company pockets; concert venues use randomized lotteries rather than pure auctions for affordable student seats. (23), utilities that pair peak-hour electricity surcharges with generous off-peak discounts frame dynamic rates as a reward for flexibility rather than a penalty.

Market design succeeds best when economists remember that prices carry (24).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Useful Map

Last summer, Ren moved to a small town with his family. He did not know anyone there. He liked riding his bicycle, so he often went out to find new places. One afternoon, he found a beautiful pond behind the station. He wanted to tell his grandmother about it, but she did not know how to get there.

Ren decided to draw a map of the town. First, he visited the library to find an old map. It showed the streets, but it did not show the new park or the pond. Ren rode around town again and took notes. He also talked to people at the shops. They told him about a quiet garden and a small bakery.

Ren put these places on his map. He drew pictures and used large letters because his grandmother could not read small writing easily. When the map was finished, he took her to the pond. She found the way by looking at his map.

Later, a librarian saw Ren's map. She asked him to make copies for the library. Ren was surprised, but he was happy to help. Now new people in town can take a free map from the library. Ren has also made friends with some children who used his map.

Preparing for Grandma's Birthday

From: Kaho
To: Uncle Dan
Subject: Grandma's birthday dinner

Dear Uncle Dan,
Everyone in our house is excited about Grandma's seventieth birthday party this Sunday! Mom reserved a quiet room at Olive Restaurant near South Station for 5:30 p.m. Because parking near the station is expensive, Dad thinks taking the train will be easier for you.

My brother Shun and I are making a photo album of our family trips. Do you have any old photos of Grandma from when you and Mom were children? If you bring two or three photos on Sunday, we can put them on the first page.

Also, please don't tell Grandma about the album yet, because we want it to be a surprise! Call our house if you need directions from the station.

Love,
Kaho

Preparing for Mountain Hiking

From: Mr. Kato
To: Outdoor Club Members
Subject: Sunday's hike on Mount Takao

Hello everyone,
The weather forecast for this Sunday looks clear and cool! Let's meet in front of the ticket machine at Central Station at 7:40 a.m. Our train leaves at 7:55 a.m., so please do not be late.

We will eat lunch near the top of the mountain. Bring rice balls or sandwiches, a large bottle of water, and a plastic sheet to sit on. Even if the morning feels warm in town, the wind at the top is cold in November. Make sure to put a light jacket in your backpack.

See you on Sunday,
Mr. Kato

Making Snow Lanterns Together

From: Uncle Shinji
To: Mao
Subject: Building mini kamakura lanterns next Saturday!

Hi Mao,
We finally got fifty centimeters of fresh powder snow here in Akita! I'm so excited that you and your parents are visiting us next weekend.

On Saturday evening before dinner, let's build five mini snow lanterns—called mini kamakura—along our front path and put small LED candles inside them. You can use your cousin's plastic bucket to pack the snow, so you don't need to bring tools—just pack waterproof snow gloves and thick wool socks!

See you at Akita Station,
Uncle Shinji

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Useful Map

Last summer, Ren moved to a small town with his family. He did not know anyone there. He liked riding his bicycle, so he often went out to find new places. One afternoon, he found a beautiful pond behind the station. He wanted to tell his grandmother about it, but she did not know how to get there.

Ren decided to draw a map of the town. First, he visited the library to find an old map. It showed the streets, but it did not show the new park or the pond. Ren rode around town again and took notes. He also talked to people at the shops. They told him about a quiet garden and a small bakery.

Ren put these places on his map. He drew pictures and used large letters because his grandmother could not read small writing easily. When the map was finished, he took her to the pond. She found the way by looking at his map.

Later, a librarian saw Ren's map. She asked him to make copies for the library. Ren was surprised, but he was happy to help. Now new people in town can take a free map from the library. Ren has also made friends with some children who used his map.

examples.script:
Learning the Sign for "Delicious"

Every Wednesday afternoon, thirteen-year-old Ren stops at Hidamari Bakery near his junior high school to buy warm walnut rolls. Two months ago, a cheerful college student named Mr. Mori started working at the register. Small cards on the counter explained that Mr. Mori was deaf, so customers pointed to bread labels or held up fingers to show how many rolls they wanted.

Ren liked Mr. Mori's bright smile, yet he felt a little sad that he could only nod when leaving. That night, Ren borrowed an introductory Japanese Sign Language book with clear illustrations from the town library. He practiced three phrases in front of his mirror: "Hello," "Thank you," and "Last week's bread was delicious!"

The following Wednesday, after receiving his bag of walnut rolls, Ren tapped his right cheek lightly and touched his chin—the sign for "delicious"—followed by "thank you." Mr. Mori's eyes lit up with surprise. He signed back slowly, teaching Ren the sign for "bread."

Now Ren learns one new sign each week, and their thirty-second chat at the counter is his favorite part of Wednesday.

examples.script:
Letters Across the Sea

Last autumn, Ms. Green's English class started a postcard exchange with a school in New Zealand. Each student got a partner. Hina's partner was a boy named Liam. In her first postcard, Hina wrote about her town's autumn festival and drew a small red lantern. However, she was worried that her English sentences were too short.

Three weeks later, postcards arrived from New Zealand. Liam loved Hina's drawing! He sent a postcard with a picture of sheep on a green hill. He wrote, "In New Zealand, October is spring, so baby lambs are everywhere now." Hina was surprised because the seasons were opposite.

For her second card, Hina wanted to share more. She went to the park, picked up two yellow ginkgo leaves, and taped one onto a card after pressing it flat in a thick dictionary. She wrote five sentences about how the trees changed color in November.

In December, Liam sent a photo of his class display board. Hina's yellow leaf was in the center, and many students wrote nice comments around it. Hina felt proud and decided to write longer letters next year.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第6回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
A Sign for the Bakery Steps

Near Midori Park, an older couple named Mr. and Mrs. Hara ran a small bread shop. Their walnut rolls were popular, and neighbors of all ages visited every morning. However, there were two stone steps at the front door. People pushing baby strollers or carrying heavy shopping bags sometimes had trouble entering.

Emi, an eighth grader who lived across the street, noticed this one Saturday. While helping a mother lift a stroller up the steps, Emi saw a wide side door facing the alley. That entrance had no steps at all!

When Emi asked Mr. Hara about it, he said, "Deliveries come through that flat door, and customers are welcome to use it too—most people just don't know it's there." With the couple's agreement, Emi made two bright wooden signs in her school woodshop club. One sign by the front steps had an arrow saying, "Step-Free Entrance Around the Corner," and the other welcomed visitors at the side door.

Mr. Hara also added a small bell beside the side door so staff could come right away. Soon, parents with strollers and older neighbors used the flat entrance comfortably every day.

Hina's art class had an interesting project in October: each student received a plain white cloth tote bag and had to decorate it using natural shapes. At first, Hina thought about pressing autumn leaves onto the cloth, just like many of her classmates.

That evening, while helping her father make curry, Hina watched him cut off the bottom of a green okra pod and the root end of a lotus root. When she looked at the leftover pieces on the cutting board, she noticed something surprising. The cut okra looked like a neat five-pointed star, and the lotus root had a ring of pretty holes like a flower!

Hina asked her father if she could wash and dry those vegetable ends instead of throwing them away. The next day in art class, she dipped the okra and lotus root into fabric paint—yellow, green, and dark blue—and stamped patterns across her bag.

Her classmates gathered around her desk in amazement. Hina gave the finished bag to her father so he could carry vegetables home from the market every week.

Grandfather's Old Radio

When Sota helped his grandmother clean the storage room, he found a small brown radio with a silver handle. "That was your grandfather's favorite radio forty years ago," his grandmother said. Sota turned the switch, but no sound came out.

Sota liked learning how machines worked. He asked if he could take the radio to Mr. Yamada, a retired electrician who lived next door. Mr. Yamada smiled and opened the back cover carefully. Inside, one thin wire had come loose, and dust covered the speaker.

For an hour, Mr. Yamada showed Sota how to brush away the dust gently and reconnect the wire safely. When they put new batteries in and turned the dial, clear jazz music filled the room! Sota was amazed by the warm sound.

That evening, Sota placed the working radio on the kitchen table. When his grandmother heard an old song from her youth, tears came to her eyes, and she thanked Sota again and again.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第13回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Repairing Grandfather's Wooden Clock

On the wall of thirteen-year-old Shun's living room hung an old octagonal wooden clock that had belonged to his great-grandfather. Every hour, its brass pendulum used to chime softly, until one winter morning the hands stopped at ten-fifteen.

Shun's mother thought they would have to throw it away because modern battery shops didn't fix wind-up clocks. That Saturday, however, Shun spotted a tiny shop near the shotengai arcade with a hand-painted sign: "Takahashi Watch & Clock Repair."

Inside, seventy-five-year-old Mr. Takahashi opened the back panel with a small screwdriver and smiled. "Nothing is broken," he told Shun. "Old oil inside the gears simply dried up in the cold." Letting Shun watch through a magnifying glass, he cleaned each brass wheel with a soft brush and added two tiny drops of fresh clock oil.

When the warm chime rang out again at home that evening, Shun's grandfather clapped with joy—and Shun decided he wanted to learn how mechanical things work too.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第6回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Returning Your Umbrella

From: Daichi
To: Riku
Subject: Thank you for yesterday!

Hi Riku,
Thank you so much for lending me your striped umbrella yesterday afternoon! The rain became really strong on my way home, so it saved my textbooks from getting wet.

I dried the umbrella well last night and folded it neatly. Tomorrow morning I have basketball practice in the gym from 7:30 a.m., so I will come to your classroom during the ten-minute break after first period to give it back.

Also, my aunt sent us a box of sweet tangerines from Ehime. I will bring three for you!

See you tomorrow,
Daichi

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第8回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Changing Piano Lesson Day

From: Ms. Morita
To: Mrs. Endo
Subject: Kaito's piano lesson next week

Dear Mrs. Endo,
Thank you for your message yesterday. Kaito played his new piece very smoothly at this week's lesson—his rhythm has improved a lot!

Next Thursday, May 21, I have to go to Osaka to play in a charity concert, so I cannot give lessons that afternoon. Could we move Kaito's 4:30 p.m. lesson to Friday, May 22, at the same time? If Friday is busy for Kaito, Saturday morning at 10:30 a.m. is also open.

Please let me know by Monday.

Warm regards,
Yoko Morita

To: Yuta

Your mother told me that you are going camping with your classmates next weekend. You are welcome to borrow my green tent! It is big enough for four people, and it is easy to set up.

Uncle Shin

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第9回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Morning Bread Delivery

Every Saturday at seven in the morning, thirteen-year-old Tsubasa rides his bicycle to his uncle's small bakery, Mugi-no-Ie. While most of his classmates are still asleep, Tsubasa helps pack warm rolls and walnut bread into paper bags for older neighbors who have trouble walking up the steep hill to the shop.

Tsubasa started helping six months ago after Mrs. Ota, an eighty-two-year-old woman living next door to his family, hurt her ankle. When Tsubasa brought her fresh bread from his uncle's shop, she smiled and said the smell of warm bread made her whole weekend brighter. Hearing that, Tsubasa's uncle decided to start a free Saturday bicycle delivery for six elderly households in the town.

Each stop takes only two or three minutes, yet Tsubasa enjoys the short chats at the front doors. Mr. Fujita often tells him stories about how the town looked fifty years ago, and Mrs. Ota sometimes gives him tangerines from her garden.

When Tsubasa returns to the bakery at eight o'clock, his uncle always rewards him with a hot cheese bun straight from the oven.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検4級 第10回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Rainy-Day Board Game Shelf

In June, heavy rain kept students indoors during lunch break almost every day at Minami Junior High School. Twelve-year-old Koharu noticed many seventh graders sitting quietly at their desks with nothing to do while the playground was muddy.

At home that weekend, Koharu opened a closet and saw three board games—othello, shogi, and a word-card game—that she and her older brother no longer played. She asked her homeroom teacher, Ms. Ota, if Class 1-A could set up a "Rainy-Day Game Corner" on the back shelf.

Ms. Ota loved the idea and added one simple rule: anyone borrowing a game wrote their name on a small whiteboard and checked that all pieces were back in the box five minutes before fifth period. Within three days, four classmates brought puzzles and card games from home too.

Soon, laughter filled the classroom even on the gloomiest June afternoons, and Koharu made friends with classmates she had barely spoken to in April.

From: Uncle Shinji
To: Mao
Subject: Building mini kamakura lanterns next Saturday!

Hi Mao,
We finally got fifty centimeters of fresh powder snow here in Akita! I'm so excited that you and your parents are visiting us next weekend.

On Saturday evening before dinner, let's build five mini snow lanterns—called mini kamakura—along our front path and put small LED candles inside them. You can use your cousin's plastic bucket to pack the snow, so you don't need to bring tools—just pack waterproof snow gloves and thick wool socks!

See you at Akita Station,
Uncle Shinji

To: Riku
Subject: Thank you for yesterday!

examples.script:
The Rainy-Day Board Games

At Aoba Junior High School, students loved playing soccer outside during lunch break. On rainy weeks in June, however, the schoolyard was closed. Many students sat quietly at their desks or crowded the hallways with nothing to do.

Kotaro, a member of the student council, talked with his classmates about this problem. He remembered that his grandfather had taught him shogi and simple card games on rainy afternoons. Kotaro asked teachers if the council could open one empty classroom on the first floor as a "Rainy-Day Game Room" during lunch.

The principal liked the idea, as long as students followed clear rules: games had to finish five minutes before afternoon classes, and everyone had to put all pieces back in their boxes. Teachers and families donated chess sets, reversi boards, and word-card games.

On the first rainy Tuesday, more than thirty students from different grades visited the room. Seventh graders played reversi against ninth graders and made new friends. Soon, some students even looked forward to rainy days!

examples.script:
The Morning Bread Delivery

Every Saturday at seven in the morning, thirteen-year-old Tsubasa rides his bicycle to his uncle's small bakery, Mugi-no-Ie. While most of his classmates are still asleep, Tsubasa helps pack warm rolls and walnut bread into paper bags for older neighbors who have trouble walking up the steep hill to the shop.

Tsubasa started helping six months ago after Mrs. Ota, an eighty-two-year-old woman living next door to his family, hurt her ankle. When Tsubasa brought her fresh bread from his uncle's shop, she smiled and said the smell of warm bread made her whole weekend brighter. Hearing that, Tsubasa's uncle decided to start a free Saturday bicycle delivery for six elderly households in the town.

Each stop takes only two or three minutes, yet Tsubasa enjoys the short chats at the front doors. Mr. Fujita often tells him stories about how the town looked fifty years ago, and Mrs. Ota sometimes gives him tangerines from her garden.

When Tsubasa returns to the bakery at eight o'clock, his uncle always rewards him with a hot cheese bun straight from the oven.

examples.script:
Repairing Grandfather's Wooden Clock

On the wall of thirteen-year-old Shun's living room hung an old octagonal wooden clock that had belonged to his great-grandfather. Every hour, its brass pendulum used to chime softly, until one winter morning the hands stopped at ten-fifteen.

Shun's mother thought they would have to throw it away because modern battery shops didn't fix wind-up clocks. That Saturday, however, Shun spotted a tiny shop near the shotengai arcade with a hand-painted sign: "Takahashi Watch & Clock Repair."

Inside, seventy-five-year-old Mr. Takahashi opened the back panel with a small screwdriver and smiled. "Nothing is broken," he told Shun. "Old oil inside the gears simply dried up in the cold." Letting Shun watch through a magnifying glass, he cleaned each brass wheel with a soft brush and added two tiny drops of fresh clock oil.

When the warm chime rang out again at home that evening, Shun's grandfather clapped with joy—and Shun decided he wanted to learn how mechanical things work too.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第2回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Seeds for Next Month

Every Saturday morning, Emi visits the Maple Community Garden with her grandfather. Residents of different ages grow vegetables and flowers there together. Last Saturday, the sky was covered with dark clouds when they left home, so her grandfather reminded Emi to pack two light raincoats in her bag.

When they arrived at the garden, they saw Mr. Lee, an older neighbor, carrying a heavy wooden box full of seed packets. Because his back was hurting a little, Emi hurried over and helped him arrange the packets neatly on a long table under a tent. Mr. Lee thanked her and explained which flowers grew well in summer.

Twenty minutes later, large drops of rain suddenly began to fall. Everyone worked quickly as a team. While the adults covered the vegetable beds with plastic sheets, Emi and two other students moved the young flowerpots under the roof of the tool shed so the strong rain would not damage them.

After the rain stopped, Emi noticed a small bookshelf inside the shed. Garden members leave gardening books there so anyone can borrow them for two weeks. Emi chose a beginner's guide to growing sunflowers. Mr. Lee also gave her a packet of sunflower seeds as a thank-you gift.

On the way home, Emi asked her grandfather if they could clear a sunny corner of their own yard. Next month, she plans to plant the seeds there and keep a photo diary of how tall the sunflowers grow.

examples.script:
Preparing Lunch for the Park Cleanup Team

From: Noah
To: Emi
Subject: Friday afternoon in the school kitchen

Hi Emi,
Thank you for joining our cooking team! As you know, community volunteers will gather early on Saturday morning to clean the pond in Central Park, and our class promised to prepare light lunch boxes for them.

We will meet in the school kitchen at 3:30 p.m. this Friday right after classes finish. I will bring fresh bread and sliced cheese from my uncle's bakery, and Hana is going to make warm carrot soup. Could you bring two clean dishcloths and a roll of aluminum foil? We need the foil to wrap the sandwiches neatly.

Also, we have to pack everything into cooler boxes before 5:00 p.m. because Mr. Takeda will lock the kitchen at 5:15 p.m. and store the boxes in the staff refrigerator overnight. Let me know if you can make it!

Best,
Noah

examples.script:
Borrowing Sports Pinnies for Field Day

From: Nanami
To: Sota
Subject: Colored vests for Grade 8 relay

Hi Sota,
Our physical education teacher, Mr. Kawai, asked our Field Day committee to check the numbered mesh vests ("pinnies") in the gym storage room today. When Reina and I counted them after school, we found plenty of red, yellow, and green vests for the eighth-grade class relay, but three of the blue vests had torn seams and missing numbers.

Luckily, the local youth soccer coach, who is Reina's uncle, said we may borrow a full set of ten clean blue vests for Field Day next Wednesday! Since you live right across the street from the community ground where his team practices on Sunday mornings, could you pick up the bag of blue vests from Coach Endo around 10:30 a.m. this Sunday?

After Field Day finishes on Wednesday, Reina and I will wash all ten vests at home and return them to her uncle, so you only need to bring the bag to school on Monday morning. Let me know if Sunday morning works!

Thanks,
Nanami

examples.script:
Rain Plan for Our Walking History Tour

From: Mr. Shinohara, History Club Adviser
To: History Club Members
Subject: Tomorrow's castle-town walking tour

Hello everyone,
Thank you for preparing your short guide speeches for tomorrow's walking tour of the old castle-town district. Each member chose a fascinating spot to introduce!

According to this evening's weather forecast, light rain will begin around 11:00 a.m. tomorrow, though the early morning will be dry. Therefore, we will reverse the order of our schedule. Instead of visiting the Folk History Museum in the morning and walking outside in the afternoon, we will meet at East Gate Square at 8:45 a.m. and do the outdoor walking route first while the streets are dry. Then, at 11:15 a.m., we will eat an early lunch in the covered rest house beside the moat and spend the afternoon inside the museum.

Please bring a folding umbrella and put your speech notes inside a clear plastic folder so raindrops won't smudge the ink. See you at East Gate Square!

Mr. Shinohara

examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第3回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Recording How Beans Grow

In April, Class Three received permission to turn an unused strip of land beside the science room into a small learning garden. At first, several students complained that pulling weeds and carrying soil was tiring. Their science teacher, Mr. Aoki, suggested dividing the work into short ten-minute shifts before morning homeroom so nobody would feel overwhelmed.

On the first Monday of May, the students planted green bean seeds in four wooden boxes. At the beginning, some students watered the boxes twice a day because they thought more water would make the seeds grow faster. However, Mr. Aoki showed them that giving too much water could actually rot the seeds underground. The class made a simple chart to check the soil with their fingers before watering.

To keep the area tidy, the students also set up two recycling bins near the tap. Dry leaves and pulled weeds went into the brown bin to become compost, while empty plastic seedling pots were washed and placed in the blue bin so next year's class could reuse them.

Two weeks later, the first bright green shoots pushed through the soil. Every Friday afternoon, students sketched the plants and measured their height with rulers. Several students who rarely spoke in science lessons became enthusiastic about comparing their weekly drawings.

In June, the Town Picture Gallery invited local schools to display student projects. Class Three selected twelve detailed plant sketches along with a short explanation of their watering chart. The students hope visitors will see that even a narrow corner of a schoolyard can become a place for discovery.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第10回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Maps You Can Touch

Last autumn, eighth-grade students at Hillside Junior High School visited the City Science Museum with a blind guest speaker, Mr. Nagai, who had talked to their class the week before about how he traveled safely around town. At the museum entrance, the students noticed something surprising: although there were colorful floor maps everywhere, none of them had raised lines or Braille labels that Mr. Nagai could read with his fingertips.

Back at school, four students in the craft club asked Mr. Nagai what kind of map truly helped him inside unfamiliar buildings. He explained that too many tiny details actually made a touch map confusing. What mattered most was clear textures, such as rough sandpaper strips for stairs, smooth raised tape for main hallways, and round wooden beads for restrooms and the information desk.

Over the next two months, the four students measured the first floor of their own school building, where guests often visited for concerts and parent meetings. They built a sturdy touch map on a wide wooden board using five distinct materials that felt completely different under a finger. Mr. Nagai tested their first version and suggested widening the space between hallway lines so two fingers could follow a route comfortably.

After the students improved the board and placed it inside the main entrance in January, not only visually impaired visitors but also young children and elderly grandparents stopped to trace the routes. Seeing how clear design helped everyone, the City Science Museum invited the students to share what they had learned with its exhibition staff.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第3回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Recording How Beans Grow

In April, Class Three received permission to turn an unused strip of land beside the science room into a small learning garden. At first, several students complained that pulling weeds and carrying soil was tiring. Their science teacher, Mr. Aoki, suggested dividing the work into short ten-minute shifts before morning homeroom so nobody would feel overwhelmed.

On the first Monday of May, the students planted green bean seeds in four wooden boxes. At the beginning, some students watered the boxes twice a day because they thought more water would make the seeds grow faster. However, Mr. Aoki showed them that giving too much water could actually rot the seeds underground. The class made a simple chart to check the soil with their fingers before watering.

To keep the area tidy, the students also set up two recycling bins near the tap. Dry leaves and pulled weeds went into the brown bin to become compost, while empty plastic seedling pots were washed and placed in the blue bin so next year's class could reuse them.

Two weeks later, the first bright green shoots pushed through the soil. Every Friday afternoon, students sketched the plants and measured their height with rulers. Several students who rarely spoke in science lessons became enthusiastic about comparing their weekly drawings.

In June, the Town Picture Gallery invited local schools to display student projects. Class Three selected twelve detailed plant sketches along with a short explanation of their watering chart. The students hope visitors will see that even a narrow corner of a schoolyard can become a place for discovery.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Wooden Book Box at Lake Green Camp

Last summer, my town opened a small outdoor library at Lake Green Camp so families staying in tents could enjoy reading without carrying heavy books from home. Volunteers built a weatherproof wooden box with a small slanted roof and placed it beside the camp dining hall. Campers were welcome to leave books they had finished reading and borrow any book from the box during their stay.

When my family stayed at the camp in August, it rained heavily on our second afternoon, canceling our canoeing lesson. Feeling bored inside our tent, my friend Jo and I walked over to the dining hall and opened the wooden book box for the first time. Inside, we discovered an illustrated guide to wild lakeside birds left by a previous camper, along with a handwritten note on the first page recommending a quiet lookout point behind the boat house.

As soon as the rain stopped the next morning, Jo and I visited that lookout point with the guide in hand. Within half an hour, we spotted three kinds of waterbirds shown in the book and sketched their feathers in our notebooks. Before leaving the camp on Sunday, we returned the bird guide and added two mystery novels of our own.

However, several first-time campers told the camp staff that they had walked past the dining hall without realizing what the wooden box was for. This spring, Jo and I offered to paint a bright sign and draw a simple camp map showing the box's location. The staff gladly accepted our idea, and our map now hangs right at the camp entrance.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第7回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Letters Across Three Oceans

When Ms. Carter became the English teacher at Harbor Junior High School in April, many eighth-grade students felt shy about writing in English. Whenever she asked them to write three sentences in their notebooks, they worried so much about making small grammar mistakes that their pages stayed almost blank.

In May, Ms. Carter arranged a pen-pal project with two partner schools (one in New Zealand and one in Portugal) where students were also learning English as a global language. Instead of exchanging instant text messages, each student designed a handmade postcard introducing one local food or seasonal event from their town. Because space on a postcard was small, students felt relaxed and focused on sharing one clear idea.

When the first bundle of colorful cards arrived from New Zealand and Portugal in June, the classroom grew lively. Harbor students noticed that their new friends occasionally crossed out a word or used simple sentences, yet their drawings and descriptions of winter rugby matches in June and grilled sardine festivals were vivid and easy to enjoy.

Realizing that communication mattered more than perfection, the students began writing longer letters in autumn. Several students looked up English words on their own to explain how their town celebrated the autumn harvest.

At the end of the term, the class displayed copies of the postcards on the hallway board with a world map and yarn connecting the three towns. Even students who once feared writing three lines now look forward to opening the mail bag every month.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Riverside Community Book Swap

RIVERSIDE COMMUNITY BOOK SWAP
Date: Saturday, June 14 (1:00 p.m. – 4:00 p.m.)
Location: Maple Hall, Main Room
Admission: Free

Do you have storybooks or magazines at home that you have already finished reading? Bring up to five clean books in good condition, and you will receive one exchange ticket for each book you bring. You can use each ticket to take one book home!

At 2:30 p.m., local actor Ms. Kato will read a short adventure story aloud for children. Children under 12 must come with an adult. For questions, call Mina at 555-0142.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第6回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Junior Bicycle Safety Check

SOUTH TOWN TRAFFIC CLUB
Free Junior Bicycle Safety Check
Date: Sunday, April 19 (9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.)
Place: South Elementary School Playground

Spring is a great season for cycling! Volunteer mechanics will check your brakes, tires, bell, and front light for free. If your tires need air or your chain needs oil, we will take care of it on the spot.

Students who pass all safety checks will receive a reflective sticker for their rear fender. No reservation is needed; just bring your bicycle before noon. If it rains, the event will be held next Sunday, April 26.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第10回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Weekend Junior First-Aid Course

HARBOR FIRE STATION
Weekend Junior First-Aid Course
Date: Saturday, August 22 (1:30 p.m. – 4:00 p.m.)
Location: Training Room, 2nd Floor
Cost: Free

Learn practical skills that can help your family and friends in an emergency! Firefighters will teach junior high school students how to treat minor burns, wrap a sprained ankle with a bandage, and use an AED machine safely.

Because participants will practice kneeling on floor mats, please wear comfortable trousers rather than skirts. Every student who completes the course will receive a pocket first-aid guide. Sign up online by August 16 (limit: 24 students).

Science Club Open Day
Saturday, May 18, 1:00–3:00 p.m.
Community Hall, Room B

Learn to build a simple weather station from things you can find at home. This event is for children aged ten to fifteen. Members of the science club will help you, so you do not need any experience. Please bring an empty plastic bottle with its cap. All other materials will be provided.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第13回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Rain Plan for Our Walking History Tour

From: Mr. Shinohara, History Club Adviser
To: History Club Members
Subject: Tomorrow's castle-town walking tour

Hello everyone,
Thank you for preparing your short guide speeches for tomorrow's walking tour of the old castle-town district. Each member chose a fascinating spot to introduce!

According to this evening's weather forecast, light rain will begin around 11:00 a.m. tomorrow, though the early morning will be dry. Therefore, we will reverse the order of our schedule. Instead of visiting the Folk History Museum in the morning and walking outside in the afternoon, we will meet at East Gate Square at 8:45 a.m. and do the outdoor walking route first while the streets are dry. Then, at 11:15 a.m., we will eat an early lunch in the covered rest house beside the moat and spend the afternoon inside the museum.

Please bring a folding umbrella and put your speech notes inside a clear plastic folder so raindrops won't smudge the ink. See you at East Gate Square!

Mr. Shinohara

examples.script:
Autumn Bird-Watching Morning Walk

GREEN LAKE NATURE PARK
Autumn Bird-Watching Morning Walk
Date: Sunday, October 18 (7:00 a.m. – 9:00 a.m.)
Meeting Spot: North Wooden Pier
Fee: 200 yen per person (free for students under 15)

October is the best season to watch wild ducks and swans arriving at Green Lake from the north! Park rangers will guide visitors quietly along the reed trail and explain how migrating birds find food before winter.

Ten pairs of binoculars are available to borrow at no extra cost, reserved on a first-come, first-served basis at the pier from 6:45 a.m. Please avoid wearing bright red or neon jackets, because sudden bright colors can frighten the birds away.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第14回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
Spring Bicycle Safety Check Day

MAPLE TOWN TRAFFIC SAFETY ASSOCIATION
Spring Bicycle Safety Check Day
Date: Sunday, April 12 (9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.)
Location: East Corner of Maple Central Park
Cost: Free for all students and residents

Before the new school term gets busy, bring your bicycle for a free ten-minute inspection! Certified mechanics from three local bike shops will check brakes, tire air pressure, chains, and front lights.

Simple adjustments such as pumping tires and oiling chains are completely free. If a worn brake pad needs to be replaced, you pay only for the part itself (300 yen). Every student whose bike passes inspection will get a reflective spoke clip for night riding!

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第1回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Second Repair

When Oliver's headphones stopped working, he put them in a drawer and planned to buy new ones. Then he saw a poster for a repair workshop at the library. Anyone could bring a broken object and learn how to repair it with help from a volunteer. Oliver thought he could save some money, so he decided to go.

At the workshop, a volunteer named Grace checked his headphones. The problem was a small wire inside them. Oliver expected Grace to do all the work, but she gave him a tool and explained how to use it safely. He was nervous at first. After several tries, however, he connected the wire. The headphones worked again.

Grace explained that repairing things could reduce the amount of rubbish people threw away. Oliver had never thought about this before. He began looking around his house for other broken things. He found a desk lamp that his sister had stopped using. It was not the same kind of problem as the headphones, so he could not fix it immediately.

The next month, Oliver returned to the workshop with the lamp. This time he asked Grace to show him how to discover the problem, rather than repair it for him. They found that a switch needed cleaning. Oliver cleaned it, and the lamp came on.

Now Oliver helps prepare the room before each workshop. He does not know enough to repair every object, but he can welcome visitors and explain what to expect. He tells them that learning is more important than finishing quickly. His sister uses the lamp again, and Oliver has kept the poster that first brought him to the library.

Junior Bicycle Safety Check

SOUTH TOWN TRAFFIC CLUB
Free Junior Bicycle Safety Check
Date: Sunday, April 19 (9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.)
Place: South Elementary School Playground

Spring is a great season for cycling! Volunteer mechanics will check your brakes, tires, bell, and front light for free. If your tires need air or your chain needs oil, we will take care of it on the spot.

Students who pass all safety checks will receive a reflective sticker for their rear fender. No reservation is needed; just bring your bicycle before noon. If it rains, the event will be held next Sunday, April 26.

Switching Our Library Duty Day

To: Maya
Subject: Library counter duty next week

Hi Maya,
Could I ask you a favor about our student library committee schedule next week? I am scheduled for lunch-break counter duty on Tuesday, May 19, and you are scheduled for Thursday, May 21.

This morning, our science teacher announced that finalists in the city robot contest will have a special practice run in the gym during lunch break on Tuesday. Thanks a lot,
Riku

examples.chapterTitle: 英検3級 第4回（3本文・計10問）
examples.script:
The Wooden Book Box at Lake Green Camp

Last summer, my town opened a small outdoor library at Lake Green Camp so families staying in tents could enjoy reading without carrying heavy books from home. Volunteers built a weatherproof wooden box with a small slanted roof and placed it beside the camp dining hall. Campers were welcome to leave books they had finished reading and borrow any book from the box during their stay.

When my family stayed at the camp in August, it rained heavily on our second afternoon, canceling our canoeing lesson. Feeling bored inside our tent, my friend Jo and I walked over to the dining hall and opened the wooden book box for the first time. Inside, we discovered an illustrated guide to wild lakeside birds left by a previous camper, along with a handwritten note on the first page recommending a quiet lookout point behind the boat house.

As soon as the rain stopped the next morning, Jo and I visited that lookout point with the guide in hand. Within half an hour, we spotted three kinds of waterbirds shown in the book and sketched their feathers in our notebooks. Before leaving the camp on Sunday, we returned the bird guide and added two mystery novels of our own.

However, several first-time campers told the camp staff that they had walked past the dining hall without realizing what the wooden box was for. This spring, Jo and I offered to paint a bright sign and draw a simple camp map showing the box's location. The staff gladly accepted our idea, and our map now hangs right at the camp entrance.

Preparing Costumes for the Drama Festival

From: Ayaka Mori, Costume Team Leader
To: Drama Club Cast Members
Subject: Costume fittings and shoe rules this week

Hi everyone,
Our regional high school drama festival is two weeks away, and all jackets and skirts for our play have now been hemmed! Individual fifteen-minute fittings will take place in Clubroom 4 on Wednesday and Thursday after school. Please check the time chart taped to the clubroom door and come wearing the thin T-shirt and leggings you will wear under your costume.

During last Saturday's run-through, the wooden stage at Civic Hall turned out to be more slippery than our school gym floor. Because leather-soled shoes slide easily when turning quickly, our advisor has asked everyone to attach thin rubber grip pads to the bottoms of their stage shoes. Our costume team bought enough pads for the whole cast; bring your stage shoes to your fitting so we can put them on together.

After Thursday's fittings, all costumes will be packed into garment bags for transport. Please do not take any costume pieces home to wash, as household detergent may change the dye color of the matching jackets.

See you Wednesday,
Ayaka

examples.script:
Borrowing tools, not buying them

At the Willow Tool Room, residents can borrow things such as drills and long ladders. At first, people chose an item online and collected it whenever the room was open. Volunteers soon noticed a problem: some people arrived without knowing how to carry a large item safely. The room now asks borrowers to describe their transport plans before a booking is confirmed. A volunteer may suggest a smaller item or a different collection time. The room has not introduced a delivery service. Its aim is to keep borrowing practical without asking volunteers to travel around town. The new question adds a step to booking, but fewer borrowers now have to return home empty-handed.

Changes to the Food Festival

From: Luis, Festival Coordinator
To: Volunteers
Subject: Please read before Saturday

Dear volunteers,
Thank you for helping at our international food festival. There have been two important changes. First, heavy rain is expected, so the festival will take place inside the community center rather than in the park. The center has enough space for all the food tables, but the entrance is narrow. Please arrive at the back door to help move supplies.

Second, the local bus company cannot provide the extra morning service we requested. Some visitors may arrive later than planned. We will therefore begin serving food at 11:30 instead of 11:00. Volunteers should still arrive at 9:00, as originally arranged. We need that time to set up the tables and check the kitchen equipment.

If you are helping at a food table, please bring a clean apron. We will provide gloves and name tags. Volunteers at the information desk do not need aprons. Those who have not yet chosen a job should contact me by Thursday evening.

Finally, please avoid bringing your own cars because parking spaces must be kept for delivery vehicles. The number 6 bus stops directly outside the center. I will send a map with the entrance marked tomorrow.

Best wishes,
Luis

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第6回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Curved Sidewalk Corners Shape Street Safety

Most pedestrians never think twice about the shape of a street corner where two sidewalks meet. Yet traffic engineers know that the radius of that curve—whether it forms a sharp ninety-degree turn or a wide, sweeping arc—has a direct effect on how fast cars turn and how safely people cross.

During the mid-twentieth century, many cities widened intersection corners into gentle curves so large trucks and buses could turn without slowing down much. While convenient for vehicles, wide curves had two drawbacks for walkers. First, drivers could swing around corners at twenty-five or thirty kilometers per hour while looking mainly for oncoming cars rather than people in the crosswalk. Second, rounding off the corner pushed the curb back, making the painted crosswalk several meters longer for children and older residents to cross.

In recent years, urban planners have been tightening residential and school-zone corners again. A tighter curb forces passenger cars to slow to walking pace before turning, giving drivers an extra second or two to spot someone stepping off the sidewalk. Extending the corner slightly—a design often called a "curb bulb"—also shortens the crossing distance and lets pedestrians see past parked cars without stepping into traffic.

What about fire engines and delivery trucks that still need room to turn? Engineers solve this in creative ways. On some corners, they build a low, textured stone apron beside the curb: ordinary cars stay off the bumpy surface, while the wide wheels of an emergency vehicle can roll slowly over it when necessary.

Small geometric changes in concrete rarely make headlines, yet reshaping a single corner can calm an entire neighborhood crossing every day of the year.

examples.script:
The quiet label

A small theatre once put a "quiet performance" label on certain shows. Staff expected it to welcome people who disliked sudden noise. However, a visitor explained that the label was unclear: did it mean the audience had to remain completely silent, or that the sound from the stage would be softer? The theatre asked several visitors to review its website. It then replaced the short label with a description of what would be different. These performances now use lower sound levels and leave a few lights on. Visitors may step outside and return. The theatre still offers ordinary performances, but it no longer expects a single label to explain every change.

The quiet label

A small theatre once put a "quiet performance" label on certain shows. Staff expected it to welcome people who disliked sudden noise. However, a visitor explained that the label was unclear: did it mean the audience had to remain completely silent, or that the sound from the stage would be softer? The theatre asked several visitors to review its website. It then replaced the short label with a description of what would be different. These performances now use lower sound levels and leave a few lights on. Visitors may step outside and return. The theatre still offers ordinary performances, but it no longer expects a single label to explain every change.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第4回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Teaching Buses and Trains to Wait Two Minutes

Missing a rural connecting bus by ninety seconds can turn a twenty-minute commute into an hour-long wait on a windy platform. In large cities, where another train arrives every four minutes, tight transfers rarely matter. Along regional rail lines and suburban bus corridors, however, vehicles run far less frequently, so a single delayed train can strand dozens of passengers who needed that connection.

Historically, bus drivers had no reliable way to know whether an approaching train was running two minutes late or twenty. Waiting blindly risked making every downstream stop late and causing passengers further along the route to miss their own appointments. As a result, most operators instructed drivers to depart strictly by the printed clock, even if a train was just pulling into the station.

Low-cost GPS trackers and shared dispatch screens have begun changing this rigid rule. In several mid-sized European and Japanese cities, trains and connecting buses now exchange live location updates automatically. If a train is delayed by three minutes or less—and the bus schedule has enough cushion on a quiet stretch of road to make up that time—the screen on the driver's dashboard flashes a "hold" request. Meanwhile, an announcement inside the train tells transferring riders that their bus is waiting at Stand 2, preventing dangerous sprinting on station stairs.

Of course, holding a bus is not always wise. When heavy snow delays a train by fifteen minutes, holding every feeder bus would paralyze the entire local network. Dispatch software therefore sets clear upper limits, typically three to five minutes, and prioritizes the last evening runs when no later bus exists.

Passenger surveys in towns using smart-hold rules show a notable jump in trust toward public transit. Knowing that operators coordinate across vehicles makes people far more willing to leave their cars at home for two-seat journeys.

examples.script:
Why Passenger Airplanes Have Tiny Holes in Their Windows

Next time you settle into a window seat on a passenger jet, look near the bottom center of the clear pane: you will spot a tiny hole scarcely wider than a toothpick. Nervous flyers sometimes wonder whether the window is cracked, yet aerospace engineers call this feature a "bleed hole," and it is built into cabin windows on purpose.

A jetliner window actually consists of three separate layers of transparent acrylic resin. The thin inner pane facing your elbow is merely a protective scratch shield, whereas the thick outer pane bears the massive air-pressure difference between the thin atmosphere ten kilometers up and the pressurized passenger cabin. If both the outer and middle panes felt full cabin pressure all the time, both would suffer wear together. The tiny hole in the middle pane equalizes air pressure safely so that (21).

The bleed hole performs a neat everyday job too. Outside air at cruising altitude drops below minus fifty degrees Celsius. Allowing dry cabin air to circulate slowly between the panes prevents moisture from freezing onto the outer glass, ensuring passengers enjoy (22).

examples.script:
A Museum You Can Hear

At the Riverside Museum, most visitors once followed signs from one glass case to another. They read short descriptions of old tools, clothes, and furniture, then moved on. The objects were interesting, but the museum staff noticed that many visitors did not stay long. Few people understood how the objects had been used in daily life.

To change this, the museum invited local residents to record stories about familiar objects. One woman described the sound of the sewing machine her mother used at home. A retired baker explained why a wooden tray had a particular shape. These recordings were added to a small audio player that visitors could borrow at the entrance. The aim was not to replace the written descriptions but to provide another way to explore the collection.

The first recordings were long and difficult to follow. Staff had assumed that visitors would listen to complete interviews. In practice, people wanted to move at their own speed. The museum therefore divided the interviews into short sections. Each section focused on one object and lasted less than two minutes. Visitors could choose only the stories that interested them.

The new system also changed the relationship between the museum and the town. Residents who had rarely visited came to hear their relatives' recordings. Some brought photographs or offered to share their own memories. The museum checked these stories against old records before using them, because personal memories are not always exact.

A visitor survey later showed that people were spending more time in the museum. However, the director did not regard longer visits as the only sign of success. She was more pleased that visitors were asking new questions about everyday life in the past. The museum now plans to add stories from younger residents as well. The staff believe that objects which seem ordinary today may help future visitors understand the present.

Subject: Footwear and arrival time for Sunday's snowshoe walk

We look forward to welcoming you to Sunday's guided snowshoe walk through Shirakaba Woods. Light snow fell yesterday, leaving forty centimeters of fresh powder along the trail—ideal conditions for beginners!

If you reserved rental snowshoes on your application form, please arrive at the nature center by 9:10 a.m., twenty minutes before the walk starts, so staff can adjust the straps to fit your boots. Note that we rent only snowshoes, not winter boots. You must wear waterproof hiking boots or tall snow boots that cover your ankles; low sneakers allow snow inside and slip out of the bindings.

Walking on snow warms the body faster than people expect. Instead of one thick down coat, wear two or three breathable layers that you can unzip or put in your backpack during uphill sections. Hot herb tea will be served in the log cabin after we return at noon; bring your own insulated mug if you have one.

Warm regards,
Kogen Nature Center Staff

Thank you for helping at our international food festival. There have been two important changes. First, heavy rain is expected, so the festival will take place inside the community center rather than in the park. The center has enough space for all the food tables, but the entrance is narrow. Please arrive at the back door to help move supplies.

Second, the local bus company cannot provide the extra morning service we requested. Some visitors may arrive later than planned. We will therefore begin serving food at 11:30 instead of 11:00. Volunteers should still arrive at 9:00, as originally arranged. We need that time to set up the tables and check the kitchen equipment.

If you are helping at a food table, please bring a clean apron. We will provide gloves and name tags. Volunteers at the information desk do not need aprons. Those who have not yet chosen a job should contact me by Thursday evening.

Finally, please avoid bringing your own cars because parking spaces must be kept for delivery vehicles. The number 6 bus stops directly outside the center. I will send a map with the entrance marked tomorrow.

Best wishes,
Luis

examples.script:
Instructions for the Astronomical Choir Recording

From: Mr. Shinohara, Chorus Club Director
To: Chorus Club Members
Subject: Sunday's recording session in the civic auditorium

Dear members,
This Sunday afternoon, a local radio technician will record two of our songs in the civic auditorium for the winter youth music broadcast. Because the auditorium's microphones are sensitive enough to pick up rustling cloth and clicking jewelry, please wear soft cotton shirts without zippers, metal buttons, or bracelets.

We will enter through the backstage door on the west side at 1:15 p.m.; the front glass doors will stay locked because no audience is attending. Warm-up exercises begin at 1:30 p.m., and recording runs from 2:15 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.

Cold winter air dries vocal cords quickly, so bring a bottle of plain room-temperature water. Please avoid milk tea or sweet juice right before singing, as sugar and dairy can coat your throat and make clear high notes harder. Cough drops may be used during breaks, not while standing on the risers.

Let's enjoy making a recording we'll remember!
Mr. Shinohara

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第7回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Mist Vegetables Gently—and Leave Others Dry

Shoppers reaching for lettuce or broccoli in the produce aisle often hear a soft rumble of thunder from hidden speakers just before fine water droplets drift over the greens. Although the sound effect is playful, the misting system itself serves a practical purpose grounded in plant biology.

Even after harvest, leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, and parsley continue losing moisture through microscopic pores on their leaves. Because these greens have a large surface area and very thin outer skins, dry store air can leave them limp within hours, forcing grocers to throw away otherwise nutritious food. Periodic bursts of cool mist keep humidity high around the leaves and slow down wilting, while the brief sound warning lets customers step back so their sleeves stay dry.

Not every vegetable benefits from a shower, however. Onions, garlic, potatoes, and winter squash are stored in dry bins far from the mist nozzles. Evolved as underground bulbs or thick-skinned storage organs, these crops naturally resist drying out; getting them wet in a warm store actually encourages mold and premature sprouting. Tomatoes and mushrooms likewise spoil faster when damp.

In recent years, several grocery chains have replaced open misting with ultrasonic humidifiers that create fog droplets too tiny to wet surfaces. Because excess water no longer pools at the bottom of display trays, stores report less bacterial rot and longer shelf life.

Knowing how different vegetables respond to moisture helps shoppers at home too: leafy greens stay crisp wrapped in a slightly damp cloth in the fridge, whereas onions belong in a cool, dry basket.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第3回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Public Libraries Are Lending Household Tools

When people think of a public library, they naturally picture rows of novels, study desks, and children's picture books. Over the past decade, however, dozens of municipal libraries have quietly added a very different section: shelves stocked with electric drills, sewing machines, hedge trimmers, and kitchen food dehydrators that residents can borrow with an ordinary library card.

The idea grew out of a simple observation about modern apartments. Many tools are essential for an occasional task, such as putting up a bookshelf, hemming curtains, or pruning a backyard tree, yet sit unused in closets for the other 364 days of the year. Buying decent equipment is expensive, and small apartments rarely have extra storage space. Sharing durable tools across a neighborhood reduces both household spending and manufacturing waste.

In the port city of Westhaven, the central library launched its "Tool Corner" three years ago with forty donated items inspected by retired electricians and carpenters. Before borrowing power tools for the first time, residents watch a five-minute safety video and sign an agreement promising to return items clean. A modest late fee encourages borrowers to bring popular items back on schedule so weekend projects are not delayed for the next person.

Interestingly, library staff noticed an unexpected benefit. Residents who visited initially to borrow a sewing machine or bicycle repair stand often left with craft manuals, gardening guides, or cookbooks as well, bringing first-time adult visitors into the building.

Running a tool library still requires dedicated space and regular maintenance checks, so not every small branch can store heavy garden equipment. Even so, Westhaven's experience shows that libraries have always been about sharing knowledge and practical resources that strengthen daily community life.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第14回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Botanical Gardens Use Wood Libraries

When visitors stroll through a botanical garden or natural history museum, pressed leaves and dried blossoms in herbarium cabinets usually come to mind as plant collections. Tucked away in climate-controlled basements from Kew Gardens in London to Kyoto and Madison, Wisconsin, however, researchers curate a lesser-known archive that looks like a carpenter's dream bookshelf: thousands of polished rectangular blocks of wood shelved spine-out like hardcover novels, known as a "xylarium."

Carved from documented trees collected around the globe over the past two centuries, each block records a species' unique cellular architecture. Slice a sliver of wood thinner than tissue paper and place it under a microscope, and its water-conducting vessels, rays, and growth rings form a fingerprint as distinctive as human DNA—even decades after a tree was felled and turned into furniture or flooring.

That anatomical library now plays a frontline role against illegal logging, one of the world's most destructive wildlife crimes. Rare tropical rosewoods, mahoganies, and ebonies protected by international treaties look nearly identical to legal plantation timber once sawn into smooth planks and stacked inside shipping containers. Customs officers at ports used to rely on paper export certificates that smugglers easily forged.

By training portable machine-vision cameras and chemical spectrometers on verified xylarium blocks, wood anatomists have given border inspectors field tools that identify protected tree species on the dock within minutes.

Old museum blocks have helped art historians and luthiers too—dating medieval oak panels and matching repair wood for historic bridges—proving that carefully cataloged specimens gain unexpected value long after they are collected.

examples.script:
Why Coastal Towns Paint Lighthouses in Distinct Stripes

Postcards of seacoasts often show a tall white lighthouse standing on a rocky headland. Travel along an actual coastline, however, and you quickly notice that neighboring lighthouses rarely look identical: one wears bold red-and-white horizontal bands, another spirals like a black-and-white barber pole, and a third is painted solid yellow.

At night, sailors identify lighthouses by their unique flash rhythm—for instance, two quick flashes every ten seconds. During daylight hours, however, a flashing lamp is hard to spot against bright sky or sea glare. Before satellite navigation existed, captains steering along a foggy coast with binoculars needed an unmistakable visual daytime marker, known to mariners as a "daymark." Giving adjacent towers contrasting patterns ensured that (21).

Background scenery also guides color choice. A pure white tower stands out sharply against dark pine forests, yet vanishes against chalk cliffs or winter snowdrifts, where red bands remain vivid. Even today, when ships carry digital chart plotters, maritime authorities maintain these painted daymarks as (22) whenever electronics fail at sea.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第10回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Bakeries Slash Bread Dough Before Baking

Look closely at a crusty French baguette or country loaf, and you will notice diagonal cuts running neatly across the golden top. Home bakers often assume these slashes—known professionally as "scoring"—are merely a baker's artistic signature. While distinct patterns do help identify different loaves, a sharp blade actually solves a basic physics problem inside a hot oven.

The moment raw dough hits a hot baking stone, yeast activity surges and trapped water turns into steam, causing the loaf to puff up rapidly during the first ten minutes. Meanwhile, dry oven heat quickly hardens the outer skin into a firm crust. If no cuts have been made, expanding gas pushes against the weakest random spot on the side or bottom, tearing an uneven blowout and leaving the interior dense in one half and hollow in the other. Scoring creates deliberate expansion joints so the loaf (21).

Angle and depth matter too. Holding the blade nearly flat creates a thin flap of dough that peels back into a crisp, caramelized ridge prized for flavor. Thus, a two-second cut just before baking controls both (22).

Hannah Cole

examples.script:
Why Stadium Grass Needs Artificial Sunlight

Modern soccer stadiums are built with steep, covered stands that shelter tens of thousands of fans from rain and wind, while keeping cheers echoing loudly around the pitch. For the groundskeepers tending the natural grass field, however, those towering roofs create a stubborn problem: even at noon on a sunny day, large sections of turf remain in deep shadow.

Grass blades need sunlight for photosynthesis, especially in winter when matches tear up wet soil and natural daylight hours are short. Without enough light, shaded goal areas quickly turn muddy and bare. To keep the turf thick and safe for players' ankles, many stadiums wheel out wide aluminum rigs fitted with high-efficiency grow lamps between matches. Sensors in the soil measure temperature and moisture so lamps warm and illuminate only the weakest patches. This targeted care (21).

Although running grow rigs uses electricity, keeping natural turf healthy avoids costly mid-season resodding, where entire truckloads of grass must be stripped and replaced. Healthy roots hold the ground together, proving that great stadium architecture must consider (22) as carefully as spectator comfort.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第15回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Manhole Covers Are Almost Always Round

Walk down almost any city street in the world, and the heavy cast-iron plates covering underground sewer and utility shafts share one unmistakable shape: they are round. Meanwhile, sidewalk grates for rainwater, subway ventilation panels, and telecom curb boxes are often rectangular. That contrast is no accident of tradition—civil engineers settled on circular manhole covers for hard-headed safety and practical reasons.

Consider what happens when workers lift a fifty-kilogram rectangular lid to climb down a ladder. Turned diagonally, a rectangle is narrower across its short side than across its corner-to-corner diagonal, meaning a careless slip could send the heavy iron plate plunging edge-first onto a technician below. A circle, by contrast, has the exact same diameter at every angle; resting on a slightly narrower circular lip inside the frame, a round cover physically (21).

Round lids simplify manufacturing and street work too. Foundries can turn circular rims smoothly on a lathe, workers never have to rotate a heavy cover to match corners when putting it back, and one worker can roll a round plate on its edge like a wheel instead of straining their back. Geometry here quietly protects (22).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第6回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Curved Sidewalk Corners Shape Street Safety

Most pedestrians never think twice about the shape of a street corner where two sidewalks meet. Yet traffic engineers know that the radius of that curve—whether it forms a sharp ninety-degree turn or a wide, sweeping arc—has a direct effect on how fast cars turn and how safely people cross.

During the mid-twentieth century, many cities widened intersection corners into gentle curves so large trucks and buses could turn without slowing down much. While convenient for vehicles, wide curves had two drawbacks for walkers. First, drivers could swing around corners at twenty-five or thirty kilometers per hour while looking mainly for oncoming cars rather than people in the crosswalk. Second, rounding off the corner pushed the curb back, making the painted crosswalk several meters longer for children and older residents to cross.

In recent years, urban planners have been tightening residential and school-zone corners again. A tighter curb forces passenger cars to slow to walking pace before turning, giving drivers an extra second or two to spot someone stepping off the sidewalk. Extending the corner slightly—a design often called a "curb bulb"—also shortens the crossing distance and lets pedestrians see past parked cars without stepping into traffic.

What about fire engines and delivery trucks that still need room to turn? Engineers solve this in creative ways. On some corners, they build a low, textured stone apron beside the curb: ordinary cars stay off the bumpy surface, while the wide wheels of an emergency vehicle can roll slowly over it when necessary.

Small geometric changes in concrete rarely make headlines, yet reshaping a single corner can calm an entire neighborhood crossing every day of the year.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第10回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Pocket Parks Cool Busy Neighborhoods

When city governments talk about expanding green space, residents often picture sprawling central parks with boating ponds and long jogging loops. Finding ten empty hectares inside an already crowded district, however, is nearly impossible. Instead, urban planners from Tokyo to Madrid are turning tiny leftover plots—a vacant corner lot, a former gas station, or two unused parking spaces—into "pocket parks."

Measuring smaller than a tennis court, a single pocket park may hold just four shade trees, a permeable brick path, a drinking fountain, and three wooden benches. Modest as that sounds, grouping dozens of small green oases a five-minute walk apart changes how a neighborhood feels in summer. Tree canopies block direct solar heat on asphalt, while soil beds soak up sudden downpours that would otherwise flood storm drains.

Social researchers have noticed equally important human effects. Large destination parks require a planned weekend trip for elderly residents or parents with toddlers, whereas a bench beneath zelkova trees fifty meters from a grocery store invites spontaneous ten-minute rests every day. Regular eye contact among neighbors watering flower beds also builds informal community trust.

Maintaining thirty scattered mini-parks can stretch municipal gardening crews thin if handled centrally. Successful cities solve this by pairing public tree pruning with neighborhood "park friends" volunteers who sweep leaves, plant seasonal bulbs, and report broken lights.

Grand city parks remain irreplaceable treasures, yet weaving tiny green pockets into everyday streets proves that nature does not have to be huge to transform urban life.

examples.script:
Teaching Buses and Trains to Wait Two Minutes

Missing a rural connecting bus by ninety seconds can turn a twenty-minute commute into an hour-long wait on a windy platform. In large cities, where another train arrives every four minutes, tight transfers rarely matter. Along regional rail lines and suburban bus corridors, however, vehicles run far less frequently, so a single delayed train can strand dozens of passengers who needed that connection.

Historically, bus drivers had no reliable way to know whether an approaching train was running two minutes late or twenty. Waiting blindly risked making every downstream stop late and causing passengers further along the route to miss their own appointments. As a result, most operators instructed drivers to depart strictly by the printed clock, even if a train was just pulling into the station.

Low-cost GPS trackers and shared dispatch screens have begun changing this rigid rule. In several mid-sized European and Japanese cities, trains and connecting buses now exchange live location updates automatically. If a train is delayed by three minutes or less—and the bus schedule has enough cushion on a quiet stretch of road to make up that time—the screen on the driver's dashboard flashes a "hold" request. Meanwhile, an announcement inside the train tells transferring riders that their bus is waiting at Stand 2, preventing dangerous sprinting on station stairs.

Of course, holding a bus is not always wise. When heavy snow delays a train by fifteen minutes, holding every feeder bus would paralyze the entire local network. Dispatch software therefore sets clear upper limits, typically three to five minutes, and prioritizes the last evening runs when no later bus exists.

Passenger surveys in towns using smart-hold rules show a notable jump in trust toward public transit. Knowing that operators coordinate across vehicles makes people far more willing to leave their cars at home for two-seat journeys.

examples.script:
Why Bakery Windows Fog Up Less Than Before

On cold winter mornings, small bakeries face a practical display problem. Warm steam rising from fresh trays of bread meets the icy glass of the front window and turns into tiny water droplets. While a misty window looks cozy in picture books, shop owners dislike it when passersby cannot see which breads have just come out of the oven.

Turning up the heater near the glass dries the window, yet dry hot air also makes uncovered croissants and crusty loaves lose moisture faster. A baker in Matsumoto found a simpler fix after talking with a neighbor who repaired eyeglasses. By installing a quiet ceiling fan that kept air moving gently across the glass and leaving a two-centimeter vent open near the top frame, the shop prevented warm damp air from sitting still against the cold pane. This adjustment (21) without drying out the bread.

Keeping the window clear had a welcome effect on morning sales. Commuters walking to the station could spot steaming walnut rolls from across the street and step inside on impulse. Sometimes solving an everyday shop problem requires (22) rather than buying a bigger heater.

Why Ambulance Sirens Change Pitch as They Pass

Stand on a sidewalk as an ambulance or express train rushes past, and you hear a familiar sound pattern: the siren sounds noticeably higher-pitched while approaching you, then drops sharply in pitch the instant the vehicle passes and speeds away. The siren speaker on the roof hasn't changed its note at all—the driver inside hears the exact same tone the whole time. Physicists call this everyday shift the "Doppler effect."

Sound travels through air as invisible waves of compressed molecules, much like ripples spreading across a pond. While an ambulance sits parked at a red light, siren waves spread outward in evenly spaced circles in every direction. Once the vehicle races forward at sixty kilometers per hour, however, it chases after its own front sound waves, squeezing consecutive wave crests closer together ahead of the bumper and stretching them farther apart behind the rear doors. Because our ears perceive closer-spaced waves as a higher musical note, bystanders ahead (21).

Astronomers and meteorologists put this exact principle to work far beyond city streets. Weather radar bounces radio waves off moving raindrops to measure wind speeds inside typhoons, while shifting starlight tells astrophysicists whether distant galaxies are (22).
