examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Mist Vegetables Gently—and Leave Others Dry

Shoppers reaching for lettuce or broccoli in the produce aisle often hear a soft rumble of thunder from hidden speakers just before fine water droplets drift over the greens. Although the sound effect is playful, the misting system itself serves a practical purpose grounded in plant biology.

Even after harvest, leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, and parsley continue losing moisture through microscopic pores on their leaves. Because these greens have a large surface area and very thin outer skins, dry store air can leave them limp within hours, forcing grocers to throw away otherwise nutritious food. Periodic bursts of cool mist keep humidity high around the leaves and slow down wilting, while the brief sound warning lets customers step back so their sleeves stay dry.

Not every vegetable benefits from a shower, however. Onions, garlic, potatoes, and winter squash are stored in dry bins far from the mist nozzles. Evolved as underground bulbs or thick-skinned storage organs, these crops naturally resist drying out; getting them wet in a warm store actually encourages mold and premature sprouting. Tomatoes and mushrooms likewise spoil faster when damp.

In recent years, several grocery chains have replaced open misting with ultrasonic humidifiers that create fog droplets too tiny to wet surfaces. Because excess water no longer pools at the bottom of display trays, stores report less bacterial rot and longer shelf life.

Knowing how different vegetables respond to moisture helps shoppers at home too: leafy greens stay crisp wrapped in a slightly damp cloth in the fridge, whereas onions belong in a cool, dry basket.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第15回（1本文・計2問）
examples.script:
Why Manhole Covers Are Almost Always Round

Walk down almost any city street in the world, and the heavy cast-iron plates covering underground sewer and utility shafts share one unmistakable shape: they are round. Meanwhile, sidewalk grates for rainwater, subway ventilation panels, and telecom curb boxes are often rectangular. That contrast is no accident of tradition—civil engineers settled on circular manhole covers for hard-headed safety and practical reasons.

Consider what happens when workers lift a fifty-kilogram rectangular lid to climb down a ladder. Turned diagonally, a rectangle is narrower across its short side than across its corner-to-corner diagonal, meaning a careless slip could send the heavy iron plate plunging edge-first onto a technician below. A circle, by contrast, has the exact same diameter at every angle; resting on a slightly narrower circular lip inside the frame, a round cover physically (21).

Round lids simplify manufacturing and street work too. Foundries can turn circular rims smoothly on a lathe, workers never have to rotate a heavy cover to match corners when putting it back, and one worker can roll a round plate on its edge like a wheel instead of straining their back. Geometry here quietly protects (22).

Changes to the Food Festival

From: Luis, Festival Coordinator
To: Volunteers
Subject: Please read before Saturday

Dear volunteers,
Thank you for helping at our international food festival. There have been two important changes. First, heavy rain is expected, so the festival will take place inside the community center rather than in the park. The center has enough space for all the food tables, but the entrance is narrow. Please arrive at the back door to help move supplies.

Second, the local bus company cannot provide the extra morning service we requested. Some visitors may arrive later than planned. We will therefore begin serving food at 11:30 instead of 11:00. Volunteers should still arrive at 9:00, as originally arranged. We need that time to set up the tables and check the kitchen equipment.

If you are helping at a food table, please bring a clean apron. We will provide gloves and name tags. Volunteers at the information desk do not need aprons. Those who have not yet chosen a job should contact me by Thursday evening.

Finally, please avoid bringing your own cars because parking spaces must be kept for delivery vehicles. The number 6 bus stops directly outside the center. I will send a map with the entrance marked tomorrow.

Best wishes,
Luis

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第2回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Small Bakeries Are Changing Their Schedules

In many towns, traditional bakeries used to display full trays of every kind of bread from early morning until closing time. Customers appreciated seeing abundant choices even late in the afternoon. Behind the scenes, however, keeping shelves full all day meant that unsold loaves frequently had to be thrown away at night, increasing ingredient costs and food waste.

Recently, a growing number of independent bakers have moved away from this model. At Sunrise Crust Bakery, for example, the owner noticed from sales records that crusty dinner rolls sold mostly after four o'clock, whereas fruit pastries were popular before ten in the morning. Instead of baking everything at dawn and hoping it would sell, the bakery began baking smaller batches tailored to each time of day.

At first, the owner worried that customers would complain if a particular item ran out early. When the bakery placed a simple chalkboard schedule outside the door showing what came out of the oven at 8:00 a.m., noon, and 4:00 p.m., customers reacted positively. Commuters started timing their visits to buy warm bread straight from the oven.

To handle the small amount of bread still left at closing time, Sunrise Crust partnered with a nearby evening soup kitchen and offered next-morning "surprise bags" at half price. While small-batch baking requires more careful planning by kitchen staff, the owner found that cutting daily waste allowed the shop to buy higher-quality local flour without raising prices.

Food researchers note that customers' expectations play a major role in reducing retail waste. When shoppers understand that an empty tray late in the day reflects careful production rather than poor service, neighborhood shops can operate far more sustainably.

Borrowing Snowshoes for the Winter Nature Walk

From: Kogen Nature Center
To: Registered Participants
Subject: Footwear and arrival time for Sunday's snowshoe walk

Dear participants,
We look forward to welcoming you to Sunday's guided snowshoe walk through Shirakaba Woods. Light snow fell yesterday, leaving forty centimeters of fresh powder along the trail—ideal conditions for beginners!

If you reserved rental snowshoes on your application form, please arrive at the nature center by 9:10 a.m., twenty minutes before the walk starts, so staff can adjust the straps to fit your boots. Note that we rent only snowshoes, not winter boots. You must wear waterproof hiking boots or tall snow boots that cover your ankles; low sneakers allow snow inside and slip out of the bindings.

Walking on snow warms the body faster than people expect. Instead of one thick down coat, wear two or three breathable layers that you can unzip or put in your backpack during uphill sections. Hot herb tea will be served in the log cabin after we return at noon; bring your own insulated mug if you have one.

Warm regards,
Kogen Nature Center Staff

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級 第5回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Public Clocks Still Matter in the Smartphone Era

Almost everyone walking through a train station plaza or town square today carries an exact atomic-synced clock in a coat pocket. At first glance, spending municipal money to maintain large analog clocks on towers, schools, and park posts might seem outdated. Yet when cities remove broken public clocks instead of repairing them, residents surprisingly often petition to bring them back.

One reason is practical convenience in moments when hands are occupied. A parent holding a toddler's hand, a cyclist waiting at an intersection, or a commuter carrying grocery bags in winter gloves can check a clock face in half a second without unzipping a pocket. Even more importantly, pulling out a smartphone just to check the time frequently leads to unintended distraction—one glance at a notification banner, and five minutes vanish.

Urban designers point to a subtler social role as well. Unlike a private screen, a public clock creates a shared reference point in physical space. Saying "Let's meet under the station clock at two" gives friends and visitors an unmistakable landmark visible from across a crowded square. During major power or cellular outages following storms, wind-up or battery-backed tower clocks have also continued marking time calmly when digital displays went dark.

Maintaining outdoor clocks does require skilled hands. Gears exposed to freezing rain, sea breeze, and nesting birds must be cleaned and lubricated regularly, and fewer young technicians train in turret clockwork today. To keep costs manageable, some towns pair modern solar-charged movements behind historic dial faces, preserving the familiar look while simplifying upkeep.

Far from being mere nostalgia, a well-placed town clock quietly supports punctual, unhurried movement through shared streets.

Borrowing Musical Scores from the Regional Archive

From: Prefectural Youth Orchestra Library
To: Section Leaders
Subject: Handling rules for borrowed orchestral sheet music

Dear section leaders,
Sheet music folders for our winter symphony program are ready to pick up starting tomorrow afternoon. Because two of the pieces are rented from a national music publisher under a strict contract, please share these handling rules with everyone in your instrument section before the first rehearsal.

Players may write bowings, breath marks, and fingerings ONLY with soft 2B or 4B lead pencils. Ballpoint pens, highlighters, and erasable friction pens are strictly forbidden—friction-pen ink can reappear in cold delivery trucks even after being rubbed out, resulting in heavy replacement fines from the publisher.

Do not remove staples or tape loose pages together. If a page tear makes turning difficult on the stand, bring the folder to the orchestra librarian before rehearsal so archival paper tape can be applied cleanly. All numbered folders must be returned with markings fully erased within three days after the December concert.

Thank you for your care,
M. Kurosawa, Orchestra Librarian

examples.script:
Preparing Audio Files for the Regional Drama Contest

From: Stage Technical Desk, Civic Theater
To: High School Drama Club Sound Operators
Subject: Sound file format and backup rules for Sunday's contest

Dear sound operators,
We look forward to supporting your technical rehearsal and performance this Sunday. Every year, at least one school experiences a playback hiccup because of file settings, so please check these requirements before Friday.

Submit all music cues and sound effects on a USB flash drive formatted in FAT32 or exFAT, saved as uncompressed WAV files (48 kHz, 16-bit). Do not rely on smartphones, Bluetooth receivers, or streaming apps in the booth—theater concrete walls block cellular signals, and notification chimes or automatic system updates can interrupt a quiet dramatic scene.

Name each file starting with a three-digit cue number in performance order (for example, "001_rain_intro.wav", "002_doorbell.wav"). In addition, bring an audio CD or a second identical USB drive in a separate bag as an emergency backup.

Stage Technical Desk

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 長文読解練習（基礎ウォームアップ・2本文・計4問）
examples.script:
An open rehearsal with a closed door

The Riverbank Orchestra wanted more local residents to attend its rehearsals. It made admission free and advertised that no knowledge of classical music was needed. Yet the audience remained mostly unchanged. A student volunteer suggested speaking to people who had never attended, rather than asking regular visitors what they enjoyed. These conversations revealed a practical problem: the building entrance was locked once rehearsal began, so anyone delayed at work could not enter. The orchestra arranged for a volunteer to remain near the entrance during the first half hour. Attendance increased, particularly among people working nearby. The free admission still mattered, but it had not solved the timing problem. The orchestra now checks whether its arrangements match the daily routines of the people it hopes to welcome.

We have pulled the six nineteenth-century coastal survey maps your teachers requested for Saturday's 1:30 p.m. research appointment in the Third-Floor Archive Reading Room.

Because hand-colored rice-paper maps tear and stain easily, all backpacks, coats, pens, highlighters, and bottled drinks must be locked in the hallway lockers before entering. examples.script:
Borrowing time

A city library introduced appointments for help with digital devices. Each appointment lasted twenty minutes. Staff could keep to the schedule easily when a visitor had one simple question. However, some visitors needed to explain a longer series of problems before staff understood the situation. Extending every appointment would have reduced the number of people the library could serve. Instead, the library added a short conversation at the booking stage. Staff now ask what the visitor hopes to do, rather than only which device they own. They can then choose a standard slot or arrange a longer session. The system is not perfect: some problems still take longer than expected. Nevertheless, fewer sessions now end before the main difficulty has even been identified.

examples.script:
Guidelines for the High School Career Shadowing Day

From: Takashi Miura, Career Guidance Coordinator
To: Second-Year Students
Subject: Next Wednesday's workplace visits

Dear students,
Next Wednesday, November 18, all second-year students will visit local workplaces, including clinics, architectural offices, bakeries, and city departments, to observe professionals at work. Please check the bulletin board outside the guidance room today to confirm your assigned host organization and travel group.

Each group will travel directly from home to its host site rather than coming to school first. Plan to arrive ten minutes before your scheduled start time. If your train or bus is delayed, call both the school office and the contact number listed on your assignment sheet immediately.

During the visit, remember that staff members are handling real patients, clients, and deadlines. You are encouraged to ask questions during the designated Q&A session, not while employees are speaking with customers. Taking written notes in your handbook is welcome, whereas taking photographs or recording audio on smartphones is strictly prohibited to protect workplace privacy.

By the following Monday, please submit a one-page reflection sheet AND a handwritten thank-you card addressed to your host supervisor. Our office will check the cards for formal wording before mailing them together.

Best regards,
Takashi Miura

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第4回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Guidelines for the Inter-School Science Poster Exchange

From: Ms. Fujita, Science Committee Coordinator
To: Presenting Student Teams
Subject: Poster tube labels and presentation timing for Saturday

Dear student teams,
Twelve high schools will gather in our gymnasium this Saturday for the Prefectural Youth Science Poster Exchange. Please read these practical details carefully so setup goes smoothly in the morning.

Each team has been assigned a numbered display panel measuring 90 centimeters wide by 120 centimeters tall. Bring your printed A0 poster rolled inside a protective tube—do not fold it, as creases cast shadows under the gym spotlights and make small graphs hard to read. We will supply removable paper tape; thumbtacks and strong double-sided tape are prohibited because the panels are rented from the city hall.

To make sure every presenter also gets to view other schools' research, the two-hour session is split into odd-numbered and even-numbered rounds. Odd-numbered teams will stand by their panels for the first hour while even-numbered teams circulate, and then roles will reverse at 11:00 a.m. At least one member of your team must remain at your panel throughout your assigned hour.

Lunch boxes may be eaten in the second-floor cafeteria, not inside the gymnasium.

Best wishes,
R. Fujita

examples.script:
Instructions for Borrowing Rare Maps in the Archive Room

From: Special Collections Desk, Prefectural Central Library
To: High School Local History Research Groups
Subject: Pencil-only rule and cotton weights for Saturday's map session

Dear student researchers,
We have pulled the six nineteenth-century coastal survey maps your teachers requested for Saturday's 1:30 p.m. research appointment in the Third-Floor Archive Reading Room.

Because hand-colored rice-paper maps tear and stain easily, all backpacks, coats, pens, highlighters, and bottled drinks must be locked in the hallway lockers before entering. You may bring only loose note sheets, a laptop or tablet (camera flash turned off), and wooden graphite pencils; mechanical pencils are not allowed because thin snapped leads can get trapped in map folds and scratch pigment.

Please use the soft cloth-covered lead "snake weights" on the tables—never your elbows or textbooks—to hold curled map corners flat.

Special Collections Staff

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 長文読解練習（基礎ウォームアップ・2本文・計4問）
examples.script:
Borrowing time

A city library introduced appointments for help with digital devices. Each appointment lasted twenty minutes. Staff could keep to the schedule easily when a visitor had one simple question. However, some visitors needed to explain a longer series of problems before staff understood the situation. Extending every appointment would have reduced the number of people the library could serve. Instead, the library added a short conversation at the booking stage. Staff now ask what the visitor hopes to do, rather than only which device they own. They can then choose a standard slot or arrange a longer session. The system is not perfect: some problems still take longer than expected. Nevertheless, fewer sessions now end before the main difficulty has even been identified.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第10回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Escalator Brushes Line the Bottom of Every Side Skirt

Look down beside your shoes the next time you ride a station escalator, and you will see stiff black nylon bristles sticking out just above the moving metal steps. Playful commuters occasionally brush dust off their sneakers against them, assuming that shoe cleaning is why engineers put them there. In reality, those "skirt deflector brushes" are a mandatory safety device.

Escalator steps must glide past stationary side panels with a tiny clearance gap of a few millimeters. Without a physical reminder, passengers standing too close to the wall risk having soft rubber rain boots, long coat hems, or dangling shoelaces pulled into that narrow gap as steps fold flat at the landing. Stiff bristles tickle ankles gently the instant a foot drifts sideways. (18), riders instinctively shift half a step toward the safe center of the tread without even looking down.

Brushes help maintenance crews indirectly as well. Coins, ticket stubs, and small pebbles dropped from pockets bounce off the angled bristles instead of wedging into moving gears underneath. (19), mechanics inspect worn or bent brush strips every month just as carefully as brakes.

A row of simple nylon bristles illustrates how subtle tactile cues can (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第3回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Borrowing Tablets for the Field Survey

From: Mr. Watanabe, Geography Department
To: Fieldwork Group Leaders
Subject: Tablet checkout and offline maps for Thursday

Hello group leaders,
For Thursday's land-use survey around Kawagoe District, each group will receive one school tablet preloaded with our mapping app. Because mobile data reception can be weak near the old canal, you must download your assigned sector's offline map onto the tablet before leaving campus. Come to the geography prep room during Wednesday lunch break to check out your device and complete the download over school Wi-Fi.

During the survey, use the app to mark building types and photograph street signs, but avoid photographing private house nameplates or pedestrians' faces. Each tablet comes with a shoulder strap; whoever is carrying the device must wear the strap at all times when walking near water.

All groups must return to school by 3:45 p.m. so data can be backed up before club activities begin at 4:15 p.m. Do not delete accidental photos in the field—you might erase shared group pins by mistake. We will sort the files together back in the classroom.

Regards,
K. Watanabe

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第2回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Audio Labels in the Supermarket

For shoppers with poor eyesight, choosing between dozens of similar-looking cans and boxes in a supermarket can be exhausting. Price tags on shelf edges are often printed in tiny type, and packaging designs change frequently without warning. Even regular customers may hesitate to pick up an unfamiliar brand if they cannot easily check cooking instructions or allergy warnings.

To address this problem, a regional grocery chain tested small raised QR stickers on its own-brand food packages. Unlike ordinary promotional codes that open long marketing pages, these tactile stickers can be located by touch and scanned from a wide angle. A smartphone immediately reads aloud the product name, weight, expiry rule, and allergy ingredients. (18), shoppers do not need to align the camera precisely with a small symbol.

Feedback from visually impaired testers led to one further improvement. Early versions read every piece of text from top to bottom, forcing listeners to wait thirty seconds before hearing whether an item contained nuts or dairy. Designers reorganized the spoken order so critical safety details came first, making the labels (19).

Unexpectedly, other customers began using the stickers too, including elderly shoppers who had left reading glasses at home and foreign residents checking unfamiliar ingredients. Designing for a specific barrier ended up creating (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準2級プラス 第5回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Keeping Bus Timetables Readable for Everyone

Public transit agencies pack an impressive amount of data onto a single bus-stop sign: weekday runs, Saturday schedules, holiday exceptions, fare zones, and route branches. For regular commuters who ride the same 7:42 a.m. bus every day, dense columns of tiny numbers soon become familiar. For an occasional rider, an older resident with declining eyesight, or a visitor standing in the rain, however, reading that grid can feel like solving a puzzle.

When a coastal city redesigned its three hundred bus-stop poles, designers began by watching people actually use the signs. Many riders traced rows with a finger because closely spaced lines caused their eyes to jump from the 8:00 row to the 9:00 row. Simply increasing font size was not enough on narrow poles, so the team removed repeated minute labels, grouped departures by morning, midday, and evening bands, and added subtle gray shading to every second row. (21), misreading errors in user tests dropped by more than half.

Equally helpful was replacing text-heavy footnotes—such as "Buses marked with a triangle bypass Harbor Hospital on Sundays"—with a small diagram showing the two route branches visually. Riders grasped where each numbered bus went in seconds rather than hunting for tiny symbols at the bottom of the board. (22), high-contrast black ink on matte yellow-white panels reduced glare under both midday sun and streetlamps.

Digital arrival apps are convenient, yet batteries die and tourists may lack data plans. Treating the humble bus-stop sign as serious information design ensures that (23).

examples.script:
How Ferries Cut Fuel Use with Wind Rotor Sails

When people picture wind-powered ships, they usually imagine canvas sails billowing from wooden masts. Modern car ferries and cargo vessels look nothing like nineteenth-century clippers, yet a growing number now carry tall, spinning white cylinders on their decks to capture wind energy alongside regular engines.

These cylinders, known as rotor sails, rely on a physical principle familiar to baseball pitchers and tennis players. When a motor spins the vertical cylinder slowly in a crosswind, air speeds up on one side of the drum and slows down on the other. The resulting pressure difference pushes the ship forward at right angles to the wind. Because the motor spinning the cylinder uses only a tiny fraction of the thrust generated, ferries crossing windy straits can throttle back their main diesel engines. (21), operators on North Sea routes have recorded fuel savings of eight to fifteen percent.

Unlike fabric sails, rotor cylinders require no extra deck crew to hoist or fold when squalls hit; bridge computers adjust rotation speed automatically as wind direction changes. (22), some designs tilt flat onto the deck at the push of a button so the ship can pass safely beneath low harbor bridges.

Rotor sails cannot power a heavy ferry on calm days, nor are they meant to work alone. Rather, combining aerodynamic physics with modern automation gives shipping lines (23) while cleaner fuels are still scaling up.

examples.script:
Why Groceries Use Curved Shopping Cart Tracks on Ramps

Multi-story supermarkets in compact city neighborhoods face a logistical puzzle: how can customers move heavy carts full of milk, rice, and vegetables smoothly between floors? Ordinary passenger elevators fill up after just two or three carts, while regular stepped escalators cannot carry wheeled baskets safely.

Many urban stores solve this with inclined moving walkways—flat, grooved metal belts that climb slowly from floor to floor. At first glance, keeping a thirty-kilogram cart from rolling backward down a twelve-degree slope looks risky, especially if a shopper lets go of the handle to check a shopping list. Yet no motors or handbrakes are attached to the carts themselves. (18), the secret lies in the precise spacing of the cart's wheels and the narrow slots cut into the walkway floor.

As a cart rolls onto the ramp, its thin rubber tires drop neatly between raised metal ribs, allowing the slightly wider brake pads beside each wheel to rest directly on top of the ribs. Friction between those pads and the metal surface locks the cart firmly in place until it reaches the flat landing at the top, where a gentle comb plate lifts the tires out again. (19), shoppers can ride hands-free without fear of a runaway basket.

Because every cart wheel must match the walkway's rib width to the millimeter, stores cannot mix carts from different manufacturers. This quiet mechanical partnership shows how (20).

Why Supermarkets Angle Aisles and End-Cap Displays Carefully

Shoppers pushing a cart down a grocery aisle often feel they are browsing freely, yet the width of lanes and the displays at the ends of shelves—known in retail as "end caps"—are planned with surprising care. Store designers study foot-traffic patterns to balance smooth movement with product discovery.

End-cap shelves facing the main perimeter walkway command huge attention because shoppers slow down to turn their carts into the next aisle. Manufacturers compete fiercely to place seasonal soup, pasta sauce, or tea on those prime corners. Shoppers frequently assume every item stacked high on an end cap is deeply discounted, even when the price tag shows the regular shelf price. (18), careful buyers check the unit price per hundred grams before tossing an end-cap item into their cart.

Aisle width shapes behavior just as strongly. Make an aisle too narrow, and whenever two carts pass, nobody dares stop to compare nutrition labels—a phenomenon retail researchers call the "butt-brush effect," where crowded shoppers hurry away without buying. Widening high-margin aisles slightly gives customers comfortable breathing room. (19), placing everyday staples like milk and eggs at the far back draws visitors past dozens of other shelves along the way.

Recognizing these quiet layout strategies lets shoppers navigate stores efficiently while (20).

examples.script:
An open rehearsal with a closed door

The Riverbank Orchestra wanted more local residents to attend its rehearsals. It made admission free and advertised that no knowledge of classical music was needed. Yet the audience remained mostly unchanged. A student volunteer suggested speaking to people who had never attended, rather than asking regular visitors what they enjoyed. These conversations revealed a practical problem: the building entrance was locked once rehearsal began, so anyone delayed at work could not enter. The orchestra arranged for a volunteer to remain near the entrance during the first half hour. Attendance increased, particularly among people working nearby. The free admission still mattered, but it had not solved the timing problem. The orchestra now checks whether its arrangements match the daily routines of the people it hopes to welcome.

Why Library Archives Freeze Wet Books After a Pipe Leak

Discovering a burst water pipe above a library's rare-book stack is every archivist's nightmare. Within forty-eight hours at room temperature, damp paper swells, leather bindings warp, ink bleeds across pages, and black mold spores erupt across irreplaceable local histories. Trying to fan-dry two thousand soaked volumes one by one with hair dryers or paper towels is physically impossible before mold wins the race.

Counterintuitively, conservation scientists respond to water emergencies not with heat, but with industrial blast freezers. Workers slip soaked books into wax-paper sleeves, pack them spine-down in crates, and rush them into cold-storage warehouses kept below minus twenty degrees Celsius. Freezing halts mold growth and ink spreading in their tracks, buying conservators months to plan careful treatment. (18), turning liquid water into solid ice sets up a remarkable drying shortcut.

Batches of frozen books move into a vacuum freeze-drying chamber modeled on equipment used for instant coffee and astronaut food. Inside a near-vacuum, ice crystals locked between paper fibers sublimate—turning directly from solid ice into water vapor without ever melting back into liquid water. (19), coated art pages that would glue themselves permanently shut if air-dried come out separate, flat, and readable.

Rapid freezing and sublimation show how applying phase-change physics can (20).

Why Libraries Lend Musical Instruments and Tools

Public libraries built their reputation on lending books, magazines, and music recordings. Over the past decade, however, hundreds of municipal libraries have added an unexpected shelf near the circulation desk—a "library of things" stocked with sewing machines, ukuleles, stargazing telescopes, and household tool kits.

The idea addresses a practical pattern of modern living. Many apartment dwellers want to mend a torn curtain once a year, test whether a child enjoys playing an instrument before buying one, or observe a lunar eclipse on a single clear evening. Buying, storing, and maintaining specialized equipment for occasional use strains both family budgets and closet space. (18), sharing sturdy items across a neighborhood keeps dozens of rarely used machines from gathering dust.

Running such a collection takes planning, of course. Librarians work with local repair volunteers to check returned drills and tune stringed instruments between loans, and borrowers sign a brief safety checklist. Surprisingly, damage rates have stayed low; patrons treat shared equipment with care because (19).

Beyond saving money, tool and instrument lending has brought new faces through library doors. Hands-on items show that a public library is ultimately dedicated to (20), whatever form learning happens to take.

From: Takashi Miura, Career Guidance Coordinator
To: Second-Year Students
Subject: Next Wednesday's workplace visits

Dear students,
Next Wednesday, November 18, all second-year students will visit local workplaces, including clinics, architectural offices, bakeries, and city departments, to observe professionals at work. Please check the bulletin board outside the guidance room today to confirm your assigned host organization and travel group.

Each group will travel directly from home to its host site rather than coming to school first. Plan to arrive ten minutes before your scheduled start time. If your train or bus is delayed, call both the school office and the contact number listed on your assignment sheet immediately.

During the visit, remember that staff members are handling real patients, clients, and deadlines. You are encouraged to ask questions during the designated Q&A session, not while employees are speaking with customers. Taking written notes in your handbook is welcome, whereas taking photographs or recording audio on smartphones is strictly prohibited to protect workplace privacy.

By the following Monday, please submit a one-page reflection sheet AND a handwritten thank-you card addressed to your host supervisor. Our office will check the cards for formal wording before mailing them together.

Best regards,
Takashi Miura

Guidelines for Borrowing Astronomical Telescopes

From: Earth Science Club Equipment Team
To: First-Year Club Members
Subject: Mandatory training and dew-shield rule for home telescope loans

Hi first-year members,
Starting June 1, members who have completed our thirty-minute setup workshop may borrow one of the club's four portable refractor telescopes over the weekend to observe the Moon and Jupiter from home!

Before signing the loan book, please remember two care rules that protect delicate optical coatings. First, attach the long black plastic dew shield to the front tube every evening you observe; clear nights cool the glass lens rapidly, causing moisture to condense on it within minutes.

Second, if morning dew or mist DOES form on the objective lens, NEVER wipe it with tissues, handkerchiefs, or shirt sleeves—tiny dust fibers scratch anti-reflection coatings permanently. Simply bring the uncapped tube indoors, point it slightly downward in a dry room until the moisture evaporates naturally, and only then put the dust cap back on.

Clear skies,
Equipment Team

examples.script:
How Acoustic Panels Quiet Noisy Restaurants

Anyone who has strained to hear a friend across a trendy café table knows the culprit: minimalist interiors with exposed concrete ceilings, glass walls, and hardwood floors. Hard, smooth surfaces look sleek in magazines, yet they reflect ninety-five percent of sound energy right back into the dining room. As background chatter rises, every table talks louder to compensate—a runaway spiral acousticians call the "Lombard effect."

Hanging heavy velvet curtains everywhere would deaden echoes, but many restaurateurs dislike bulky fabrics that trap cooking odors or clash with modern lighting. Acoustic engineers have responded with stealth sound absorbers disguised as everyday architecture. Micro-perforated wooden slats, recycled PET felt baffles painted to match ceiling beams, and even framed wall art backed with mineral wool swallow mid-range speech frequencies instead of bouncing them around. (21), placing thin felt pads under chair legs and rubber mounts beneath espresso grinders stops structure-borne clatter at its source.

Crucially, the goal in a lively bistro is not library silence; a room that is too dead makes diners feel self-conscious that neighboring tables can hear every whisper. Tuning absorption to keep reverberation under roughly half a second preserves a warm buzz while restoring effortless conversation. (22), guests linger comfortably for dessert, and servers make fewer order mistakes.

Thoughtful acoustic design proves that how a room sounds shapes hospitality (23).

Rethinking Nighttime Lighting in Parks

Bright streetlamps have long been installed in urban parks to help pedestrians see footpaths and feel secure after sunset. In recent years, however, ecologists and lighting engineers have pointed out an unintended side effect: unshielded white lamps scatter glare into surrounding trees and ponds, disrupting nocturnal insects, bats, and roosting birds.

When a riverside town decided to replace its aging park lamps, officials initially assumed they had to choose between human safety and wildlife protection. Turning lights off completely made evening joggers uneasy. Yet consultations with lighting specialists revealed a third approach. By fitting hoods that directed light strictly downward and shifting from harsh blue-white LEDs to warmer amber tones, the town could keep paths clearly visible while leaving tree canopies dark. (18), motion sensors dimmed secondary trails late at night when nobody was walking past.

Six months after the upgrade, insect surveys along the riverbank showed a marked recovery in moth diversity compared with brightly lit neighboring streets. Residents also responded positively; many noted that shielded lamps actually made it easier to see obstacles on the ground because (19).

The project demonstrated that environmental care does not always demand giving up public convenience. Often, the real problem lies in wasted energy—in this case, light shining into the sky where no walker needs it. Careful design allowed the park to (20).

examples.script:
How Pumped-Storage Hydropower Acts as a Giant Water Battery

Solar panels and wind turbines now generate affordable clean electricity across much of the world, yet both share a familiar limitation: clouds hide the sun, calm evenings stall wind blades, and peak household demand arrives after sunset when people cook dinner and heat baths. Storing gigawatts of daytime surplus power for evening use has become one of the central engineering challenges of modern grids. Surprisingly, more than ninety percent of large-scale energy storage operating globally today relies not on chemical lithium batteries, but on gravity and water.

Known as "pumped-storage hydropower," the concept uses two water reservoirs sitting at different elevations—typically separated by several hundred meters of vertical mountainside and connected by a steep underground tunnel. At midday, when rooftop solar panels flood the grid with cheap electricity, reversible turbines spin backward as pumps, pushing millions of cubic meters of water from the lower lake up into the mountain reservoir. After dusk, when power demand spikes, operators open the intake gates: stored water rushes back downhill through the same turbines, spinning generators that reach full output within ninety seconds.

Round-trip efficiency reaches roughly seventy-five to eighty percent—meaning three-quarters of the electricity used to pump water uphill comes back onto the grid—and concrete reservoirs last well over half a century without losing capacity the way phone batteries degrade after a thousand charge cycles.

Geography sets strict limits, of course. Flat coastal plains lack the elevation drop needed, and flooding pristine mountain valleys for new reservoirs raises serious ecological concerns. Engineers are therefore exploring closed-loop designs in abandoned deep-pit mines that never touch natural rivers.

Chemical batteries will keep growing rapidly for cars and neighborhood substations, yet wherever mountains meet sunny grids, uphill water remains clean energy's heaviest lifter.

How Repair Cafés Extend Product Lifespans and Neighborhood Ties

Buy an electric toaster, desk fan, or winter coat today, and a single snapped switch or stuck zipper often sends the entire item to the trash bin. Manufacturers frequently seal plastic housings with glue rather than screws, while commercial repair shops must charge labor fees that rival the price of a cheap replacement. Across more than two thousand towns worldwide—having started in Amsterdam in 2009—community volunteers have built a welcoming response: the monthly "Repair Café."

Held in libraries, church basements, or civic centers on Saturday afternoons, a Repair Café pairs retired engineers, tailors, carpenters, and tech-savvy students with neighbors carrying broken household goods. Visitors pay nothing except optional donations for spare fuses or thread. Crucially, the café is not a drop-off counter; owners pull up a chair and hold the flashlight or screwdriver alongside the fixer. (21), demystifying how a coffee maker or bicycle brake works gives people confidence to tackle minor upkeep at home.

Volunteer groups log every attempted repair in a shared international database, successfully reviving roughly two-thirds of items brought in. Beyond keeping tons of metals and textiles out of landfills, those records now inform "right-to-repair" lawmakers pressing appliance makers to supply spare parts and screw-together designs. (22), elderly craftspeople living alone gain a lively monthly venue where younger neighbors genuinely value their decades of practical skill.

Sharing tools over a cup of tea shows how local grassroots action can (23).

From: Ms. Fujita, Science Committee Coordinator
To: Presenting Student Teams
Subject: Poster tube labels and presentation timing for Saturday

Dear student teams,
Twelve high schools will gather in our gymnasium this Saturday for the Prefectural Youth Science Poster Exchange. Please read these practical details carefully so setup goes smoothly in the morning.

Each team has been assigned a numbered display panel measuring 90 centimeters wide by 120 centimeters tall. Bring your printed A0 poster rolled inside a protective tube—do not fold it, as creases cast shadows under the gym spotlights and make small graphs hard to read. We will supply removable paper tape; thumbtacks and strong double-sided tape are prohibited because the panels are rented from the city hall.

To make sure every presenter also gets to view other schools' research, the two-hour session is split into odd-numbered and even-numbered rounds. Odd-numbered teams will stand by their panels for the first hour while even-numbered teams circulate, and then roles will reverse at 11:00 a.m. At least one member of your team must remain at your panel throughout your assigned hour.

Lunch boxes may be eaten in the second-floor cafeteria, not inside the gymnasium.

Best wishes,
R. Fujita

How Sponge Sidewalks Help Cities Handle Cloudbursts

Summer weather in many temperate cities has grown more uneven: weeks of dry heat are increasingly interrupted by intense one-hour cloudbursts that dump a month's rain in a single afternoon. Conventional streets paved from wall to wall with waterproof asphalt funnel every liter of rain straight into underground storm pipes. When pipes reach capacity, intersections flood while tree roots two meters below the pavement remain bone-dry.

To break this paradox, civil engineers are redesigning sidewalks as "rain gardens" and permeable pavements—part of what urban hydrologists call "sponge cities." Replacing solid concrete slabs along curb lanes with porous interlocking bricks, crushed-gravel trenches, and shallow planted basins lets rainwater soak straight into engineered soil beds beneath pedestrians' feet. (21), peak runoff entering municipal storm drains during a sudden downpour can drop by forty percent or more.

Storing moisture underground pays off weeks later when clear, hot weather returns. Street trees draw on that trapped soil water and release cool vapor through their leaves, lowering sidewalk temperatures noticeably. (22), gravel layers and plant roots filter brake dust and oil droplets out of street water before it seeps toward rivers.

Retrofitting every avenue takes years of utility coordination, so cities prioritize flood-prone low spots first. Step by step, porous streets turn sudden rain from an urban hazard into (23).

examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Angle Aisles and End-Cap Displays Carefully

Shoppers pushing a cart down a grocery aisle often feel they are browsing freely, yet the width of lanes and the displays at the ends of shelves—known in retail as "end caps"—are planned with surprising care. Store designers study foot-traffic patterns to balance smooth movement with product discovery.

End-cap shelves facing the main perimeter walkway command huge attention because shoppers slow down to turn their carts into the next aisle. Manufacturers compete fiercely to place seasonal soup, pasta sauce, or tea on those prime corners. Shoppers frequently assume every item stacked high on an end cap is deeply discounted, even when the price tag shows the regular shelf price. (18), careful buyers check the unit price per hundred grams before tossing an end-cap item into their cart.

Aisle width shapes behavior just as strongly. Make an aisle too narrow, and whenever two carts pass, nobody dares stop to compare nutrition labels—a phenomenon retail researchers call the "butt-brush effect," where crowded shoppers hurry away without buying. Widening high-margin aisles slightly gives customers comfortable breathing room. (19), placing everyday staples like milk and eggs at the far back draws visitors past dozens of other shelves along the way.

Recognizing these quiet layout strategies lets shoppers navigate stores efficiently while (20).

examples.script:
Why Escalators Leave One Side Debate Behind

In many busy subway stations, commuters follow an unwritten rule on escalators: stand on one side and leave the other lane clear for people in a hurry. At first glance, this arrangement seems polite and efficient. In recent years, however, transit operators from Tokyo to London have begun asking riders to stand in both lanes and refrain from walking on moving steps.

Safety was the initial concern. Escalator steps are much taller than ordinary stairs, so a single misstep by someone carrying a bag can cause a chain of falls. Yet engineers studying station crowds found a second, surprising problem. When ninety percent of riders prefer to stand, reserving half the escalator for the few who walk leaves the walking lane mostly empty. (18), queues at the bottom grow longer during rush hour.

Field trials confirmed the math. Stations that guided commuters to stand two abreast moved roughly twenty-five percent more people per minute than stations using the stand-and-walk split. Standing evenly also reduced uneven mechanical wear on rollers and chains, because (19).

Changing habits formed over decades takes patience, of course. Clear floor footprints and calm voice reminders work better than scolding posters, helping riders understand that (20).

Borrowing More Than Books

A small library wanted to attract residents who rarely borrowed books. Instead of expanding its shelves, it began lending useful household objects, including a sewing machine and a set of gardening tools. The staff hoped that residents could try an object before deciding whether to buy one. People could also borrow items they needed only occasionally.

At first, the library accepted almost every donated object. This created an unexpected problem. Some items were missing parts, while others required repairs that the staff could not perform. The service soon became difficult to manage. The library therefore introduced a rule: every object had to be inspected before it was accepted. (18), donations became easier to handle, even though the library received fewer of them.

Another concern was that borrowers might return objects late. The library considered charging large fines, but staff worried this would discourage people from trying the service. Instead, borrowers received a reminder a day before an item was due. If they needed more time, they could request an extension unless someone else was waiting. The library found that clear communication was (19).

The service is still small. Staff have not claimed that it will replace shopping or solve all the town's waste problems. However, residents have started discussing which objects could usefully be shared. For the library, one important result has been (20). People who had never met now exchange advice about using and repairing the objects they borrow.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第4回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Airport Carpets Quietly Calm Travelers

Major rail terminals tend to favor polished stone floors that withstand millions of rolling suitcases, yet many international airports still cover long departure piers with miles of patterned carpet. Cleaning carpet takes extra effort, so travelers sometimes wonder why operators keep installing soft flooring beyond security checkpoints.

Acoustics and pacing explain the choice. Hard stone corridors bounce announcements, footsteps, and wheel clatter back and forth, raising stress among passengers already worried about boarding times. Carpet absorbs high-frequency noise so gate calls remain intelligible at lower volume. Softer underfoot resistance also slows walking speed slightly without people realizing it. (18), crowds move more smoothly and waiting areas feel calmer.

Maintenance teams manage wear by laying modular carpet squares rather than single giant rolls. When coffee spills near a café or wheel tracks wear down a central lane, crews swap out only the damaged fifty-centimeter tiles overnight. (19), subtle wave patterns inspired by local coastlines hide minor scuffs between deep cleanings.

Airport flooring shows how material choices quietly shape behavior, proving that (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第1回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
A Space for the River

For many years, the people of Bellford regarded their river mainly as a threat. High walls separated it from nearby streets, and a narrow channel carried water quickly through the center of town. The design had protected buildings during many ordinary storms. However, as the town expanded, more roofs and paved surfaces prevented rain from soaking into the ground. Water reached the river faster, and maintaining safety became increasingly difficult.

One response would have been to make the walls higher. Instead, planners proposed allowing the river more room at a former industrial site upstream. Old warehouses there had been removed, leaving land that could temporarily hold water during heavy rain. In dry weather, most of the area could be used as a public park. The proposal did not eliminate the need for walls elsewhere; it was intended to complement existing defenses.

Some residents objected that a park designed to flood was a waste of money. They feared that equipment would be damaged and the area would be closed too often. The design team responded by placing expensive electrical equipment above expected water levels and choosing surfaces that could be cleaned after flooding. Path signs explained that lower routes might close, while a higher route would remain available under most conditions.

A more difficult question concerned who would benefit. The park was near a neighborhood with few green spaces, but many people living there had not attended the early planning meetings. The meetings had been held during working hours and relied on technical presentations. The town changed the schedule and used a temporary model that residents could walk around. This led to requests for better lighting, places to sit, and a safer crossing to the park.

After the park opened, a severe storm tested the design. Water spread across the lower ground as intended, and some paths were closed for cleaning afterward. Officials resisted describing this as a failure of the park: temporary flooding was part of its protective function. At the same time, they acknowledged that the cleanup had taken longer than expected and revised the maintenance plan.

Bellford's experience illustrates why adapting to floods involves more than building a single structure. The physical design, the ability to maintain it, and the ways people understand and use it all matter. A project can serve several purposes, but those purposes need to be explained honestly. Calling a floodable park permanently dry would create false expectations; treating it only as empty storage would overlook its everyday value to residents.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第15回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
How Porous Pavement Tames Urban Flash Floods

When an intense summer thunderstorm dumps fifty millimeters of rain onto a forested hillside, spongy leaf litter and tree-root channels soak up most of the downpour, releasing clear water slowly into streams over days. Drop that same cloudburst onto a conventional city neighborhood—where roofs, parking lots, and asphalt streets seal eighty percent of the ground—and rainwater has nowhere to sink. Torrents race across oily pavement into storm drains within minutes, overwhelming sewer pipes, flooding underpasses, and flushing tire dust and litter straight into urban rivers.

Rather than digging ever-wider concrete storm tunnels beneath crowded streets, civil engineers are redesigning pavement itself to mimic forest soil. Conventional asphalt and concrete mix coarse gravel with fine sand that packs every tiny gap shut. Pervious concrete and porous asphalt, by contrast, deliberately omit fine sand particles, leaving an interconnected honeycomb of air voids—roughly twenty percent of the slab's volume—through which rainwater drains straight downward into a thick crushed-stone reservoir bed underneath.

Beneath parking bays, plazas, and low-speed residential lanes, that gravel bed acts as both sponge and biofilter. Stormwater pauses among irregular stone surfaces for hours before seeping into native subsoil or perforated overflow pipes, shaving dangerous flood peaks during cloudbursts. Meanwhile, naturally occurring bacteria coating the stones break down trace motor-oil hydrocarbons, and cooler moisture evaporating after storms trims surface pavement heat.

Porous surfaces are not maintenance-free miracles, nor do they suit eighty-kilometer-per-hour truck highways where heavy braking shears open-graded stone loose. Without semiannual cleaning by vacuum sweeper trucks, windblown silt and autumn leaves can clog surface pores within a few years—and well-meaning crews must never sealcoat porous lots with black tar.

Matched to the right streets and upkeep schedules, however, permeable paving turns acres of hard city crust back into living watershed.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 長文読解練習（基礎ウォームアップ・2本文・計4問）
examples.script:
When fewer messages are not better

A housing association introduced an online repair form to reduce the time staff spent answering telephone calls. After three months, calls had fallen sharply, and managers initially described the change as a success. A maintenance worker, however, noticed that some serious problems were reaching the repair team later than before. Interviews suggested that residents sometimes abandoned the form because it required them to identify the technical category of a fault. They could describe a leaking ceiling but did not know which category to choose. The association simplified the form and restored a clearly advertised telephone option. Calls increased again, but fewer urgent repairs were reported late. The form had still saved staff time on routine requests. What changed was the measure of success: managers began examining how quickly problems reached the appropriate team, rather than treating every avoided call as a benefit.
Before signing a two-year apartment lease, newcomers are wise to look (     ) hidden monthly fees for bicycle parking and hallway maintenance.

examples.script:
When Saving Water Changes Habits

A housing cooperative fitted low-flow shower heads in its apartments. The equipment was designed to use less water each minute while still providing a comfortable shower. Based on the devices' technical specifications, the cooperative expected a substantial reduction in total water use. However, the first three months produced a smaller reduction than expected.

Interviews with residents helped explain the difference. Some people said the new shower felt pleasant and therefore stayed in it longer. Others believed the equipment made water use so small that there was little reason to worry about time. In both cases, a technical improvement had been partly offset by (18). The equipment was working as designed, but this alone did not determine the final result.

The cooperative did not remove the shower heads or blame residents for behaving badly. Instead, it shared simple information about the difference between water used per minute and water used during an entire shower. Residents were also given a way to see their own household's weekly use, rather than compare themselves with a single average household. (19), a family with several children would naturally use more water than someone living alone.

Later results suggested that combining efficient equipment with understandable feedback was more useful than relying on equipment alone. The lesson was not that efficient technology has no value. Rather, organizations should (20) when estimating its benefits. A device can make conservation easier, but the choices people make around it remain important.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第2回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Hospital Signs Stopped Using Medical Department Names

Large hospitals can be intimidating places to navigate, especially for anxious patients arriving for the first time. Traditionally, corridor signs directed visitors using formal medical terms such as "Otolaryngology," "Nephrology," or "Ophthalmology." To doctors and nurses, these names were precise and unambiguous. To many patients and family members, however, the unfamiliar Latin and Greek words slowed them down and forced them to stop staff in hallways for directions.

When a regional medical center renovated its main building, a communication researcher observed visitors at the entrance desk for two weeks. Nearly forty percent of inquiries came from people who already held appointment slips yet could not match the technical department name to everyday language. The hospital had inadvertently designed its signs for people who already worked there rather than for (18).

During the redesign, planners replaced complex terminology on main hallway signs with plain descriptions such as "Ear, Nose & Throat," "Kidney Care," and "Eye Clinic," accompanied by numbered color bands along the walls. Specialist terms were still printed in smaller letters underneath so medical referrals remained exact. (19), nurses spent far less time giving basic directions, and fewer patients arrived late for appointments.

The project demonstrated that accuracy and clarity need not conflict. Keeping technical terms on medical records while using everyday words on public signs allowed the hospital to (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第1回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
A Space for the River

For many years, the people of Bellford regarded their river mainly as a threat. High walls separated it from nearby streets, and a narrow channel carried water quickly through the center of town. The design had protected buildings during many ordinary storms. However, as the town expanded, more roofs and paved surfaces prevented rain from soaking into the ground. Water reached the river faster, and maintaining safety became increasingly difficult.

One response would have been to make the walls higher. Instead, planners proposed allowing the river more room at a former industrial site upstream. Old warehouses there had been removed, leaving land that could temporarily hold water during heavy rain. In dry weather, most of the area could be used as a public park. The proposal did not eliminate the need for walls elsewhere; it was intended to complement existing defenses.

Some residents objected that a park designed to flood was a waste of money. They feared that equipment would be damaged and the area would be closed too often. The design team responded by placing expensive electrical equipment above expected water levels and choosing surfaces that could be cleaned after flooding. Path signs explained that lower routes might close, while a higher route would remain available under most conditions.

A more difficult question concerned who would benefit. The park was near a neighborhood with few green spaces, but many people living there had not attended the early planning meetings. The meetings had been held during working hours and relied on technical presentations. The town changed the schedule and used a temporary model that residents could walk around. This led to requests for better lighting, places to sit, and a safer crossing to the park.

After the park opened, a severe storm tested the design. Water spread across the lower ground as intended, and some paths were closed for cleaning afterward. Officials resisted describing this as a failure of the park: temporary flooding was part of its protective function. At the same time, they acknowledged that the cleanup had taken longer than expected and revised the maintenance plan.

Bellford's experience illustrates why adapting to floods involves more than building a single structure. The physical design, the ability to maintain it, and the ways people understand and use it all matter. A project can serve several purposes, but those purposes need to be explained honestly. Calling a floodable park permanently dry would create false expectations; treating it only as empty storage would overlook its everyday value to residents.

examples.script:
Planting Pocket Forests in Industrial Districts

Urban tree-planting campaigns often place single young trees at regular intervals along concrete sidewalks. While tidy in appearance, isolated street trees frequently struggle in compacted soil, suffer from heat reflected off asphalt, and grow slowly. In paved industrial districts where summer temperatures rise sharply, planners have begun testing an alternative approach known as "pocket forests."

Instead of spacing one species evenly along a curb, landscapers loosen a plot of soil no larger than a tennis court, enrich it with compost, and plant dozens of native tree and shrub species close together. Because the young plants compete gently for sunlight while shading the soil beneath them, moisture evaporates more slowly and roots establish themselves rapidly. Within three years, a dense multi-layered canopy can form, creating (21).

Critics initially questioned whether tiny plots could make any measurable difference beside busy warehouses. Temperature sensors installed by university researchers showed that air directly inside and downwind of the pocket forests was several degrees cooler on summer afternoons than surrounding parking lots. (22), factory workers began using benches beside the plots during lunch breaks, and songbirds returned to areas where they had rarely been seen.

Planners emphasize that pocket forests are not a substitute for large suburban parks, which offer sports fields and long walking trails. Rather, their strength lies in (23) where large expanses of open land are simply unavailable.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第13回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Why Hospital Architects Replace Long Echoing Halls

Step into a hospital ward built in the 1970s, and its floor plan usually follows a "racetrack" or single straight corridor stretching sixty meters from end to end, lined with glossy vinyl tiles and hard plaster ceilings. Architects back then prized unbroken sightlines and easy mopping. Acoustic measurements conducted over the past twenty years, however, revealed an unintended side effect: hard parallel walls bounce footsteps, pager beeps, and rolling cart clatter down the entire ward, pushing nighttime decibel levels far above World Health Organization guidelines for restorative sleep.

Elevated ward noise harms more than patient comfort. Sleep studies in cardiac and surgical recovery units show that repeated fifty-five-decibel noise spikes trigger brief surges in heart rate and stress hormones even when patients do not consciously recall waking up. Fragmented rest slows immune recovery and makes delirium more common among older adults. Nurses suffer too: in reverberant corridors where conversations blur together, staff report higher mental fatigue and must double-check spoken medication numbers more carefully to prevent misheard doses.

Modern hospital designers now attack corridor noise through both geometry and materials. Instead of one unbroken tunnel, wards are divided into shorter decentralized clusters curved gently around small nursing alcoves, cutting the distance sound can travel unchecked. Overhead, micro-perforated mineral tiles swallow speech frequencies while still meeting strict infection-control wiping standards, and poured rubber subfloors cushion stretcher wheels.

Several Scandinavian and Japanese teaching hospitals have paired structural redesign with "quiet-night protocols"—switching nurse call alerts from corridor loudspeakers to vibrating wrist badges after 9:00 p.m. and grouping routine blood-pressure checks so sleeping patients are disturbed less often.

Healing requires skilled medicine, yet architecture that guards quiet rest turns every night on the ward into part of the treatment.

examples.script:
How Beaver Dams Restore Drying Mountain Meadows

Across western North America and parts of Europe, summer streamflows in mountain valleys have grown more erratic as winter snowpacks melt weeks earlier in spring. Streams that once meandered slowly across lush wet meadows now rush down eroded gullies in April, leaving valleys parched and fire-prone by August. To hold precious snowmelt higher in watersheds, land managers are enlisting a furry native engineer once trapped as a nuisance: the beaver.

Where beavers return—or where conservation crews weave starter "beaver dam analogs" from willow posts to invite them back—the landscape transforms within two seasons. Gnawing small streamside aspens and packing mud against branches, a single beaver family builds leaky stick dams that slow rushing water into stair-stepped ponds. Water spreads sideways into floodplain soils, raising the local water table by up to a meter. (21), cold groundwater seeps back into the creek gradually through late summer, keeping downstream trout cool during heat waves.

Satellite photos of recent western wildfires revealed a dramatic bonus. While surrounding dry pine ridges burned black, wide emerald ribbons of beaver-irrigated willow marsh stayed too wet to ignite, offering safe refuge for deer, amphibians, and songbirds. (22), beaver ponds trap silt and ash washed down after storms, protecting town drinking-water intakes farther downstream.

Coexisting with beavers near roads requires simple culvert guards so ponds don't flood highways, yet working alongside nature's builders offers (23).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第2回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Rethinking How Cities Measure Bus Punctuality

Most city bus networks judge their performance by a familiar standard: whether each bus arrives at stops at the exact minute printed on the timetable. On quiet suburban routes that run twice an hour, this measure makes complete sense. Missing the 9:10 bus means waiting thirty minutes in the cold, so passengers check the clock before leaving home.

On busy urban corridors where buses are scheduled every five or six minutes, however, passengers behave differently. Commuters rarely consult a timetable; they simply walk to the stop expecting a bus to appear shortly. Yet heavy traffic frequently causes a frustrating pattern known as "bus bunching." If one bus is delayed for ninety seconds by a delivery van, slightly more passengers gather at the next stop. Boarding takes longer, delaying that bus further, while the following bus encounters almost empty stops and catches up. Soon two or three buses travel nose to tail, followed by a fifteen-minute gap.

Curiously, under traditional punctuality rules, an operator could try to keep drivers tied to fixed clock times even after traffic disrupted the pattern, or penalize drivers who paused briefly to restore spacing. When transit planners in Harborview analyzed passenger complaints, they realized riders on high-frequency routes did not care which specific bus they boarded; they cared about how long they waited on the sidewalk.

Harborview subsequently switched its evaluation of six-minute routes from timetable adherence to "headway regularity," which means keeping the time interval between consecutive buses steady. Dispatchers gained authority to ask an ahead-of-schedule bus to wait forty seconds at a transfer hub so a gap would not widen downstream. Digital signs at stops also began showing "Every 6 minutes" alongside live countdowns rather than long lists of clock times.

Average waiting times fell by nearly twenty percent without adding extra vehicles or drivers. Nevertheless, transit specialists note that headway management works only when routes are frequent and dispatchers communicate clearly with passengers on board; nobody likes sitting at a stop for forty seconds unless the driver explains why. Choosing the right metric, they conclude, depends on matching measurement to how passengers actually experience a journey.

examples.script:
Why Hospital Signs Stopped Using Medical Department Names

Large hospitals can be intimidating places to navigate, especially for anxious patients arriving for the first time. Traditionally, corridor signs directed visitors using formal medical terms such as "Otolaryngology," "Nephrology," or "Ophthalmology." To doctors and nurses, these names were precise and unambiguous. To many patients and family members, however, the unfamiliar Latin and Greek words slowed them down and forced them to stop staff in hallways for directions.

When a regional medical center renovated its main building, a communication researcher observed visitors at the entrance desk for two weeks. Nearly forty percent of inquiries came from people who already held appointment slips yet could not match the technical department name to everyday language. The hospital had inadvertently designed its signs for people who already worked there rather than for (18).

During the redesign, planners replaced complex terminology on main hallway signs with plain descriptions such as "Ear, Nose & Throat," "Kidney Care," and "Eye Clinic," accompanied by numbered color bands along the walls. Specialist terms were still printed in smaller letters underneath so medical referrals remained exact. (19), nurses spent far less time giving basic directions, and fewer patients arrived late for appointments.

The project demonstrated that accuracy and clarity need not conflict. Keeping technical terms on medical records while using everyday words on public signs allowed the hospital to (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第5回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
When Soil Microbes Leave Clues for Archaeologists

Archaeologists searching for ancient timber buildings often face a frustrating reality: in damp, mild climates, wooden posts rot away completely within centuries, leaving neither stone walls nor brick foundations behind. Traditionally, excavators locate vanished halls by scraping away topsoil and looking for faint dark circles—known as postholes—where decayed wood stained the earth.

Visual stains, however, can be hard to distinguish from animal burrows or tree roots. Recently, geoarchaeologists have begun analyzing the DNA and chemical traces of soil bacteria living in buried layers. Centuries of human or livestock activity alter soil phosphorus, acidity, and organic matter in lasting ways. Even two thousand years after a wooden stable disappeared, the microbial community thriving in that patch of dirt differs measurably from the microbes three meters outside the wall. (21), researchers can tell whether a vanished room once housed cattle, stored grain, or served as a clean sleeping area.

Sampling tiny cores of soil with a hand auger also protects fragile sites. Rather than digging wide trenches across an entire meadow, teams test small pinprick samples first to map where activity was concentrated. (22), full excavation can be limited to the corners most likely to answer historical questions.

Microbial mapping does not replace trowels and pottery analysis, of course. Still, reading living microscopic ecosystems allows archaeologists to (23) long after timber walls have turned back to dust.

examples.script:
Updated Policy for Borrowing Field Recording Kits

From: Media Lab Desk, Faculty of Cultural Studies
To: Undergraduate Fieldwork Students
Subject: Windscreens and memory-card rules for oral-history kits

Dear students,
Starting next Monday, six upgraded stereo audio kits will be available for two-week loan to students conducting local oral-history interviews this semester. Before reserving a kit online, please note two updated borrowing rules based on issues from last autumn.

First, every kit now includes a furry "deadcat" wind muff alongside the standard foam sponge cover. Foam covers stop indoor breath pops, but they cannot block wind rumble on porches, farms, or fishing piers; three outdoor interviews last term were almost impossible to transcribe because of wind noise. Whenever you record outdoors, slip the furry wind muff over the microphone before pressing record.

Second, the Media Lab no longer lends SD memory cards inside the cases. Last year, two students accidentally returned kits before copying their files, and our automatic formatting bench erased a week's worth of recordings. Please purchase your own Class-10 SD card (32 GB or 64 GB) at the campus co-op and test it in the recorder at the pickup counter before leaving.

Happy interviewing,
Media Lab Staff

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第2回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Planting Pocket Forests in Industrial Districts

Urban tree-planting campaigns often place single young trees at regular intervals along concrete sidewalks. While tidy in appearance, isolated street trees frequently struggle in compacted soil, suffer from heat reflected off asphalt, and grow slowly. In paved industrial districts where summer temperatures rise sharply, planners have begun testing an alternative approach known as "pocket forests."

Instead of spacing one species evenly along a curb, landscapers loosen a plot of soil no larger than a tennis court, enrich it with compost, and plant dozens of native tree and shrub species close together. Because the young plants compete gently for sunlight while shading the soil beneath them, moisture evaporates more slowly and roots establish themselves rapidly. Within three years, a dense multi-layered canopy can form, creating (21).

Critics initially questioned whether tiny plots could make any measurable difference beside busy warehouses. Temperature sensors installed by university researchers showed that air directly inside and downwind of the pocket forests was several degrees cooler on summer afternoons than surrounding parking lots. (22), factory workers began using benches beside the plots during lunch breaks, and songbirds returned to areas where they had rarely been seen.

Planners emphasize that pocket forests are not a substitute for large suburban parks, which offer sports fields and long walking trails. Rather, their strength lies in (23) where large expanses of open land are simply unavailable.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第6回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
Why Translating Humor Across Languages Is an Art

Automated translation software has grown remarkably adept at turning weather bulletins, user manuals, and shipping contracts from one language into another within seconds. In domains where every term maps cleanly onto a fixed counterpart, literal accuracy is the highest virtue. Hand the same software a comic novel, an animated film script, or a witty newspaper column, however, and the output frequently lands with a dull thud.

Humor rarely resides in dictionary definitions alone. Puns exploit accidental collisions of sound inside a single language: an English joke built on "knight" and "night" evaporates the moment those words become two unrelated nouns in Japanese or Spanish. Comedic timing also leans heavily on grammar. Languages that place the main verb at the very end of a sentence reveal a surprise twist in a different rhythm than languages that announce action upfront. Even cultural assumptions matter—a joke about polite elevator small talk falls flat in places where riders stand in respectful silence.

Skilled literary and audiovisual translators therefore approach comedy closer to musical arrangement than word-for-word substitution. Instead of explaining a pun in an awkward footnote—which kills laughter instantly—a seasoned translator asks what emotional effect the author intended in that scene, then crafts a fresh play on words rooted in the target language's own idioms. Subtitle translators face stricter constraints still: viewers must read the line in three seconds while watching the actor's eyebrows and hearing the cadence of the original voice.

Paradoxically, departing from the literal surface is often the only way to remain faithful to a comic work's spirit. If an original line made readers chuckle at a character's pompous wordplay, a translation that is lexically exact yet lifeless betrays the text far more than an inventive local pun.

Machines may suggest vocabulary candidates quickly, yet sensing why a room laughs still demands human judgment steeped in two living cultures.
