examples.script:
Why Supermarkets Are Rethinking "Best-Before" Date Labels

Walk down any grocery aisle and you will see dozens of date stamps printed on milk cartons, canned beans, and bags of rice. Shoppers naturally assume these dates mark the exact day food becomes unsafe to eat. Food safety agencies point out, however, that two very different labels are often confused. While "use-by" dates apply to highly perishable items like raw fish, "best-before" dates on dry or canned goods indicate peak flavor and texture rather than spoilage.

Household surveys across several countries have revealed that nearly a third of still-edible groceries are thrown out simply because a "best-before" date has passed by a day or two. Consumers want to keep their families safe, yet inconsistent wording such as "sell by," "enjoy by," and "best if used before" leaves people guessing and encourages (18).

To clear up this confusion, several supermarket chains have standardized their packaging down to just two phrases: "Use By" for safety-critical chilled foods, and "Best Quality Before (Often Good Longer)" for shelf-stable items. Some dairy producers even add simple reminders instructing shoppers to look and smell before discarding unopened yogurt. (19), households participating in pilot studies threw away significantly less pantry food over six months.

Experts emphasize that clearer wording never lowers hygiene standards. Instead, distinguishing genuine safety deadlines from quality estimates helps consumers (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第9回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Escalator Handrails Move Slightly Faster Than the Steps

Anyone who holds onto an escalator handrail during a long subway ride has probably noticed a tiny quirk: after twenty seconds, your hand has crept a couple of centimeters ahead of your body, forcing you to move your fingers back. Commuters often assume the belt is poorly calibrated. In reality, technicians adjust many escalators so the rubber handrail runs roughly one to two percent faster than the metal steps.

Mechanical wear explains part of the design. While the steps are driven by toothed steel chains that never slip, the rubber handrail is pulled over smooth rollers by friction. As rollers age, slight slippage naturally slows the belt down. Setting a new handrail marginally fast ensures it will not lag behind the steps months later. (18), safety researchers point out an important human-balance reason behind that forward bias.

Imagine standing on steep steps rising at thirty degrees if the handrail moved slower than your feet: your arm would gradually get pulled backward, tipping your center of gravity toward the open stairs behind you—the most dangerous direction to fall. A handrail that inches slightly ahead, by contrast, gently nudges posture upright or slightly forward, where knees and ankles can catch a stumble easily. (19), building codes typically allow handrails to run up to two percent faster than steps, while forbidding them to run noticeably slower.

What feels like a minor mechanical mismatch actually reflects (20).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第10回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Escalator Steps Have Deep Grooves Along Their Treads

Look down at the moving metal steps of any train-station escalator, and you will see dozens of narrow parallel ridges and grooves running from back to front—never side to side. Passengers sometimes assume those grooves exist mainly to give wet sneakers extra grip on rainy days. While texture does help drainage, mechanical engineers designed those deep longitudinal cleats primarily so the steps can disappear safely at the end of the ride.

At the top and bottom landings of an escalator, moving steps slide beneath a stationary metal plate edged with sharp teeth, called the "comb plate." Those comb teeth mesh right inside the grooves of each passing step with less than two millimeters to spare. Instead of hitting a flat edge where shoe soles, umbrella tips, or wheeled luggage could catch, passengers glide smoothly off the ridges onto the solid floor. (18), small objects like gravel or dropped coins are scooped upward onto the landing rather than dragged down into the return machinery.

Keeping that comb-and-groove partnership safe requires watchful upkeep. If a heavy steel cart chips even two adjacent comb teeth, a dangerous snagging gap opens up. Modern escalators wire sensitive switches behind the comb plate that halt the motor instantly if anything jams under a tooth. (19), yellow painted borders frame each tread to warn riders away from the hinge seams between steps.

Every detail of an escalator step shows how everyday transit hardware (20).

Trial of the Flexible Workspace

From: Priya Shah, Facilities Manager
To: Staff in the West Building
Subject: Four-week workspace trial

Dear colleagues,
From next Monday, the third-floor meeting room will be used as a quiet workspace during the morning. This is a four-week trial, not a permanent change. Staff feedback has shown that some tasks require longer periods without interruption than our open office currently allows. The room will remain available for meetings after 1 p.m.

You may reserve a desk through the internal booking page up to two working days ahead. To give more people a chance to participate, please book no more than two mornings per week. If you no longer need a booking, cancel it promptly. Desks cannot be reserved by leaving personal belongings overnight.

During the trial, the room is intended for individual work. Please take telephone and video calls elsewhere, even if you use headphones. There will be no charge to your department for using the room. However, this does not include printing costs, which will continue to be charged in the usual way.

We will record how often desks are used, but the number of bookings will not be our only measure of success. At the end of the trial, participants and their team leaders will be asked whether the arrangement helped them complete suitable tasks and whether it created difficulties for their teams. We also want to hear from staff who wanted to participate but could not find a suitable time.

Please do not assume that the booking rules will remain unchanged after the trial. They will be reviewed along with the room's future use. Send any urgent concerns directly to me rather than waiting for the final survey.

Priya

examples.chapterTitle: 英検2級 第9回（2本文・計8問）
examples.script:
How Quiet Asphalt Reduces Highway Tire Roar

Stand beside a suburban expressway where cars cruise at eighty kilometers per hour, and you might assume engines and exhaust pipes create most of the noise. For passenger cars built over the past twenty years, however, tire-pavement noise actually overtakes engine sound once speeds pass roughly forty to fifty kilometers per hour—a fact made even clearer as quiet electric vehicles still produce a steady roar at highway speeds.

Much of that highway roar comes from "air pumping." As a spinning rubber tire flattens against smooth, dense asphalt, air trapped inside the tire's tread grooves is squeezed violently and shoots out to the sides like thousands of tiny whistles per second, amplified by the curved horn shape between tire and road. On rain-slicked dense pavement, surface water also sprays upward, reducing driver visibility and increasing hydroplaning risk.

Road engineers in the Netherlands, Japan, and Scandinavia developed an effective acoustic remedy: porous elastic road surfaces, often called "quiet asphalt." By leaving out fine sand particles and binding coarse crushed stone with polymer-modified bitumen, crews lay a top wearing course riddled with interconnected tiny air voids—roughly twenty percent open pore space. Instead of squirting sideways with a hiss, compressed air under the tire escapes harmlessly downward into the porous mat. Rainwater drains straight through those same channels to roadside gutters, cutting splash spray dramatically.

Porous asphalt comes with real upkeep trade-offs, though. Dust, tire rubber crumbs, and autumn mud gradually clog the tiny pores within five to eight years unless specialized high-pressure vacuum trucks flush them clean. In snowy mountain passes, water freezing inside clogged pores can loosen stones under snowplow blades.

Even with shorter resurfacing cycles, cities bordering busy ring roads value porous pavements highly: cutting traffic noise by four to six decibels sounds to the human ear much like cutting traffic volume in half.

Planting Pocket Forests in Industrial Districts

Urban tree-planting campaigns often place single young trees at regular intervals along concrete sidewalks. While tidy in appearance, isolated street trees frequently struggle in compacted soil, suffer from heat reflected off asphalt, and grow slowly. In paved industrial districts where summer temperatures rise sharply, planners have begun testing an alternative approach known as "pocket forests."

Instead of spacing one species evenly along a curb, landscapers loosen a plot of soil no larger than a tennis court, enrich it with compost, and plant dozens of native tree and shrub species close together. Because the young plants compete gently for sunlight while shading the soil beneath them, moisture evaporates more slowly and roots establish themselves rapidly. Within three years, a dense multi-layered canopy can form, creating (21).

Critics initially questioned whether tiny plots could make any measurable difference beside busy warehouses. Temperature sensors installed by university researchers showed that air directly inside and downwind of the pocket forests was several degrees cooler on summer afternoons than surrounding parking lots. (22), factory workers began using benches beside the plots during lunch breaks, and songbirds returned to areas where they had rarely been seen.

Planners emphasize that pocket forests are not a substitute for large suburban parks, which offer sports fields and long walking trails. Rather, their strength lies in (23) where large expanses of open land are simply unavailable.

examples.script:
When Seaweed Farms Help Shellfish Neighbours

Along rocky coasts from Hokkaido to Maine, shellfish growers raising oysters and scallops face a quiet chemical challenge. As oceans absorb excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, coastal waters become slightly more acidic, making it harder for young shellfish larvae to build sturdy calcium shells during their first weeks of life.

Marine researchers testing ways to buffer local waters noticed a promising partner already familiar to coastal cuisine: fast-growing kelp and other seaweeds. Like land plants, kelp draws dissolved carbon dioxide out of seawater during daylight hours as it photosynthesizes. Hanging curtains of kelp on ropes just upstream of oyster cages measurably raises water pH in the surrounding bay while releasing oxygen. (21), juvenile oysters raised beside seaweed lines develop thicker shells than those grown in open water nearby.

Sharing ocean leases benefits farmers economically as well. Kelp grows fastest in cold winter and early spring months when shellfish work is relatively quiet, allowing crews to use the same boats, buoys, and anchor lines across seasons. Harvested seaweed can be sold for food, fertilizer, or animal feed supplements. (22), kelp blades absorb excess nitrogen washing off farmland, reducing summer algae blooms that otherwise suffocate coastal beds.

Co-cultivating seaweed and shellfish will not reverse global ocean chemistry on its own. Even so, pairing complementary marine crops gives coastal communities (23).

examples.script:
How Hospital Courtyards Speed Up Patient Recovery

For much of the twentieth century, modern hospital architecture prioritized clinical efficiency above almost everything else. Long windowless corridors minimized walking distances between operating rooms and laboratories, while outdoor courtyards were often paved over to expand equipment wings or staff parking. Architects treated trees and gardens as pleasant decorations that were worth keeping only if money was left over.

That view began to change after health researchers compared surgical patients whose rooms overlooked a small grove of maple trees with similar patients facing a plain brick wall. Reviewing hospital charts over several years, researchers noticed a consistent pattern: patients with a view of greenery requested fewer strong painkillers, reported lower anxiety, and were discharged nearly a day earlier on average than those facing brick.

Subsequent studies examined what happened when patients, visiting relatives, and nurses could actually step outside into a sheltered courtyard for fifteen minutes. Measuring heart rates and stress hormones showed that sitting near running water and varied foliage helped the nervous system recover from the constant beeping of medical monitors. Equally important, nurses who took breaks in green courtyards made fewer clerical errors during afternoon shifts than colleagues who rested in windowless basement lounges.

Designing an effective healing garden involves more than scattering flowerpots on concrete. Landscape specialists work closely with physical therapists to build wide, non-slip pathways gentle enough for wheelchairs and IV poles, provide shaded seating every ten meters so recovering patients can rest easily, and avoid heavily scented flowers that might discomfort people experiencing nausea.

Today, hospital administrators increasingly view therapeutic gardens not as luxury ornaments, but as practical medical infrastructure that supports patients, families, and exhausted clinical staff alike.

examples.script:
Why Hospital Signs Stopped Using Medical Department Names

Large hospitals can be intimidating places to navigate, especially for anxious patients arriving for the first time. Traditionally, corridor signs directed visitors using formal medical terms such as "Otolaryngology," "Nephrology," or "Ophthalmology." To doctors and nurses, these names were precise and unambiguous. To many patients and family members, however, the unfamiliar Latin and Greek words slowed them down and forced them to stop staff in hallways for directions.

When a regional medical center renovated its main building, a communication researcher observed visitors at the entrance desk for two weeks. Nearly forty percent of inquiries came from people who already held appointment slips yet could not match the technical department name to everyday language. The hospital had inadvertently designed its signs for people who already worked there rather than for (18).

During the redesign, planners replaced complex terminology on main hallway signs with plain descriptions such as "Ear, Nose & Throat," "Kidney Care," and "Eye Clinic," accompanied by numbered color bands along the walls. Specialist terms were still printed in smaller letters underneath so medical referrals remained exact. (19), nurses spent far less time giving basic directions, and fewer patients arrived late for appointments.

The project demonstrated that accuracy and clarity need not conflict. Keeping technical terms on medical records while using everyday words on public signs allowed the hospital to (20).

examples.script:
The Silence in the Archive

Historical collections are sometimes treated as though they were transparent windows onto the past. A researcher asks a question, locates the relevant papers, and extracts an answer. Yet the existence of a document reflects a chain of decisions: someone had to produce it, someone had to retain it, and an institution eventually had to consider it worth preserving. Groups whose daily activities generated few written records may consequently be difficult to study, even when their contribution to a community was substantial.

Consider a project reconstructing the history of a neighborhood market. Official files might contain detailed records of licenses and inspections, while offering almost nothing about informal arrangements through which traders shared transport or helped a sick colleague. If researchers relied exclusively on official files, they could (19). What was easiest to document would acquire disproportionate importance simply because it had survived in an accessible form.

Oral interviews can help broaden such a project, but they do not provide an uncomplicated solution. People may interpret earlier experiences through the concerns of the present. Different accounts may disagree without either speaker deliberately misleading the interviewer. (20), recordings should be accompanied by information about when and under what circumstances they were made. This enables later users to assess the accounts instead of treating them as context-free statements.

An honest archive therefore makes its own limitations visible. It can identify gaps, explain selection policies, and preserve disagreements rather than forcing every account into a single version of events. This does not make historical research impossible. On the contrary, recognizing how a collection was assembled allows researchers to (21). The aim is not to abandon evidence but to ask more precise questions of it.

examples.script:
Who Benefits from a Quieter Street?

Reducing traffic on a residential street may seem an uncomplicated improvement. Fewer vehicles can mean less noise, cleaner air, and more space for people walking or cycling. Yet the evaluation of a traffic scheme depends on where its boundaries are drawn. A street that becomes quieter may sit beside another that receives the diverted vehicles. An assessment limited to the first street can therefore tell a convincing but incomplete story.

Suppose a district introduces barriers that prevent through-traffic from using several residential roads. Initial monitoring shows a sharp decline in vehicles inside the area. Residents living near the barriers report that children can cross more easily and that conversations are no longer interrupted by engine noise. These are genuine benefits, not merely perceptions to be dismissed. However, residents along the main roads outside the area report longer queues. They question why their experience is absent from the first evaluation.

One response is to enlarge the monitoring area. This is necessary, but a larger average alone may still obscure important differences. If a substantial improvement for several thousand people outweighs a smaller deterioration for a few hundred, the overall figure may look favorable. That calculation does not by itself establish whether the distribution of costs is acceptable, especially if those facing deterioration already experience the greatest pollution. Choosing a measurement boundary is therefore not a neutral substitute for considering fairness.

Timing introduces another complication. Drivers may initially follow familiar routes and later change their journey, travel at another hour, or choose another means of transport. The first week may consequently exaggerate permanent disruption. Conversely, waiting for people to adapt cannot justify disregarding persistent problems indefinitely. An evaluation should state in advance when it will be repeated and which findings would trigger a change. Otherwise, every unfavorable result can be described as temporary and every favorable result as final.

A credible process combines measurements with ways for affected people to challenge the interpretation. Residents may identify a school entrance that monitors have missed or explain why a supposedly convenient alternative route is unusable for someone with limited mobility. Their accounts do not replace traffic counts, but they can reveal what the counts fail to capture.

The choice is not simply between accepting every scheme and rejecting any scheme with uneven effects. It is between treating evaluation as a defense of a completed decision and using it to revise that decision. A project can retain its original aims while adding protection for neighboring roads, adjusting delivery access, or removing a barrier that causes disproportionate harm. A quieter street is worth pursuing, but the claim of success becomes stronger when it accounts for people beyond that street.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第2回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Why Negative Scientific Results Deserve Publication

Pick up almost any prominent scientific journal and you will read predominantly about experiments that worked: a compound that slowed disease progression in mice, a teaching intervention that raised test scores, or a catalyst that accelerated a chemical reaction. Studies in which a plausible hypothesis produced no statistically meaningful effect are far more likely to remain unpublished in laboratory drawers, a phenomenon methodologists call the "file-drawer problem."

This publication pattern rarely stems from deliberate dishonesty. Journals compete for attention and citations, editors favor striking breakthroughs, and researchers under career pressure understandably prioritize manuscripts with a high chance of acceptance. Writing up a rigorous null result takes nearly as much time as writing up a positive discovery, yet brings far less professional recognition. Individual incentives therefore align to filter out negative findings.

The collective cost to science, however, is substantial. When five independent laboratories test the same promising idea and four find no effect while one obtains a positive result by chance, publishing only the fifth study creates a distorted impression of effectiveness. Other teams may then spend years and public grant money repeating dead-end experiments they had no way of knowing had already failed. Worse still, clinical or policy reviews that pool published studies risk overestimating the benefits of an intervention.

One promising reform is the "registered report." Under this format, peer reviewers evaluate a study's research question, sample size, and experimental protocol before data are collected. If the design is sound and the question important, the journal commits in principle to publishing the paper regardless of how the numbers turn out, provided the researchers follow the approved plan. Early evaluations suggest that registered reports contain a much higher proportion of null findings than conventional journals while maintaining high methodological quality.

Registered reports do not suit purely exploratory research where methods evolve mid-experiment, nor do they eliminate the need for replication. Yet they address a structural flaw that exhortations to individual virtue cannot fix alone: shifting prestige from whether a result looks dramatic to whether an investigation was worth conducting and carefully executed.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第3回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Negative Results Belong in the Record

Scientific journals naturally gravitate toward studies that report clear, positive findings. Discovering that a compound inhibits a pathogen or that a teaching method raises test scores makes a compelling narrative for editors and readers alike. Yet most experiments conducted in laboratories and field sites do not confirm their initial hypothesis. When well-designed studies showing no measurable effect remain locked in file drawers, the published literature presents a distorted map of reality.

This publication bias carries practical costs. Independent teams across different universities may unknowingly repeat the same fruitless experiment, spending years of grant funding and volunteer effort on questions already answered in the negative elsewhere. Worse still, if ten laboratories test an ineffective intervention and only the single team that observes a fluke correlation publishes its paper, reviewers surveying the journals may conclude that the intervention works. A skewed record can thus (19).

Recognizing the problem, several funding agencies and journals have introduced "registered reports," in which reviewers evaluate a study's research question and statistical design before data are collected. If the protocol is rigorous, the journal commits in principle to publishing the outcome regardless of how the numbers turn out. (20), researchers face less pressure to slice datasets creatively until a statistically striking pattern appears.

Valuing null results does not mean celebrating sloppy experiments that fail merely because instruments were miscalibrated or samples were tiny. Methodological rigor matters even more when claiming the absence of an effect. Requiring open registries and pre-specified plans allows science to (21), turning instructive dead ends into shared public knowledge rather than private disappointments.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第7回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
When Academic Journals Publish Null Results

Open almost any prestigious science or psychology journal, and the table of contents brims with breakthroughs: a compound that shrinks tumors in mice, a classroom technique that boosts test scores, or a catalyst that doubles battery life. Rarely will you read a headline announcing that a plausible hypothesis made no measurable difference at all. Behind that lopsided reading list lies a long-standing distortion known to methodologists as the "file-drawer problem."

For decades, peer reviewers and editors favored eye-catching positive findings while rejecting rigorous studies whose outcomes were statistically flat, leaving disappointed researchers to tuck negative data away in desk drawers. That habit quietly skews collective knowledge. If twenty laboratories independently test whether a herbal extract improves memory, and nineteen find zero effect while one sees a fluke improvement by chance, publishing only that lone success misleads doctors and patients alike. (22), other scientists waste years and grant money repeating failed experiments nobody warned them about.

To correct this bias, a growing coalition of journals has introduced "Registered Reports." Under this format, reviewers judge a study's research question, sample size, and statistical plan BEFORE a single measurement is collected. Once the protocol passes peer review, the journal commits in principle to publishing the paper regardless of how the numbers turn out, provided the team follows its approved plan. (23), shifting evaluation from flashy outcomes to methodological rigor removes the temptation to cherry-pick favorable data.

Null results rarely win newspaper headlines, yet making them visible is vital to helping science (24).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第5回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
When Municipal Procurement Shapes Green Markets

Discussions of environmental policy usually spotlight household choices—carrying reusable bags, sorting bottles, or turning down thermostats—alongside national taxes and regulations. Between individual shoppers and lawmakers, however, sits an economic actor whose routine purchasing decisions quietly steer entire industries: public procurement. Across most industrialized nations, central ministries, cities, public hospitals, and school districts spend between twelve and twenty percent of gross domestic product buying everything from concrete and streetlamps to school meals and fleet vehicles.

For emerging low-carbon technologies, the hardest barrier is rarely laboratory invention; it is crossing the commercial gap between costly small-batch prototypes and affordable mass production. Private contractors understandably hesitate to retool a cement plant or electrify heavy refuse trucks if customer demand looks uncertain. When a coalition of cities commits to buying low-clinker concrete for bridge decks over five years, suppliers gain the predictable order book needed to finance new kilns and train crews, driving unit costs down for private builders as well.

Using public tenders to encourage innovation requires careful contract design, though. Traditional bidding rules often specify exact materials and award contracts solely to the lowest upfront price—a formula that locks in familiar high-emission products even when cleaner alternatives cost less to run over twenty years. Conversely, writing specifications around a single patented process risks shutting out rival approaches and inflating taxpayer bills. Forward-looking agencies therefore set performance outcomes—such as maximum embodied carbon per square meter or lifetime energy consumption—and let competing engineers propose how best to meet them.

Verifying those claims demands administrative capacity that small towns rarely possess alone. Regional purchasing consortia and standardized third-party environmental product declarations have become crucial, allowing rural school boards and clinics to apply rigorous lifecycle criteria without hiring specialist engineers of their own.

examples.script:
When Historical Maps Guide Modern Ecological Restoration

Ecologists asked to restore degraded wetlands or floodplains often confront a baseline puzzle: what did a "healthy" landscape actually look like before industrial drainage and embankment? Living memory rarely stretches back more than seventy years, so river valleys straightened in the nineteenth century can appear entirely natural to current residents.

Archival cartography has emerged as an unexpected scientific ally. Military surveyors, tax assessors, and estate engineers working two or three centuries ago recorded marsh boundaries, oxbow ponds, and coppiced woodlands with painstaking care—not out of environmental concern, but because taxable pasture, timber yields, and troop crossings depended on ground conditions. Digitizing and layering those hand-drawn sheets over modern satellite elevation models reveals vanished channels that still subtly govern where floodwater pools after storms. (22), restoration teams can reconnect buried meanders rather than digging artificial ponds in arbitrary spots.

Old maps require critical interpretation, of course. Early surveyors occasionally exaggerated cliff heights, omitted seasonal brooks dry in August, or used land categories whose meanings shifted over generations. Cross-checking maps against sediment cores, pollen grains, and parish flood chronicles prevents planners from mistaking a surveyor's shorthand for literal truth. (23), recognizing that preindustrial landscapes were themselves shaped by grazing, reed cutting, and small millponds reminds conservationists that ecosystems were rarely untouched wilderness.

Historical baselines cannot—and should not—be copied mechanically under a warming climate. Rather, reading archival maps alongside field data helps communities (24) while designing landscapes resilient enough for future extremes.

examples.script:
The record is not the relationship

A grant programme rewarded neighbourhood organisations according to the number of residents they contacted. The measure was attractive because it was inexpensive to collect and easy to compare across projects. Over time, however, some organisations shifted staff towards brief encounters that could be recorded quickly. Activities requiring repeated visits to gain residents’ trust produced fewer countable contacts, even when those relationships helped people access essential support. A review panel proposed retaining the contact count but combining it with follow-up evidence and accounts from residents. Critics warned that such material would be harder to standardise and might favour organisations skilled at presenting persuasive stories. The panel acknowledged the risk and recommended common questions, independent sampling and explicit uncertainty in the reports. It did not claim that the revised approach would produce a perfectly objective ranking. Its argument was that a narrow, precise number could systematically misrepresent the work, while a broader assessment could expose more of the relevant trade-offs. The central choice was therefore not between measurement and no measurement, but between different compromises in what the programme made visible and what it encouraged organisations to do.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第2回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
The Hidden Bias in Citizen Pothole Apps

Many municipal governments now offer smartphone applications that let residents photograph damaged pavement, broken streetlights, or blocked drains and send the exact GPS coordinates to repair crews. At first glance, crowdsourced reporting looks like a triumph of responsive governance: problems are spotted faster than inspectors could patrol every street, and citizens can track repair progress online.

When urban researchers compared app submissions against independent street-condition surveys across an entire city, however, a troubling discrepancy emerged. Wealthier districts with younger, tech-savvy commuters generated four times as many reports per kilometer of damaged road as older, lower-income neighborhoods where fewer residents used municipal apps or trusted rapid official action. Dispatching crews strictly in the order reports arrived meant that technology had inadvertently (22).

Recognizing this pattern did not mean shutting down the reporting platform. Citizen photos still saved inspectors valuable time on urgent hazards such as fallen branches after a storm. Instead, the public works department combined app reports with scheduled baseline inspections weighted toward neighborhoods with older infrastructure and historically low reporting rates. (23), maintenance budgets were no longer driven solely by who complained fastest on a smartphone.

Digital participation tools often promise neutrality because anyone is theoretically free to download them. Yet equal permission to use a channel rarely produces equal representation in the resulting dataset. Responsible public administration therefore requires officials to (24) before turning user-generated maps into spending priorities.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第3回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Negative Results Belong in the Record

Scientific journals naturally gravitate toward studies that report clear, positive findings. Discovering that a compound inhibits a pathogen or that a teaching method raises test scores makes a compelling narrative for editors and readers alike. Yet most experiments conducted in laboratories and field sites do not confirm their initial hypothesis. When well-designed studies showing no measurable effect remain locked in file drawers, the published literature presents a distorted map of reality.

This publication bias carries practical costs. Independent teams across different universities may unknowingly repeat the same fruitless experiment, spending years of grant funding and volunteer effort on questions already answered in the negative elsewhere. Worse still, if ten laboratories test an ineffective intervention and only the single team that observes a fluke correlation publishes its paper, reviewers surveying the journals may conclude that the intervention works. A skewed record can thus (19).

Recognizing the problem, several funding agencies and journals have introduced "registered reports," in which reviewers evaluate a study's research question and statistical design before data are collected. If the protocol is rigorous, the journal commits in principle to publishing the outcome regardless of how the numbers turn out. (20), researchers face less pressure to slice datasets creatively until a statistically striking pattern appears.

Valuing null results does not mean celebrating sloppy experiments that fail merely because instruments were miscalibrated or samples were tiny. Methodological rigor matters even more when claiming the absence of an effect. Requiring open registries and pre-specified plans allows science to (21), turning instructive dead ends into shared public knowledge rather than private disappointments.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第7回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
When Academic Journals Publish Null Results

Open almost any prestigious science or psychology journal, and the table of contents brims with breakthroughs: a compound that shrinks tumors in mice, a classroom technique that boosts test scores, or a catalyst that doubles battery life. Rarely will you read a headline announcing that a plausible hypothesis made no measurable difference at all. Behind that lopsided reading list lies a long-standing distortion known to methodologists as the "file-drawer problem."

For decades, peer reviewers and editors favored eye-catching positive findings while rejecting rigorous studies whose outcomes were statistically flat, leaving disappointed researchers to tuck negative data away in desk drawers. That habit quietly skews collective knowledge. If twenty laboratories independently test whether a herbal extract improves memory, and nineteen find zero effect while one sees a fluke improvement by chance, publishing only that lone success misleads doctors and patients alike. (22), other scientists waste years and grant money repeating failed experiments nobody warned them about.

To correct this bias, a growing coalition of journals has introduced "Registered Reports." Under this format, reviewers judge a study's research question, sample size, and statistical plan BEFORE a single measurement is collected. Once the protocol passes peer review, the journal commits in principle to publishing the paper regardless of how the numbers turn out, provided the team follows its approved plan. (23), shifting evaluation from flashy outcomes to methodological rigor removes the temptation to cherry-pick favorable data.

Null results rarely win newspaper headlines, yet making them visible is vital to helping science (24).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第1回（全12問）
examples.script:
Woman: Come in, Garrett. Looking at your first delta checkup chart, your blood work came back completely normal, yet you mentioned persistent afternoon headaches.
Man: Yes, Doctor Helena. It started right after our accounting team moved to a paperless system and my screen hours doubled.
Woman: That timing tells us a lot. People often jump straight to strong painkillers, which I would rather avoid in your case.
Man: I prefer avoiding unnecessary pills too. What do you recommend I start with instead?
Woman: First, please switch to an anti-glare monitor filter and take brief breaks every hour, and let us reassess your progress in a fortnight.
Question. What does the doctor advise the man to do first?
examples.translation: 血液検査は正常だったが「persistent afternoon headaches」が続いている患者に対し、強い鎮痛薬は避け、まず「反射防止モニターフィルターに替え、1時間ごとに小休止を取る」を行って2週間後に再評価するよう医師が助言した。

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第1回（6音源・計12問）
examples.script:
Conservation Note First Echo: Displaying sixteenth-century silk tapestries presents curators with a persistent dilemma: bright light reveals delicate brushwork to visitors, yet cumulative exposure irreversibly alters organic dyes. Historically, museums rotated fragile works into dark storage after just six weeks on view. Recently, conservation scientists tested motion-activated dimming systems that lower light levels whenever galleries are empty. Spectrophotometer readings after twelve months confirmed negligible color shift while preserving crisp visual contrast for viewers. Even so, conservators still enforce strict total-exposure budgets for irreplaceable masterpieces.
Question one. How did museums traditionally protect sixteenth-century silk tapestries from light damage?
Question two. What did conservation scientists recently test with positive results?
examples.translation: sixteenth-century silk tapestriesの展示保存におけるジレンマと新技術。「展示室が無人のときに照度を下げる人感調光システム」を試験導入したところ、12か月後の分光測色でも色変化がごくわずかに抑えられ視認性も保たれた。それでも代替不可能な名品には総露光量の上限管理が継続されている。

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第1回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
Who Benefits from a Quieter Street?

Reducing traffic on a residential street may seem an uncomplicated improvement. Fewer vehicles can mean less noise, cleaner air, and more space for people walking or cycling. Yet the evaluation of a traffic scheme depends on where its boundaries are drawn. A street that becomes quieter may sit beside another that receives the diverted vehicles. An assessment limited to the first street can therefore tell a convincing but incomplete story.

Suppose a district introduces barriers that prevent through-traffic from using several residential roads. Initial monitoring shows a sharp decline in vehicles inside the area. Residents living near the barriers report that children can cross more easily and that conversations are no longer interrupted by engine noise. These are genuine benefits, not merely perceptions to be dismissed. However, residents along the main roads outside the area report longer queues. They question why their experience is absent from the first evaluation.

One response is to enlarge the monitoring area. This is necessary, but a larger average alone may still obscure important differences. If a substantial improvement for several thousand people outweighs a smaller deterioration for a few hundred, the overall figure may look favorable. That calculation does not by itself establish whether the distribution of costs is acceptable, especially if those facing deterioration already experience the greatest pollution. Choosing a measurement boundary is therefore not a neutral substitute for considering fairness.

Timing introduces another complication. Drivers may initially follow familiar routes and later change their journey, travel at another hour, or choose another means of transport. The first week may consequently exaggerate permanent disruption. Conversely, waiting for people to adapt cannot justify disregarding persistent problems indefinitely. An evaluation should state in advance when it will be repeated and which findings would trigger a change. Otherwise, every unfavorable result can be described as temporary and every favorable result as final.

A credible process combines measurements with ways for affected people to challenge the interpretation. Residents may identify a school entrance that monitors have missed or explain why a supposedly convenient alternative route is unusable for someone with limited mobility. Their accounts do not replace traffic counts, but they can reveal what the counts fail to capture.

The choice is not simply between accepting every scheme and rejecting any scheme with uneven effects. It is between treating evaluation as a defense of a completed decision and using it to revise that decision. A project can retain its original aims while adding protection for neighboring roads, adjusting delivery access, or removing a barrier that causes disproportionate harm. A quieter street is worth pursuing, but the claim of success becomes stronger when it accounts for people beyond that street.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第7回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
How Artificial Night Light Disrupts Pollinators

Discussions of declining insect pollinators typically center on habitat loss, pesticides, and climate shifts, with honeybees and bumblebees taking center stage in public campaigns. Over the past decade, however, ecologists tracking wild meadows after sundown have documented an overlooked disruption: artificial light at night from streetlamps, warehouse floodlights, and highway interchanges. Far from falling quiet at dusk, temperate ecosystems rely on a vast nocturnal shift of moths, beetles, and hoverflies that visit pale, fragrant blossoms while daytime bees sleep.

Field experiments in Swiss valleys illuminated half of a series of dark alpine meadows with standard white LED streetlamps while leaving matched control plots dark. Using night-vision cameras, researchers observed sixty-two percent fewer nocturnal pollinator visits to wild thistle and campion flowers under lit poles. Moths drawn upward into lamp glare spent hours circling fixtures or became easy prey for bats, leaving flowers below unpollinated. Even more unexpectedly, the damage spilled into the next afternoon: plants that missed nighttime pollination produced less nectar and fewer viable seeds, attracting fewer daytime bumblebees as well.

Replacing all outdoor lighting is neither realistic nor desirable where pedestrian safety is at stake, yet engineers and biologists have found room for compromise. Broad-spectrum blue-white LEDs disrupt insect vision most severely because short wavelengths strongly stimulate nocturnal compound eyes. Shielding fixtures so light points strictly downward onto pavement, dimming lamps during pre-dawn hours via motion sensors, and shifting toward warmer amber spectra substantially reduce insect attraction without leaving sidewalks in darkness.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第4回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
When Historical Maps Guide Modern Ecological Restoration

Ecologists asked to restore degraded wetlands or floodplains often confront a baseline puzzle: what did a "healthy" landscape actually look like before industrial drainage and embankment? Living memory rarely stretches back more than seventy years, so river valleys straightened in the nineteenth century can appear entirely natural to current residents.

Archival cartography has emerged as an unexpected scientific ally. Military surveyors, tax assessors, and estate engineers working two or three centuries ago recorded marsh boundaries, oxbow ponds, and coppiced woodlands with painstaking care—not out of environmental concern, but because taxable pasture, timber yields, and troop crossings depended on ground conditions. Digitizing and layering those hand-drawn sheets over modern satellite elevation models reveals vanished channels that still subtly govern where floodwater pools after storms. (22), restoration teams can reconnect buried meanders rather than digging artificial ponds in arbitrary spots.

Old maps require critical interpretation, of course. Early surveyors occasionally exaggerated cliff heights, omitted seasonal brooks dry in August, or used land categories whose meanings shifted over generations. Cross-checking maps against sediment cores, pollen grains, and parish flood chronicles prevents planners from mistaking a surveyor's shorthand for literal truth. (23), recognizing that preindustrial landscapes were themselves shaped by grazing, reed cutting, and small millponds reminds conservationists that ecosystems were rarely untouched wilderness.

Historical baselines cannot—and should not—be copied mechanically under a warming climate. Rather, reading archival maps alongside field data helps communities (24) while designing landscapes resilient enough for future extremes.

examples.script:
The Hidden Bias in Citizen Pothole Apps

Many municipal governments now offer smartphone applications that let residents photograph damaged pavement, broken streetlights, or blocked drains and send the exact GPS coordinates to repair crews. At first glance, crowdsourced reporting looks like a triumph of responsive governance: problems are spotted faster than inspectors could patrol every street, and citizens can track repair progress online.

When urban researchers compared app submissions against independent street-condition surveys across an entire city, however, a troubling discrepancy emerged. Wealthier districts with younger, tech-savvy commuters generated four times as many reports per kilometer of damaged road as older, lower-income neighborhoods where fewer residents used municipal apps or trusted rapid official action. Dispatching crews strictly in the order reports arrived meant that technology had inadvertently (22).

Recognizing this pattern did not mean shutting down the reporting platform. Citizen photos still saved inspectors valuable time on urgent hazards such as fallen branches after a storm. Instead, the public works department combined app reports with scheduled baseline inspections weighted toward neighborhoods with older infrastructure and historically low reporting rates. (23), maintenance budgets were no longer driven solely by who complained fastest on a smartphone.

Digital participation tools often promise neutrality because anyone is theoretically free to download them. Yet equal permission to use a channel rarely produces equal representation in the resulting dataset. Responsible public administration therefore requires officials to (24) before turning user-generated maps into spending priorities.

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第6回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Restoring Old Buildings Often Beats Rebuilding

When municipal boards debate the fate of an aging school or brick warehouse, demolishing the structure and erecting a sleek low-energy replacement frequently sounds like the greenest path forward. New glass-and-steel buildings advertise solar roofs, triple glazing, and tight insulation that slash annual heating bills. Yet lifecycle engineers who tally carbon from quarry to landfill warn that focusing solely on future utility bills overlooks a massive upfront debt: the "embodied carbon" already locked inside existing walls.

Producing fresh cement, smelting structural steel, and hauling demolition rubble release enormous pulses of greenhouse gases before a new building welcomes its first occupant. Even an ultra-efficient replacement can take thirty to fifty years of operational energy savings just to offset the emissions generated during its construction—precisely the decades in which climate scientists say emissions cuts matter most. Retrofitting an intact masonry or timber frame with interior insulation, heat pumps, and repaired sash windows typically emits a fraction of that upfront carbon. (19), adaptive reuse preserves neighborhood streetscapes and finishes months sooner than ground-up construction.

Preservation is not unconditionally superior, of course. Structures riddled with seismic hazards, toxic asbestos, or crumbling foundations may cost prohibitive sums to make safe, and poorly planned retrofits can trap dampness inside historic walls. Sound policy therefore weighs structural integrity alongside whole-life carbon accounting rather than taxing repairs more heavily than new builds, as some tax codes inadvertently do. (20), training carpenters and engineers in diagnostic retrofit skills has become just as urgent as designing flagship net-zero towers.

Viewing existing buildings as repositories of material and energy already paid for helps cities (21).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第12回（2本文・計6問）
examples.script:
Why Surge Pricing Provokes Moral Outrage

To a textbook microeconomist, raising prices dynamically when demand suddenly outstrips supply looks like plain common sense. If a torrential rainstorm hits a commuter rail station at six p.m. and three hundred drenched passengers compete for thirty nearby taxis, tripling fares does two useful things at once: travellers who can easily wait indoors stay put, while off-duty drivers two neighborhoods away gain a strong incentive to head toward the storm. Within half an hour, the queue clears.

In real life, however, dynamic "surge pricing" regularly triggers furious public backlash—especially when hardware stores raise snow-shovel prices after a blizzard or ride-hailing apps quadruple fares during transit breakdowns. Behavioral economists led by Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler traced this anger to an unwritten social norm they termed "reference-transaction fairness." Consumers accept that companies raise prices when wholesale costs rise—say, if cocoa beans double in price after crop disease. Exploiting a sudden spike in customer desperation without any matching rise in the seller's own costs, by contrast, violates deep intuitive rules of community reciprocity. (22), firms that cash in on a one-week emergency often forfeit years of hard-won customer loyalty.

Smart operators therefore look for ways to allocate scarce capacity without appearing predatory. Ride-hailing platforms cap multipliers during declared natural disasters while paying drivers bonuses out of company pockets; concert venues use randomized lotteries rather than pure auctions for affordable student seats. (23), utilities that pair peak-hour electricity surcharges with generous off-peak discounts frame dynamic rates as a reward for flexibility rather than a penalty.

Market design succeeds best when economists remember that prices carry (24).

examples.chapterTitle: 英検準1級 第8回（2本文・計7問）
examples.script:
The Subtle Pitfalls of Algorithmic Dynamic Pricing

Airlines and hotels have adjusted fares according to season and remaining capacity for half a century; travelers readily accept that a beach room costs more in August than in rainy November, or that booking a seat the night before departure carries a premium. Powered by real-time inventory software and electronic shelf labels, however, rapid "dynamic pricing" has begun spreading into everyday arenas—from commuter toll lanes and ride-hailing apps to concert tickets, restaurant menus, and even neighborhood supermarkets.

In textbook microeconomics, flexible prices allocate scarce goods efficiently. Raising ride-hail fares during a Friday downpour entices off-duty drivers onto the streets while nudging price-sensitive riders with umbrellas toward the subway, shrinking wait times for people with urgent trips. Similarly, automated markdowns on yogurt or fish approaching its sell-by date at seven p.m. curb food waste while rewarding thrifty evening shoppers.

Yet behavioral economists warn that treating every consumer transaction like a live stock exchange overlooks how deeply long-term retail relationships depend on perceived fairness. In classic surveys pioneered by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues, respondents judged it acceptable for a hardware store to discontinue a seasonal discount when snow shovels ran low, yet overwhelmingly condemned raising the regular price of shovels the morning after a blizzard. Consumers distinguish sharply between rationing scarce luxuries and exploiting sudden necessity.

Opaque algorithms compound that resentment when prices jump unpredictably within minutes or appear personalized to a shopper's battery level or postcode. Firms chasing short-term surge revenue in staple goods have repeatedly suffered reputational backlashes far costlier than the extra margin earned on a busy afternoon. Smart pricing design therefore pairs transparency and clear upper caps with genuine customer value—using discounts to smooth off-peak demand rather than ambushing captive buyers.
